name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: README headline: up to 1300x faster construction and reserve() than std::vector and up to 3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector. Results image: reserve microbenchmark 939.81x-1380.19x faster than std::vector (one outlier of 4762.93x at large2) and 2.65x-3.63x faster than pmr::vector; emplace 1.20x-1.61x faster than std; selective construct path 1.21x-15.40x faster than std; churn simulation ranges from 1.58x slower to 1.66x faster than std; raw alloc 1.81x-287.40x faster than malloc.
compiler_and_flags: clang 20.1.8; -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1000x+ figures come only from the reserve microbenchmark, where each frame creates one std::vector, calls reserve(count), and frees it. glibc malloc/free of large blocks likely dominates that path, so it is not general alloc/free churn. In the more realistic tables the gains shrink to 1.2x-1.6x (emplace), and churn simulation is 1.06x-1.58x slower than std for 4096B and 16384B elements. Results are published only as a PNG image. New project (created Aug 2025, 37 stars) with no independent verification found.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ pool allocator faster than std::allocator benchmark github'

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code is public in benchmark/ (benchmark_micro.hpp, benchmark_selective.hpp, CMakeLists.txt, build.sh), and the README states clang 20.1.8, -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto, and an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U. It compares directly against std::vector with std::allocator and against std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource. Flags are stated, so the >50x cap does not apply.
verification.notes: Headline numbers match the README text and the results image. baseline_stdlib = libstdc++ is inferred: build.sh adds -stdlib=libc++ only on macOS, and the test system is Arch Linux clang, which defaults to libstdc++. Per-case numbers were read from the results PNG (https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c7692e54-...).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: up to ~1300x faster construction/reserve than std::vector (std::allocator); up to ~3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector (pool resource)
corrected_fields.caveats: The ~1300x figure comes from a narrow construction+reserve microbenchmark (bypassing malloc/realloc growth entirely), not sustained alloc/free churn; the ~3.5x-vs-pmr figure is more representative of general use. New project (created Aug 2025), 37 stars, no independent third-party verification found.

name: NUMAlloc
workload: PARSEC (native inputs), five CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI apps (Nekbone, QMCPACK, LAMMPS, AMG, Quicksilver) and real apps (Apache httpd, MySQL, Memcached, SQLite, Aget, Pfscan, Pbzip2) at 128 threads on an 8-node NUMA machine, plus Hoard synthetic scalability tests (threadtest, larson, cache-scratch, cache-thrash)
claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc-1.6.7) and 20.9% faster than the default Linux allocator (glibc 2.28) across PARSEC, CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI and real applications. 26.1% faster than glibc on the OpenMP/MPI apps alone. Best case fluidanimate: up to 5.3x faster than glibc, 4.8x faster than TBB and 4.6x faster than mimalloc (ISMM'23 manuscript). The earlier SC'22 draft (SC2022/evaluation.tex) reported 19.0% vs glibc, 6.8x vs Scalloc, and a Rodinia average of 2.44x vs glibc / 2.33x vs mimalloc. The Rodinia claim is commented out of the ISMM'23 manuscript.
compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0 on Linux Debian 10. The paper gives no optimization flags; the repo's source/Makefile builds the allocator with -g -O2 -std=c++14. Hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count).
hardware: Intel Xeon(R) Platinum 8153, 2.00GHz, 8 NUMA nodes x 16 physical cores (128 cores total), 512GB RAM, 32KB L1/1MB L2 per core, 22MB LLC per node
tradeoffs: About 10-12% higher memory footprint than the default allocator due to transparent-huge-page use (drops to comparable with THP disabled); designed around NUMA-aware node/thread binding, so benefits are largest on multi-socket/multi-node machines and smaller on single-socket systems; needs origin-aware object return and an interleaved heap that can hurt serial-phase-heavy applications.
caveats: No top-level LICENSE. Some source files (e.g. libnumalloc.cpp, inherited from FreeGuard) carry GPL-2.0-or-later headers, but most NUMA-specific files (pernodeheap, perthreadheap, interheap) have no license header, so the license is unclear (usability=reference). The repo bundles sources and paper drafts for about 10 UTSASRG projects plus many source-* variant folders, and source/Makefile is configured for NUMA_NODES=2, so which build produced the paper numbers is not obvious. The original benchmark_url was an unpublished SC'22 draft whose numbers differ from the later ISMM'23 manuscript (19.0% vs 20.9% over glibc; Rodinia claim dropped). The draft also contradicts itself on fluidanimate (5.3x vs 2.9x over glibc). Last push 2023-03-01 (>3 years ago): abandoned.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'memory allocator faster than std::allocator malloc evaluation paper' -> gh search repos "numalloc" -> UTSASRG/numalloc SC2022/evaluation.tex, abstract.tex, intro.tex

verification.tier_reason: The allocator source is public (source/) and GCC-8.3.0 plus the Xeon Platinum 8153 CPU are stated. But no optimization flags are given for the benchmarks, and the PARSEC/CORAL-2/Rodinia harness is not in the repo, so it is not A. The work was published peer-reviewed at ISMM 2023 (DOI 10.1145/3591195.3595276, confirmed via Crossref), so it is B.
verification.notes: The numbers in the original record do appear verbatim in SC2022/evaluation.tex, but that is a pre-publication draft. The peer-reviewed venue is ISMM 2023, so benchmark_url and claimed_speedup were re-pointed to the ISMM2023 manuscript in the repo; the published ACM text itself was not opened. Downgraded from A to B because the paper states no compile flags and the repo has no benchmark harness.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc) and 19% faster than the default Linux allocator across evaluated apps; up to 6.8x faster than Scalloc and 5.3x faster than the default allocator in the best case (fluidanimate); 2.9x faster than default / 4.6x faster than TCMalloc specifically on fluidanimate; on the Rodinia suite, 2.33x faster on average than mimalloc and 2.44x faster than the default allocator
corrected_fields.workload: PARSEC + Rodinia OpenMP/MPI multithreaded applications and Hoard-suite microbenchmarks (threadtest, larson, false-sharing) run with up to 128 threads across an 8-node NUMA machine
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0, Linux Debian 10, hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count)
corrected_fields.caveats: Repo has no top-level LICENSE file even though the SC'22 paper text says the code 'will be opened source using GNU GPL V2 license... upon acceptance' -- treat as unclear/no license (usability=reference) rather than assuming GPL-2.0. The repository bundles source and papers for roughly 10 different UTSASRG projects (SC22, ISMM22/23, EuroSys22/23, HPCA22, OOPSLA20/21, TPDS, plus a patent folder), so which exact source subfolder is 'the' released NUMAlloc build is not obvious from the repo alone. name: SuperMalloc
baseline: best of DLmalloc, JEmalloc, Hoard, and TBBmalloc
workload: malloc-test multithreaded allocate/free microbenchmark at 1, 8 (with hardware transactional memory), and 32 threads on 64-bit Linux
claimed_speedup: ~2.1x faster than the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc with 1 thread; 2.75x faster with 8 threads + HTM; 3.4x faster with 32 threads (no HTM)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20), per the paper. Release build flags -O3 -flto -pthread -fPIC, plus -mrtm for the HTM build (release/Makefile, Makefile.include). Compared against Hoard 3.10, jemalloc 3.6.0, tbb43_20140724 and DLmalloc 2.8.6.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 4 cores / 8 HW threads, 3.4GHz, 1 socket) for the HTM results; 2-socket 16-core Intel Xeon E5-2665 (Sandy Bridge, 2.4GHz, 32 HW threads) for the non-HTM 32-thread results
tradeoffs: Full-speed path requires Haswell+ hardware transactional memory; ships a separate pthread-lock build (libsupermalloc_pthread.so) for machines without HTM. Uses more virtual address space via a superblock design. Author Bradley Kuszmaul's ISMM'15 paper implementation, not a maintained production allocator.
caveats: The benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015. The last commit on any branch is 2017-10-25 (GitHub pushed_at of 2019-11-15 has no matching commit), and there is no recent head-to-head vs mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. The numbers come from the author's own malloc-test variant in the ISMM'15 paper. The paper's 'DLmalloc' is standalone Doug Lea dlmalloc 2.8.6 linked separately, not glibc's ptmalloc2-based default malloc, so glibc malloc itself was not measured. The fastest path relies on Haswell TSX/HTM; a pthread-mutex build also exists. Dual-licensed: MIT (expat) or GPLv3-or-later.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "supermalloc" -> repo paper/ismm15/supermalloc.tex

verification.tier_reason: The ISMM'15 paper source states gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20 and the CPUs (i7-4770, Xeon E5-2665). The benchmark code is public in the same repo (tests/new-malloc-test.c, with raw data in paper/ismm15/*.data), and release/Makefile sets -O3 -flto (-mrtm for HTM). That meets A.
verification.notes: The abstract states 2.1x / 2.75x / 3.4x over the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc verbatim. Metadata fixes: the license is MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later (the GPL text says 'or any later version'), and last_commit is 2017-10-25, not 2019-11-15. compared_against_cpp_std_directly is set to false because the 'DLmalloc' baseline is standalone dlmalloc 2.8.6, not the system glibc malloc.

corrected_fields.hardware: 4-core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 3.4GHz, 1 socket + hyperthreading) for the HTM results; 16-core 2-socket 2.4GHz Xeon-class machine for the larger-thread-count results
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20); also uses Haswell hardware transactional memory (HTM) intrinsics for the lock-elision fast path
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015; repo has had no commits since 2019-11-15 so there is no recent head-to-head vs jemalloc/mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. Numbers come from the project's own malloc-test benchmark (bundled in the same repo as the paper source), not an independent third party, but compiler, flags-equivalent build config, and exact CPU models are all stated in the paper text, so it meets tier A.

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator on 14 processors, and up to 18x over the next best allocator tested. At 14 processors: Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc, threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc, shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc. Uniprocessor: BEMengine 10.3% faster than the Solaris allocator, but the average over the uniprocessor benchmarks is 6.2% slower than Solaris.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary evidence is the ASPLOS 2000 paper, run on 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC with Solaris 7 against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era; the GNU C++ version is unstated. Uniprocessor, Hoard averaged 6.2% slower than the Solaris allocator (shbench +49.2%, espresso +15.9%, Ghostscript +10.6% runtime). The current README adds first-party modern results (code in benchmarks/, 192-core 2-node AMD EPYC, exact CPU model, compiler, and flags unstated, charts only). Those results claim 1.3-1.5x higher Larson throughput than glibc, mimalloc, and jemalloc, and 1.6x faster than glibc at 128 threads on NUMA. The README concedes that jemalloc wins linux-scalability. Hoard is also in daanx/mimalloc-bench as 'hd', but those results are chart images only.
found_via: GitHub: found via daanx/mimalloc-bench README allocator list ('hd' = Hoard); followed citation to the ASPLOS 2000 paper

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper compares Hoard against the Solaris 7 default allocator and Ptmalloc (glibc) on a 14-way Sun Enterprise 5000 with GNU C++ -O6. The compiler version is unstated and the benchmark code is not tied to the paper, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: The old record had '10.6% faster (BEMengine)'. The paper's BEMengine figure is 10.3% faster; 10.6% is Ghostscript, where Hoard is slower. The earlier caveat said no modern reproduction exists, but the README now has modern first-party benchmarks against glibc. Those are tier C material, so the paper keeps this entry at B.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator and up to 18x over the next-best allocator (Ptmalloc) at 14 processors (paper abstract); threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; BEMengine 10.6% faster than Solaris allocator uniprocessor
corrected_fields.caveats: Primary quantitative evidence is a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper run on 26-year-old hardware (UltraSPARC/Solaris 7) against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era, not a modern libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL build; no current reproduction with stated modern compiler/flags/hardware was found this session, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The GitHub repo itself is actively maintained in 2026 as a drop-in malloc replacement, and Hoard is also included (as 'hd') in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite, though that page's results are chart images only, not text numbers.

name: scalloc
baseline: ptmalloc2 (glibc's default malloc, part of GNU libc; extends Doug Lea's dlmalloc)
workload: SPEC CPU2006 483.xalancbmk single-threaded allocation-intensive workload, plus threadtest/shbench/larson multithreaded microbenchmarks and an ACDC-generated producer-consumer workload
claimed_speedup: About 1.28x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (read from the Figure 5 bar chart, derived from page data). Here scalloc is mid-pack, below TCMalloc (~1.345), llalloc (~1.33), TBB (~1.29) and SuperMalloc (~1.285), and the paper says the differences among the best allocators are small. For multithreaded workloads the paper claims scalloc 'increases performance on average while consuming less memory than the previously fastest allocator (TBB)' and outperforms/outscales all allocators for varying object sizes that fit virtual spans.
hardware: UMA machine, 4x 10-core 2GHz Intel Xeon E7-4850 (2 hardware threads/core), 32KB L1D, 32KB L1I, 256KB L2/core, 24MB L3/processor, 128GB RAM, Linux kernel 3.8.0
tradeoffs: Reserves up to 32TB of virtual address space per arena (relies on on-demand paging / madvise to keep physical memory low); distributed via LD_PRELOAD on Linux / DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES on OSX; needs overcommit accounting and transparent-huge-pages tuned for best results.
caveats: The OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is 10+ years old. The current README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and says to benchmark the current version; the separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo was last updated 2018-03-20. Today's numbers may therefore differ from the paper's. The paper states no compiler or optimization flags. The xalancbmk values exist only as bars in Figure 5, not as printed numbers.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "scalloc" -> arxiv.org/pdf/1503.09006

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed OOPSLA'15 paper (Artifact Evaluated) comparing against ptmalloc2 on SPEC 483.xalancbmk and threadtest/shbench/larson/ACDC, with hardware (4x Xeon E7-4850) stated. Neither the paper nor the artifact README (only 'tested on Ubuntu 14.04') gives the compiler or flags, so it is B, not A.
verification.notes: The record's '~1.33x, on par with TCMalloc ~1.34x' misread Figure 5: the ~1.33 bar is llalloc, and scalloc's bar is about 1.28. claimed_speedup was corrected and verdict downgraded (tier stays B). The 'artifact not updated since 2019' caveat was corrected to 2018-03-20.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ~1.33x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (Figure 5, on par with TCMalloc's ~1.34x); among the fastest and most memory-efficient allocators (previously TBB was fastest) across the multithreaded threadtest/shbench/larson suite
corrected_fields.caveats: OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is now 10+ years old; the current repo README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and points benchmarking at a separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo that has not been updated since 2019, so today's numbers may differ from the paper's. Exact compiler/version and optimization flags used for the SPEC run were not found in the extracted paper text, so tier is capped at B rather than A.

name: arena-allocator (ShortAlloc)
baseline: operator new/delete (GNU/glibc malloc via std::vector's default std::allocator)
workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)
compiler_and_flags: clang 17.0, -O3, -std=c++20, libstdc++ ('gnu' lib), per the QuickBench options of the linked benchmarks (not stated in the README)
hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool: the QuickBench result context shows 1 CPU at 2300 MHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2, 45MB L3; CPU model unstated. The README includes QuickBench's disclaimer that absolute timings are unreliable.
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; featured in a Hacker News 'Show HN' post
tradeoffs: Bump allocator: cannot free individual objects out of order, only the whole arena at once (or most-recent-first); backed by a fixed-size std::array, so capacity is bounded by the configured arena size; not thread-safe.
caveats: The README does not state compiler or flags, but the QuickBench runs used clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown and QuickBench's shared AWS pool makes absolute durations unreliable, so it stays at Tier C. The 93x-230x ratios for 1KB-8KB objects coincide with crossing glibc's mmap threshold (as the README explains), so they are not a general allocator speed claim. The arena cannot free non-top allocations. There is no LICENSE file, so usability is 'reference' only.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'arena allocator C++ github faster than operator new' -> Hacker News 'Show HN: C++ Arena Allocator That's 200x+ Faster Than GNU Malloc'

verification.tier_reason: First-party QuickBench numbers compare against std::vector with the default allocator (glibc malloc). The code is public (arena-benchmark.cpp and the QuickBench links), and the QuickBench options show clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown (shared AWS pool), so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: All README table numbers match (2.2x-4.4x up to 512B; 93x, 150x, 190x, 230x for 1K-8K). Compiler and flags were retrieved from the QuickBench API (quick-bench.com/quick/<id>). The Show HN post exists (2025-03-13, 2 points).

corrected_fields.hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool; CPU model and load unstated (README includes explicit disclaimer that absolute QuickBench timings are unreliable)
corrected_fields.caveats: Compiler and optimization flags are not stated, and several ratios (93x-230x) exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, coinciding with crossing glibc's mmap allocation threshold (a known artifact of that one size range, not a general allocator speed claim) -- capped at Tier C rather than A. QuickBench's own disclaimer says absolute durations on its shared AWS pool are 'meaningless' beyond relative comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo, so usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.

name: arena-allocator (yaroslavaristov)
baseline: malloc/free (system C allocator; the benchmark calls malloc/free directly, not operator new/delete)
workload: Google Benchmark: allocate N (1-1024) 64-byte objects then release them in bulk (arena reset() vs N free() calls, both inside the timed loop), plus a mixed 8/64/256-byte alloc+release batch
claimed_speedup: 10x-27x faster sequential allocation than malloc on AMD EPYC 7763 (N=1 to 1024 objects), 15x faster on a mixed-size batch; on Apple M1 (virtualized) 32x-342x faster sequential allocation and 15x on the mixed batch
compiler_and_flags: g++-14 (hard-coded via CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER in CMakeLists.txt; exact minor version not stated), C++23, Release: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub Codespaces, x86_64, native); Apple M1 (aarch64, via OrbStack virtualization -- author notes 'not native hardware')
tradeoffs: Bump-pointer only: no per-object free, just a bulk reset(); fixed power-of-two capacity decided at construction; not a general-purpose allocator (no fragmentation handling, no shrink/grow); single header, single contributor, unaudited.
caveats: Very new (last commit 2026-07-21), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. EPYC 7763 numbers come from a shared GitHub Codespaces VM. The largest multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured under OrbStack virtualization, which the README itself calls not native hardware; the malloc side there may be a non-glibc libc. The workload favors a bump allocator by construction: the arena releases everything with one O(1) reset while malloc pays N individual frees, and the arena has no per-object free.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: gh search repos "arena allocator" "faster than malloc"

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench.cpp, Google Benchmark, arena vs malloc/free), and CMakeLists.txt pins the compiler to g++-14 with Release flags -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG. The README names the CPUs (AMD EPYC 7763; Apple M1 under OrbStack). The >50x cap does not apply because flags are stated.
verification.notes: All README numbers match the record (10x-27x and 15x on EPYC; 32x-342x and 15x on M1). The tier is upgraded to A because the compiler (g++-14) is pinned in CMakeLists.txt and flags plus CPU are stated. If the pipeline requires the compiler to be named on the results page itself, it drops back to C.

corrected_fields.baseline: operator new/delete (malloc)
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG (compiler name/version not stated)
corrected_fields.workload: Sequential allocation of 1-1024 fixed-size objects and a mixed small/medium/large-object batch, arena bump-pointer vs plain malloc
corrected_fields.caveats: Very new (pushed within the last ~2 months), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. The largest claimed multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured on virtualized (OrbStack) hardware that the README itself calls non-native/unreliable, and exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, so tier is capped at C rather than A/B despite stated compiler flags and hardware. Comparing a no-free bump allocator against general-purpose malloc is a favorable, narrow workload (arena wins almost by construction once frees are removed from the critical path).

name: Lockless Memory Allocator
baseline: glibc malloc (ptmalloc, the built-in allocator of Ruby 2.6.5 and 2.5.1 on Linux); jemalloc and tcmalloc also run
workload: Third-party Ruby allocation stress script (12 million small string allocations with 600,000 retained and periodic large allocations up to 100 KB), run with LD_PRELOAD of each allocator, wall seconds and peak RSS, for 1 and 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby 2.6.5, lockless 1.4 versus built-in glibc malloc): 8 threads 2.859 s versus 3.423 s (1.20x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 249,540 KB versus 186,336 KB (34% more, the highest RSS of every allocator in that run); 1 thread 2.874 s versus 3.296 s (1.15x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 164,468 KB versus 169,444 KB. Older runs: Ruby 2.5.1, lockless 1.4 3.568 s versus 4.928 s (1.38x, derived from page data); Ruby 2.3.3, lockless 1.3 3.689 s versus 5.463 s (1.48x, derived from page data). Lockless is mid-pack among the alternatives: at 8 threads tcmalloc 2.5 (2.764 s), tcmalloc 2.0 (2.797 s), rpmalloc (2.824 s) and jemalloc 5.2.0 (2.837 s) are faster and jemalloc 5.2.1 is within 2% (2.922 s); at 1 thread tcmalloc 2.6.3 (2.526 s) and several other tcmalloc/jemalloc versions are faster. The vendor's own page (blocked, snippet only) compares against eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1 and tcmalloc 1.7 with the t-test1 benchmark.
stars_or_usage: benchmark repo (allocator_bench) has 56 stars; no stars figure for the vendor site
tradeoffs: Preload or link replacement of malloc; the benchmark shows a larger memory footprint than glibc (about 34% higher RSS at 8 threads) and Percona's MySQL test is quoted in search snippets as showing over 5 GB RSS for mysqld. GPL (with a commercial licence sold by the vendor) rules out some uses.
caveats: Evidence is one personal Ruby benchmark repo (SamSaffron/allocator_bench, public scripts, last commit 2020-07-06) with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated, so tier C; the results are single runs without variance. The workload is Ruby string allocation under the GVL, so the '8 threads' runs do not allocate truly in parallel and the allocator margin is small (1.15 to 1.48x); lockless also used the most memory of any allocator at 8 threads (34% more RSS than glibc). Many tcmalloc and jemalloc versions match or beat it. The vendor page https://locklessinc.com/benchmarks_allocator.shtml and the whole locklessinc.com domain (including mail.locklessinc.com) are egress-blocked, so vendor numbers (t-test1 versus eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1, tcmalloc 1.7) are known from search snippets only. Licence GPL-3.0-or-later is confirmed from the vendor README and ll_alloc.c header carried in the GitHub mirror jl2922/lockless_allocator ('GPL version 3 (or any later version)'; commercial licences offered by the vendor); the source copyright reads 2009-2011, and the vendor what's-new page (snippet only) lists the last allocator update on 23 Jul 2012 (aligned_alloc support), so the code is effectively abandoned. GPL means linking obliges source redistribution. [retier] Third-party SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby, GVL-serialised threads, single runs, no CPU or compiler): 1.15-1.48x vs glibc but 10th of 37 on time (tcmalloc 2.0-2.7, rpmalloc and jemalloc 5.2.0 faster) and second-highest 8-thread RSS of 37 (rpmalloc master higher). The 'mem' column is end-of-run RSS from ps, not peak; retained sizes use an unseeded Random.rand so the workload differs per run; tcmalloc 2.1 vs 2.2 differ by 14.5% at 1 thread, the same size as lockless's margin. The bench preloaded libllalloc.so.1.4 while the jl2922/lockless_allocator mirror (2017, 0 stars) builds .so.1.3. x86-only assembly, real sbrk slabs, mallopt/malloc_trim ignore their parameters, a fork child leaks other threads' heaps. Vendor numbers (locklessinc.com, blocked) and Percona 2012 (best throughput group, mysqld RSS +5 GB) seen as snippets only. GPL-3.0-or-later; code copyright 2009-2011, last update July 2012, abandoned.

name: Boost.Fiber
workload: skynet microbenchmark (ported from atemerev/skynet): spawn 10 threads-of-execution recursively until 1,000,000 total actors/fibers are created (only 10,000 for std::thread/std::async/pthread due to resource exhaustion); each returns its ordinal number, summed back up to the root; average time-per-unit measured with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock
claimed_speedup: fiber (16C/32T, work-stealing, tcmalloc): 0.05-0.09 us/fiber (average over 1,000,000) vs std::thread 52-73 us/thread and std::async 106-122 us/thread (average over 10,000, because 1,000,000 threads exhausted resources); ~580-1460x lower time-per-unit vs std::thread and ~1180-2440x vs std::async (derived from page data). Single-thread round-robin fiber (1C/1T): 1.69-1.79 us/fiber, still ~30-40x lower than std::thread (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1, variant=release, optimization=speed
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2GHz, 16 cores/32 threads, 64GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 511 stars on the standalone mirror; ships as part of the Boost C++ Libraries collection used industry-wide
tradeoffs: Cooperative user-space scheduling: a blocking syscall or CPU-bound fiber can stall all fibers on its worker thread unless paired with async I/O (e.g. Boost.Asio integration); best numbers require a non-default allocator (tcmalloc) and a work-stealing scheduler configuration; different programming model (fiber-per-task) than raw std::thread/std::async call sites.
caveats: Numbers come from Boost's own project documentation (first party), though the benchmark code itself (performance/thread/skynet_std.cpp and the fiber counterpart in the same repo) is public and the compiler/flags/hardware are all stated, meeting the tier-A bar despite the source being first-party. The raw ratio (>50x) looks extreme, but it is explained by mechanism (fiber creation/context switch avoids syscalls and stack-guard-page setup that std::thread/std::async incur) rather than a flawed methodology; std::thread could only be tested at 10,000 units instead of 1,000,000 due to OS resource exhaustion, so the two are not run at identical scale. Measurements were taken with gcc-6.3.1, an old compiler (circa 2017); the fiber library and hardware landscape have moved on since, and the doc gives no indication the numbers were re-run on newer toolchains.

name: utl::parallel (UTL ThreadPool)
workload: Four microbenchmark scenarios, 1000 tasks each: (1) small non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 0-100us, (2) large non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 1000-3000us, (3) shallow recursive tasks (0-100us with 70% chance of spawning+awaiting one more such task), (4) deep recursive tasks (0-100us with 49% chance of spawning+awaiting two more such tasks, averaging ~50 subtasks); reports ms/op and op/s relative to a serial baseline
claimed_speedup: Small non-recursive: utl::parallel::ThreadPool 573.3% vs std::async() 214.0% of serial speed (~2.7x faster than std::async, derived from page data). Large non-recursive: 597.0% vs 564.2% (~1.06x, roughly tied). Shallow recursive: 583.0% vs 161.1% (~3.6x faster than std::async; BS::thread_pool and progschj/ThreadPool deadlock entirely on this workload). Deep recursive: 565.1% vs 154.7% (~3.65x faster than std::async, derived from page data).
hardware: 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 5600H, hyper-threading disabled
tradeoffs: Uses a custom future type instead of std::future so recursive awaiting doesn't deadlock, so it is not a drop-in std::future replacement; ships as one module inside a larger multi-module header-only utility collection (UTL) rather than a standalone package; explicitly a niche tool for recursive/scatter-gather workloads, not a general vendor-optimized scheduler like TBB/OpenMP.
caveats: Author explicitly disclaims superiority over vendor-optimized frameworks (OpenMP/TBB). On large non-recursive tasks the advantage over std::async almost disappears (~1.06x) since thread-creation overhead is amortized; the large speedups are concentrated in small-task and recursive-task scenarios, exactly where std::async's per-call thread-spawn cost dominates. claimed_speedup: up to 29% faster runtime, 1.5x less memory, and 1.9x higher throughput than oneTBB on the ML workload

hardware: 40 Intel Xeon CPU cores at 2.00 GHz (exact model not stated), 4 GeForce RTX 2080 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux 5.0.0-21-generic

baseline: Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 1.2.2 (CPU, MKL); also TensorFlow 1.0.0 (CPU) and tiny-dnn

name: fbthrift
baseline: Protocol Buffers C++ (protobuf; version not stated), measured with SerializeToArray, SerializeAsString and SerializeToZeroCopyStream
workload: folly::Benchmark microbenchmark in thrift/lib/cpp2/protocol/benchmark: serialize and deserialize a struct of repeated field groups (i32, i64, 8-byte string, list<i32> of 10, map<string,i32> of 5, bool, double) in Small (1 group), Medium (3 groups) and Large (9 groups) sizes, Thrift Binary, Compact and cursor-based (CurSe) protocols against Protobuf equivalents (and an internal Carbon format).
claimed_speedup: Source comment 'Results for last run: 2025-11-18', time per iteration. Serialize Small: Thrift Binary 380.11 ns, Compact 395.36 ns, CurSe 230.85 ns versus Protobuf Array 945.69 ns, String 832.30 ns, ZeroCopy 998.08 ns (Binary about 2.2-2.6x faster, derived from page data). Serialize Medium: Binary 936.16 ns, Compact 948.40 ns, CurSe 456.09 ns versus Protobuf 2.94 us / 2.55 us / 3.04 us (Binary about 2.7-3.2x, derived). Serialize Large: Binary 2.72 us, Compact 2.75 us, CurSe 1.23 us versus Protobuf 9.54 us / 8.32 us / 9.60 us (Binary about 3.1-3.5x, derived). The CurSe serialize rows skip building the struct (see caveats), so their 3.6-4.3x over Protobuf is not like-for-like. Deserialize Small: Binary 396.13 ns, Compact 424.35 ns, CurSe 427.60 ns versus Protobuf 660.66-681.08 ns (Binary about 1.7x, derived). Deserialize Medium: Binary 1.06 us, Compact 1.10 us versus Protobuf 2.08-2.18 us (about 1.9-2.1x, derived). Deserialize Large: Binary 3.15 us, Compact 3.29 us versus Protobuf 6.58-6.68 us (about 2.1x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: buck2 mode opt-clang-lto (Meta-internal fbcode build; clang version and protobuf version not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires the folly dependency stack and the Thrift compiler and IDL, which is a heavier build than protobuf; fbthrift diverged from Apache Thrift with its own cpp2 code generator, field_ref API, adapters and CursorBasedSerializer. Wire formats differ (Thrift Binary/Compact are larger or comparable but not identical to protobuf varint encoding).
caveats: First-party results pasted into a source comment (dated 2025-11-18); the benchmark code is public but CPU model, core count, clang and protobuf versions are not stated, and it needs the Meta fbcode/buck2 build (mode/opt-clang-lto), so it is not reproducible as published (tier C). Serialize benchmarks build the test object inside the timed loop for Thrift Binary/Compact and Protobuf (createThriftTestData / createProtobufTestData run every iteration), so the ratios mix object population with encoding, and population is not symmetric: Thrift copy-assigns the prebuilt std::vector and std::map, while Protobuf appends the 10 list elements one by one and inserts the 5 map entries one by one into a protobuf Map. The CurSe serialize rows write the constants straight to the cursor writer with no struct built at all, so CurSe-vs-Protobuf serialize ratios are not like-for-like, and the CurSe deserialize row discards what it reads (no doNotOptimizeAway). Deserialize runs exclude serialization via BenchmarkSuspender; the Protobuf String path copies the IOBuf into a std::string inside the timed region, while the Array path parses in place. Protobuf SerializeToArray writes directly into a pre-sized IOBuf (no extra copy); only the SerializeAsString row adds a copyBuffer copy. No protobuf Arena is used. One tiny synthetic schema (i32, i64, 8-byte string, list<i32> of 10, map<string,i32> of 5, bool, double per group; 1, 3 or 9 groups), no realistic string lengths. fbthrift is Facebook's branch of Apache Thrift (GitHub does not mark it a fork; is_fork_of left null).

name: CRoaring (Roaring Bitmaps)
baseline: std::unordered_set<uint32_t> and sorted std::vector<uint32_t> with STL set algorithms (std::set_intersection/union/difference, std::binary_search) from the standard library bundled with GCC 5.4; also an uncompressed bitset (the authors' portable C 'cbitset', same word-array layout as std::bitset/std::vector<bool>)
workload: 8 realistic integer-set datasets (CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Census1881, Census1881-sorted, Weather, Weather-sorted, Wikileaks, Wikileaks-sorted; 200 sets each, universe sizes 200K-4.3M): sequential iteration/cardinality, random-access membership queries at n/4, n/2, 3n/4, and 199 pairwise intersections/unions/differences/symmetric differences between successive sets. name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: Ping-pong latency on Ryzen 5950X (SMT): AtomicQueue mean 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). 1-producer/1-consumer throughput on 5950X: AtomicQueue ~142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex ~4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue mean ~1.23B msg/s (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). With 2-16 producer/consumer pairs, OptimistAtomicQueue stays ~4-24x ahead of std::mutex (52.9M vs 13.0M msg/s at 2; 55.3M vs 2.3M at 16), while plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (Ryzen 5950X/5825U); gcc-8.4.0 (legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold 6132). Current Makefile gcc release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG -fno-stack-protector -fno-stack-clash-protection -fno-tree-ch -fno-move-loop-invariants -fno-plt -fno-math-errno -ffinite-math-only -pthread; benchmarks.cc is compiled with -std=c++17, which is appended after the base -std=c++14.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 'std::mutex' baseline is atomic_queue's own fixed-size ring buffer guarded by std::mutex (AtomicQueueMutex), polled through try_push/try_pop retry loops. It is not std::queue with a condition variable. The ~1.23B msg/s 1P/1C OptimistAtomicQueue figure varies a lot (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). The page says throughput exceeds the inverse of latency on purpose, because the throughput loop has no dependency chains. Treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the conservative claim. With 2+ producer/consumer pairs on the 5950X, plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex: std::mutex leads at 2 pairs (13.0M vs 10.1M msg/s) and ties at 4. Only OptimistAtomicQueue keeps a large throughput lead under contention.

name: contention_free_shared_mutex (AlexeyAB/object_threadsafe safe_ptr library)
workload: Concurrent read/write locking benchmark (bench_contfree / benchmark / CDS_test folders) comparing contention_free_shared_mutex<> to std::shared_mutex under multi-threaded mixed read/write contention on a shared object; exact operation counts and thread counts are shown only in chart images in the README, not as text/tables.
claimed_speedup: README headline: "contention_free_shared_mutex<> - 10 X times faster than std::shared_mutex". CodeProject Article 2 (archived), 16 threads on Xeon E5-2660 v3, std::map guarded by the lock: 0% modifications 34.60 Mops (contfree_safe_ptr<map>) vs 2.44 Mops (safe_ptr<map, std::shared_mutex>), stated as 14x; 15% modifications 5.16 vs 0.74 Mops, stated as 7x. The README charts (90% update/5% insert/5% delete, 20 usec forced delay, 2x Xeon E5-2686 v4) show about 1.9 vs about 0.4 MOps at 64 threads (~5x, read approximately from the chart image) and near-parity at 16 threads or fewer.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3.0 on Linux, g++ -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 (bench_contfree/Makefile). The article also offers an MSVS 2015 build, but the published run command (numactl ... ./benchmark 16) is Linux.

tradeoffs: contention_free_shared_mutex shards locking state per-thread to avoid contention, which increases memory usage relative to std::shared_mutex; safe_ptr<>/contfree_safe_ptr<> wrap objects and change access syntax (operator-> based locking) rather than being a drop-in mutex replacement; recursive-lock semantics differ from std::shared_mutex.

The 10x headline is a middle value: the article shows 14x at 0% writes and 7x at 15% writes, and the lock is contention-free only up to 36 threads (template parameter). Above that it acts as an exclusive lock. The README's real-app chart (20 usec delay) shows parity up to 16 threads and ~5x only at 64 threads. name: eventpp::SpinLock (eventpp GeneralThreading policy)

claimed_speedup: 10M events, 100 event types/listeners (doc/benchmark.md): 1 enqueue/1 process thread: SpinLock 1303 ms vs std::mutex 1824 ms (~1.4x faster, derived from page data); 1/3: 3186 vs 2989 ms (SpinLock slower); 2/2: 3049 vs 3151 ms (slightly faster); 4/4: 1659 vs 1657 ms (tie); 16/16: 1891 vs 708 ms (SpinLock ~2.7x SLOWER, derived from page data).

name: libcsp
baseline: Go goroutines (Go 1.14, sync.WaitGroup); pthreads also run at a reduced size
workload: Divide-and-conquer sum(0, 10,000,000) spawning two lightweight processes per node (about 20 million short-lived processes), 10 rounds, seconds per round and memory share, for 1 to 8 CPU cores.
claimed_speedup: libcsp versus Go seconds per round: 3.047 versus 31.145 on 1 core (10.2x), 0.847 versus 11.172 on 4 cores (13.2x), 0.726 versus 8.030 on 8 cores (11.1x) (ratios derived from page data). Memory of the machine: 2.3% versus 31.2% at 8 cores. The docs say libcsp is 'at least 10 times faster and use less memory than golang'. Repo description: 'A concurrency C library 10x faster than Golang'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.0 with -Wall -O3 and the libcsp gcc plugin (cspcli analyze); Go v1.14 'go build' defaults
hardware: 8 CPU cores, 8192 MB memory, Linux 4.15.0-88-generic x86_64 (ubuntu-bionic); CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a GCC plugin plus the cspcli tool to analyse stack sizes at compile time, so stack use must be statically analysable; C only, GCC only; custom syntax (proc, sync, async macros); includes netpoll and timers.
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (benchmarks/sum_libcsp.c, sum_go.go, sum_thread.c and benchmarks/Makefile), but the CPU model is not stated; the environment is listed only as 8 cores, 8192 MB, Linux ubuntu-bionic 4.15.0-88-generic (the hostname and round memory size suggest a VM, not confirmed). The workload is a pure process-spawn microbenchmark (two child processes per node, about 20 million per round) with no cutoff, so it measures create-schedule-destroy overhead rather than real applications; the Go side allocates two closures and a WaitGroup per node that escape to the heap, so Go's GC and growable-stack costs are included, while libcsp's stacks are sized at compile time by its GCC plugin and 'cspcli analyze' (the memory column reflects that static sizing). Building needs the libcsp GCC plugin plus the cspcli analysis step with a fixed core count. Go 1.14 dates from 2020; no newer Go was tested. The pthread comparison could not run at the same size: sum_thread.c comments say MAX had to be cut to 10,000 (3.2 s per round) because 10^7 exceeds the Linux thread limit. LICENSE file is MIT while source headers carry ISC-style permission text (both OSI-permissive). Single author; last commit 2023-06-30, so abandoned.

name: Wirehair
baseline: CM256 (catid/cm256, O(N^2) Cauchy-matrix MDS Reed-Solomon codec; Longhair measured alongside)
workload: Erasure-code encode and decode throughput for 128 data pieces of 64,000 bytes with 128 recovery pieces (code rate 1/2), WH256 (Wirehair with the GF256 inner loops) vs CM256, Longhair, FEC-AL and Leopard, on the author's AVX2 laptop.
claimed_speedup: Leopard's Benchmarks.md: WH256 wirehair_encode(N = 128) 661.644 MB/s and wirehair_decode 830.103 MB/s vs CM256 encode 99.6658 MBps and decode 104.651 MBps (Longhair 100.342 and 96.3757 MB/s), i.e. about 6.6x faster encode and 7.9x faster decode than CM256 (derived from page data). Text: Wirehair 'Encodes at 660 MB/s, and decodes at 830 MB/s for ALL cases' and is the fastest decoder in that comparison; Wirehair's README also states it scales as O(N) rather than O(N log N) (Leopard) or O(N^2) (Fecal).
hardware: Author's 'few year old' laptop with AVX2 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not an MDS code: needs N + 0.02 packets on average and sometimes N + 1 or N + 2 (Benchmarks.md says about a 3% chance of one extra block). Rateless fountain code for large block counts (up to 64,000). Same page shows Leopard encodes about 3x faster (1.96 GB/s) at k=m=128, and the Fecal README shows FEC-AL encoding about 2x faster than Wirehair at N=1000 with about 100 losses and 4x faster with about 30 losses (Wirehair decodes about 2x faster at 100 losses, but 2x slower at 30). The Wirehair README itself calls it a pretty inefficient codec for N below about 128 compared with Fecal. Public C API; versioned wire profiles in the current tree.
caveats: First-party numbers from the same author as CM256, 'not being very rigorous' on one laptop, with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and one configuration (k=m=128, 64 KB pieces). The measured code is catid/wh256, a pre-production GF256 branch; github.com/catid/wh256 now returns 404, so the benchmarked code is not public (current Wirehair 2 is described as a pure-GF(256) API, but its equivalence to WH256 is not shown). The numbers sit in the Leopard repo, not Wirehair's. The comparison covers only the author's own codecs; in the same table the author's Leopard encodes faster (1964.98 MB/s vs 661.644 MB/s), so Wirehair is fastest only at decode. Reed-Solomon (MDS, practical only up to 255 pieces) and a fountain code (about 0.025 extra blocks of overhead on average) are not like-for-like. Baseline is the author's own CM256 rather than Jerasure, ISA-L or Zfec, and the author notes CM256's inner loops could still be improved with GF256. Wirehair's own README benchmarks only compare Wirehair 1 with Wirehair 2 (GCC 13.3, AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9985WX, per docs/benchmarks/README.md) and show WH2 slower at 64-byte blocks, so they are no evidence against an outside baseline. Category erasure-codes is not one of the wave categories; filed under compression-and-encoding as the nearest domain.

name: libarchive (bsdtar)
workload: Jan Psota's TCP script (tcp.sh) timing bsdtar (libarchive 2.3.4), GNU tar 1.19 and star 1.5a85 creating, listing and extracting a pax-format archive; four data sets on two machines: Linux 2.6.23 source (291 MB, 23,867 files) on tmpfs, best of 5, and a 3.2 GB home directory on reiserfs disk on a 64-bit Athlon 64 X2; a 119 MB driver tree and a 2.1 GB home directory on a 32-bit Athlon, best of 3.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, mostly not faster. 64-bit Athlon 64 X2, tmpfs, Linux 2.6.23 tree (291 MB, best of 5): list 0.164 s versus GNU tar 0.218 s (bsdtar 1.33x faster, derived from page data); create 0.764 s versus 0.743 s (GNU tar 1.03x faster); extract 0.733 s versus 0.625 s (GNU tar 1.17x faster). 64-bit, disk, 3.2 GB in 7,447 files (best of 3): list 0.053 s versus 56.535 s (unexplained, since the script passes --seek to GNU tar); create 184.680 s versus 159.240 s (GNU tar 1.16x faster); extract 78.914 s versus 78.480 s (tie). 32-bit 1.5 GHz Athlon, drivers tree (119 MB, best of 3): list 0.167 s versus 0.161 s, create 1.329 s versus 1.223 s, extract 1.186 s versus 1.064 s (GNU tar faster in all three). 32-bit, disk, 2.1 GB (best of 3): list 0.214 s versus 0.210 s, create 182.171 s versus 174.999 s, extract 94.912 s versus 94.657 s (GNU tar marginally faster in all three). Tim Kientzle's note attributes bsdtar's list wins to lseek() skipping over entry bodies, which GNU tar also offers. The project itself only claims 'efficient'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.2.2 (Gentoo), CFLAGS="-O2 -march=k8 -pipe" (64-bit machine); -march=athlon-xp -mfpmath=sse on the 32-bit machine
hardware: AMD Athlon 64 X2 Dual Core 4200+ 2.2 GHz, 2012 MB RAM, Linux 2.6.22 (Gentoo); also a 1.5 GHz 32-bit AMD Athlon with 504 MB
stars_or_usage: 3.6k stars; ships as bsdtar, bsdcpio, bsdunzip on FreeBSD, macOS and Windows
tradeoffs: Streaming multi-format reader and writer (tar, zip, 7z, rar, iso9660 and more), so the generality costs some create and extract speed relative to a tar-only tool. README notes thread safety depends on the platform (archive_write_disk_header needs an external mutex on POSIX).
caveats: Not a speed claim by the project: the data is a 2007 mailing-list post by a third party (Jan Psota, Bug-tar list), archived in contrib/psota-benchmark with the TCP script (tcp.sh) beside it; the committed script sets n=3 while the first result set says best of 5. Versions are libarchive 2.3.4 and GNU tar 1.19, so the numbers are stale by almost twenty years. The 'compare' rows are invalid: Tim Kientzle's note says bsdtar does not support that operation (the script does not abort on its failure), so its 0.001 s is a no-op. bsdtar is slower than GNU tar for create and extract on all four data sets; its list win appears on the two 64-bit sets only and comes from lseek() skipping, a feature GNU tar has too; the script passes --seek to GNU tar, so the 1000x list gap on the 3.2 GB disk run is not explained by the file. Covers only uncompressed archives; compressed or tape cases are untested. Licence: COPYING is a 2-clause BSD notice for most sources, with a few files under 3-clause UC Regents, public domain or CC0/OpenSSL/Apache-2.0, all permissive. Filed so the shortcoming is recorded; libarchive is not shown to be faster than GNU tar overall.

name: pixz
baseline: xz (XZ Utils), run multi-threaded by pRDS with the same core count as pixz (xz -zcT<cores> -6 to compress, xz -cdT<cores> to decompress)
workload: Write and read an R object holding a 3 GB CSV of about 17 million tweets through the R package pRDS, which pipes R's serialization stream into external compressors at default levels: pixz -tp<cores> -6 versus xz -zcT<cores> -6 for writing, pixz -dp<cores> versus xz -cdT<cores> for reading (cores = mc.cores option, or detectCores()/2 when unset), on a 4-core, 8-thread i7 Mac. Benchmark committed 2020-06-02.
claimed_speedup: pRDS README benchmark table: pixz write 443 s, read 63 s, size 805 MB versus multi-threaded xz write 469 s, read 64 s, size 795 MB (pixz about 1.06x faster to compress and about 1.02x faster to decompress, output about 1.3% larger, derived from page data). Other xz-format rows: 7z (-mmt) 580 s write, 83 s read, 741 MB; R native xzfile 2626 s write, 105 s read, 772 MB (pixz about 5.9x faster than R's built-in single-threaded xz, but multi-threaded xz itself is about 5.6x faster than R native, derived from page data, so that gap is threading, not pixz). R native uncompressed write and read take 99 s and 42 s, which bounds the read rows.
hardware: i7 Mac, 4 cores / 8 threads (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Splits input into independent xz blocks (loses some compression ratio versus one large block, 805 MB versus 795 MB in the table above), adds a tarball index for fast listing and single-file extraction, output is a normal .xz stream with an added index; needs libarchive and liblzma; flags differ from xz (-z, -c, -f, -l, -q, -t mean different things).
caveats: Weak evidence: one loosely controlled run by a third party in an obscure R package (pRDS, GPL-2.0, 0 stars; the pRDS author says 'not in an entirely scientific manner', 'loosely controlled environment', and that four tools did not work as intended on the machine), no tool versions, no flags, no CPU model, no repeat runs. pRDS's command table (R/zzz.R) runs xz as 'xz -zcT# -%' and 'xz -cdT#' and pixz as 'pixz -tp# -%' and 'pixz -dp#' with the same core count, so the xz row is multi-threaded xz, not single-threaded: the result is pixz versus xz -T at equal threads, a 6% compression gap that a single run cannot separate from noise. Reads go through R's deserializer from a pipe (uncompressed read alone takes 42 s), so the 63 s versus 64 s read rows are R-bound and say little about pixz's parallel decompression; the benchmark predates xz 5.4's multi-threaded decompression. The pixz README makes no speed numbers; its claims are that it parallelizes decompression, indexes tarballs for random access, and defaults to all cores while xz defaults to one (modern xz has -T and -T0, so that is a default difference). No stronger public pixz-versus-xz measurement was found (two WebSearch queries returned only README mirrors). Not clearly faster than multi-threaded xz; its distinct value is the block index for random access to tarball members.

Other rows: 7z 580 s write, 83 s read, 741 MB; R native xz 2626 s write, 105 s read, 772 MB (pixz about 5.9x faster than R's built-in xz, derived from page data). The pixz README itself gives no numbers, only the claims that pixz parallelizes decompression and defaults to all cores while xz defaults to one.
corrected_fields.caveats: Weak evidence: one loosely controlled run by a third party (the pRDS author says 'not in an entirely scientific manner', 'loosely controlled environment', and that four tools did not work as intended on the machine), no tool versions, no flags, no CPU model, no repeat runs. The 'xz' row is not stated to be single-threaded or multi-threaded (the 469 s figure is plausible for single-threaded xz -6 on 3 GB), and a 6% gain from 8 threads suggests pixz was not parallelizing well in that setup. Modern xz (5.2 and later) has its own -T threading, so the pixz README's 'xz defaults to one core' framing is now only a default difference. The pixz repo has no benchmark of its own and the README makes no speed numbers. Directional only; filed to record that no stronger public pixz-versus-xz measurement was reachable (pxz and pigz benchmark pages found by search were not pixz-specific, and the neurolabusc/pigz-bench README does not cover xz or pixz).

name: TurboRLE (TRLE and SRLE)
baseline: rle8 (rainerzufalldererste/rle8 as of 2019, an SSE/AVX2 8-bit run length encoder, one configuration 'rle8 1'; that repository has since become hypersonic-rle-kit) and Mespotine RLE (MRLE); memcpy shown as a reference row. None of the general-lossless category baselines (zlib, zstd, lz4, brotli, xz) appear in the README tables.
workload: Single-thread run length encode and decode throughput (MB/s) and compressed size on three large files: girl.bmp (RLE64Samples), a checkers end-game tablebase file (1034.db), and enwik9 after a Burrows-Wheeler transform (enwik9bwt), measured with TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: README claim: 'Compress better and up to 12 times faster and decompress up to 6 times faster than other fast RLEs'; 'Can be faster than memcpy!'. Skylake table (MB/s, C = compress, D = decompress): girl.bmp trle C 2089 / D 11385, srle 8 C 11307 / D 13205 (4744806 bytes) vs rle8 C 890 / D 11998 (5901235 bytes) and mrle C 378 / D 12302; enwik9bwt trle C 472 / D 1743, srle 8 C 568 / D 4310 vs rle8 C 260 / D 675 and mrle C 207 / D 553; 1034.db trle C 774 / D 3020 vs rle8 C 456 / D 2669 and mrle C 262 / D 1491. Derived from page data: srle 8 compresses girl.bmp about 12.7x faster than rle8 and decompresses enwik9bwt about 6.4x faster than rle8; trle compresses girl.bmp about 2.3x faster than rle8 while decompressing slightly slower (11385 vs 11998 MB/s). srle 64 compresses girl.bmp at 16269 MB/s vs memcpy 13978 MB/s (output is larger, 19839711 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3 (tables dated 2019-08); flags not stated in the README. The current TurboBench makefile builds the TurboRLE objects with -O3 -march=haswell -w -fstrict-aliasing -falign-loops=32 -DNDEBUG on x86_64, but that is the HEAD makefile, not the 2019 revision. The in-repo ./trle test tool (trle.c) benchmarks trle, srle and mrle but not rle8, so the rle8 rows can only come from TurboBench.
hardware: Intel Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (x86 tables for girl.bmp, 1034.db and enwik9bwt); ARM A73 ODROID-N2 1.8GHz (second set of tables covering only girl.bmp and enwik9bwt, with no rle8 row since rle8 is x86 SSE/AVX2 only)
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft; a commercial licence is not described in the README). Pure C with no inline assembly, SIMD paths for SSE/AVX2/NEON plus a RISC-V scalar fallback, and Java JNI bindings. Several variants (srle 8/16/32/64) trade compression ratio for speed, so the fastest rows compress much worse than rle8 or mrle: the 12x and 6x figures pair different output sizes.
caveats: Tier C: first-party tables dated 2019-08 with compiler and CPU stated but no flags in the README; TurboBench is public but its 2019 build flags are not documented, and TurboRLE's own code has changed since (decoder commits as recent as 2026-07). The baselines are other RLE libraries, not the general-lossless category incumbents (zlib, zstd, lz4, brotli, xz). The 'up to 12x / 6x' claims cherry-pick the best variant per file (srle 8 vs rle8 on girl.bmp compression; srle 8 vs rle8 on enwik9bwt decompression); trle decompresses girl.bmp slower than rle8 and mrle (11385 vs 11998 and 12302 MB/s). The rle8 baseline is stale: its successor, hypersonic-rle-kit (same repository, BSD-2-Clause), benchmarks TurboRLE commit 7f6e486 (April 2023, AVX2 enabled) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X with Visual Studio 2022, and its own 8-bit codecs decode several times faster than trle and srle 8 at similar ratios (enwik9.bwt: '8 Bit 3LUT Short' 40.34% ratio, 765.3 MiB/s encode, 3,046.5 MiB/s decode vs trle 42.0%, 697.6 and 2,062.9 MiB/s; '8 Bit' decodes at 16,097.6 MiB/s vs srle 8 6,095.1 MiB/s); trle keeps the best plain-RLE ratio on 1034.db (17.4% vs 18.55%). That contradicts the README's 'No other RLE compress or decompress faster with better compression'. The memcpy row and the 'faster than memcpy' claim apply only to srle 64 compression of highly compressible data (girl.bmp: 16269 vs 13978 MB/s, output 4.9% of input). GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft).

name: Versor (geometric algebra library)
baseline: other C++ geometric algebra solutions: GluCat (framed and matrix), TbGAL, Garamon, Gaalet, Gaalop, GATL
workload: ga-benchmark: 10 unary and 12 binary geometric algebra operations (geometric product, outer product, inner products, dualization, inversion and others) on conformal, Euclidean (2-5 D) and Minkowski models plus a conformal inverse kinematics algorithm, ranked by mean CPU time with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: ga-benchmark 2020-02-05 run, wall-clock real_time (derived from the run JSONs): Versor geomean 0.88x GATL speed (GATL faster in 1,239 of 1,816 cases; inverse kinematics 242 vs 857 ns), 0.96-0.98x Gaalop and Gaalet; Versor 18x faster than Garamon, 37x TbGAL, 162x GluCat (framed), 2,588x GluCat (matrix). Wall-clock golds: GATL 111, Gaalet 76, Gaalop 55, Versor 23. The published medal table (GATL 247 golds, Versor 246) ranks by CPU time read from a 15.625 ms WSL1 tick, so its golds are zero-time ties.
compiler_and_flags: GNU Compiler Collection 7.4.0 in 'release' mode (CMake Release; exact flags not stated in the result pages)
hardware: 8 x 1992 MHz CPUs, CPU model not stated, Linux 4.4.0-18362-Microsoft (Windows Subsystem for Linux), CPU scaling off, metric CPU time
stars_or_usage: 327 stars, 54 forks; one of seven solutions in ga-benchmark
tradeoffs: Template-metaprogramming library for Euclidean, Conformal, Projective and Minkowski geometric algebras with arbitrary metrics; needs C++11 (gcc 4.7+, clang 3.2+); heavy compile times were reported as improved in the README; includes OpenGL drawing helpers; the lead developer's PhD project.
caveats: Tier B: independent community suite (ga-developers/ga-benchmark, GPL-3.0, code public, run published in ga-benchmark-runs) but the context line gives no CPU model (8 x 1992 MHz, WSL1 kernel 4.4.0-18362-Microsoft) and no flags beyond CMake Release with GCC 7.4.0, and the run is from February 2020, so the Versor revision tested may differ from current devel. The result is a medal ranking against other geometric algebra libraries, not a speedup against the geometry-spatial category incumbents (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS) or any standard-library facility, and gives no time ratios. Medals are positions by exact equality of mean CPU time (gabm.py make_ranking), and 1,043 golds were awarded over 323 cases (derived from page data), so GATL, Versor, Gaalop and Gaalet share first place in most cases: a Versor gold means tied-fastest, not uniquely fastest, and its 246 golds vs GATL's 247 is a tie. Gaalop and Gaalet counts are depressed by 59 compilation-error faults each. The inverse-kinematics algorithm is excluded from the medal table (IGNORED_GROUPS). The gafro paper (Loew and Calinon, IEEE Robotics and Automation Magazine 2024, arXiv 2310.19090) forked ga-benchmark and states that GATL and Versor were previously reported to be the fastest GA libraries (read from search snippets only; arXiv and idiap.ch are blocked). The suite's install script clones github.com/wolftype/versor; the Versor README itself has no numbers (prose 'fast' and 'on steroids' only). [retier] Medal table ranks by CPU time on WSL1 (15.625 ms tick) while each repetition runs 20-200 us, so 89-93% of cases read 0.0 and golds are ties; wall-clock data shows Versor fourth behind GATL, Gaalet and Gaalop. Commutator is two geometric products; operator! only for blades/versors; silent zeroing on implicit conversion (#20); Rotor typedef wrong above 3D (#22); 5 of 12 binary ops missing from the harness.

name: geogram (ParallelDelaunay3d)
baseline: CGAL 3D Delaunay / regular triangulation, single-threaded and CGAL Parallel; the paper also has SciPy, Voro++, HXT (Gmsh) and gDel3D (GPU) columns
workload: Runtime of 3D Voronoi / Delaunay construction on synthetic white-noise and density-gradient point sets and of power-diagram (weighted, regular triangulation) construction on clustered point sets, 0.1M to 15M points, plus real-world neural-rendering point sets, in a third-party SIGGRAPH 2026 GPU Voronoi paper (Taveira, Lindstrom, Fatemi, Hammarstrand, Kahl) that uses SciPy, CGAL, CGAL Parallel, Geogram, Voro++ and HXT as CPU baselines on 16 cores.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (paper not opened). Clustered weighted point sets, Geogram on 16 cores versus single-threaded CGAL: 100k points 0.060 s vs 0.449 s (about 7.5x, derived); 500k 0.250 vs 2.299 (about 9.2x); 1M 0.413 vs 4.808 (about 11.6x); 15M 5.890 vs 74.723 (about 12.7x), but these ratios compare 16 threads with one thread. Against CGAL Parallel on the same 16 cores the gap is far smaller: white noise 15M points, Geogram 6.138 s vs CGAL Parallel 6.903 s (about 1.12x, derived from snippet data); clustered 100k points, Geogram 0.060 s vs CGAL Parallel 0.533 s. HXT (Gmsh) beats Geogram at scale: 2.259 s at 15M points, white noise (Geogram about 2.7x slower, derived from snippet data); the paper calls HXT the best CPU baseline, closely followed by Geogram.
hardware: CPU methods on 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 9534 (WebSearch snippet only; GPU not captured)
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; Symposium on Geometry Processing Software Award 2023
tradeoffs: Geogram's ParallelDelaunay3d uses floating-point predicates with exact-arithmetic fallback (expansion_nt/PCK) and is multithreaded; it is a general geometry-processing toolkit with its own mesh data structures rather than CGAL's generic kernel framework. Input points may be perturbed or duplicated points handled differently from CGAL (not checked).
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org, research.chalmers.se (full-text PDF), research.zenseact.com (project page), emergentmind.com and themoonlight.io are blocked in this environment, so the paper (Taveira, Lindstrom, Fatemi, Hammarstrand, Kahl, 'Scalable GPU Construction of 3D Voronoi and Power Diagrams', SIGGRAPH 2026, arXiv 2605.06408, ACM DOI 10.1145/3799902.3811229) was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch result text summarising its tables. CPU baselines ran on 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 9534 (snippet); compiler, flags, thread settings, Geogram and CGAL versions are unknown. The headline 7.5-12.7x compares 16-thread Geogram with single-threaded CGAL; against CGAL Parallel on the same cores Geogram is only about 1.12x faster at 15M white-noise points (6.138 s vs 6.903 s). The clustered table is power-diagram (weighted) construction, not plain Delaunay. Geogram is not the fastest CPU code in the comparison: HXT (Gmsh, already listed) took 2.259 s at 15M points, and the HXT paper reports a serial kernel about 3x faster than Geogram. The paper's purpose is a GPU method, with Geogram and CGAL as baselines. Geogram's own README and wiki pages carry no numbers.

name: igraph
baseline: NetworkX 2.4 (pure Python); SNAP 5.0.0 as a second row
workload: Median wall time of graph loading, single-source shortest path, PageRank (damping 0.85, tol 1e-3), k-core and strongly connected components on the SNAP datasets amazon0302, web-Google and soc-Pokec, through the Python bindings (python-igraph 0.8.2 against networkx 2.4, Python 3.8).
claimed_speedup: Median seconds, igraph vs NetworkX (Amazon / Google / Pokec), from runtime_results.png: PageRank 0.57 / 2.42 / 23.39 vs 8.59 / 33.5 / 239.75 (about 15x / 14x / 10x, derived from page data); k-core 0.15 / 0.92 / 5.99 vs 3.63 / 42.6 / 296.26 (about 24x / 46x / 49x, derived); strongly connected components 0.22 / 1.38 / 3.96 vs 2.22 / 7.77 / 61.74 (about 10x / 5.6x / 16x, derived); loading 0.57 / 3.87 / 25.75 vs 4.72 / 19.24 / 140.19 (about 8x / 5x / 5x, derived); shortest path 0.05 / 0.41 vs 1.37 / 3.41 on Amazon / Google (about 27x / 8x, derived). The Pokec shortest-path row (igraph 0.6 s vs NetworkX 5.65 s, SNAP 2.3 s) is not like-for-like: the igraph and SNAP scripts start from vertex 0 while the NetworkX script switches to node '1' for Pokec. Versus SNAP: loading 25.75 vs 52.73 s on Pokec (about 2x, derived); SNAP is faster on PageRank.
compiler_and_flags: not stated; python-igraph 0.8.2 installed as a conda-forge binary (setup/setup.md), Python 3.8
hardware: Google Compute n1-standard-16 (16 vCPU Haswell 2.3 GHz, 60 GB); exact CPU model not given
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars (igraph/igraph); widely used R, Python and Mathematica bindings
tradeoffs: GPL license (copyleft) limits embedding in permissive projects. The C core is called through wrappers (R, Python, Mathematica); the benchmark measures the Python binding, so interpreter overhead and type conversion are included.
caveats: Numbers are third-party (timlrx/graph-benchmarks, MIT, 85 stars, 2020) and appear only in the README image runtime_results.png; the linked timlrx.com blog post is egress-blocked here. The win is against pure-Python NetworkX, not a C or C++ library. In the same table igraph is slower than graph-tool, LightGraphs (Julia) and NetworKit on nearly every algorithm (Google PageRank 2.42 s vs 0.36 / 0.06 / 0.10 s; Pokec PageRank 23.39 s vs 1.1 / 0.21 / 0.24 s) and slower than SNAP on PageRank (Google 2.42 vs 2.31 s, Pokec 23.39 vs 8.62 s) and on Google shortest path (0.41 vs 0.26 s); only loading is faster than graph-tool and LightGraphs. Harness flaw on Pokec shortest path: networkx_profile.py starts at node '1' for Pokec (soc-pokec ids are not 0-based; download_data.sh only strips comment lines, no remapping), but igraph_profile.py runs g.shortest_paths([g.vs[0]]) and Graph.Read(format='edges') creates vertices 0..max id, so igraph's 0.6 s is a search from an isolated phantom vertex plus building a 1.6M-entry distance row, not a real traversal; snap_profile.py also asks for node 0. The Pokec shortest-path ratios (about 9x vs NetworkX, 0.6 vs 2.3 s vs SNAP) should not be cited. igraph returns a full 1 x N distance list while NetworkX returns a dict of reachable nodes. Versions are from 2020 (python-igraph 0.8.2 from conda-forge, networkx 2.4, SNAP 5.0.0 on Python 3.7); igraph has changed since. NetworkX loading uses read_edgelist into a DiGraph. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model are not stated, hence tier B not A. Medians over 100 runs (Amazon, Google) or 10 runs (Pokec); NetworkX was run fewer times (count not stated). The category graph-algorithms is a suggestion: the guessed sequence-containers does not fit.

name: klib khash (khash.h)
workload: udb2 micro-benchmark: count occurrences of N 32-bit integer keys (about 25% distinct) in a uint32-to-uint32 hash map, with identity hash for both tables, six rounds with N = 10M, 18M, 26M, 34M, 42M, 50M, so rehashing growth is included; reports CPU time and peak-RSS delta.
claimed_speedup: udb2 180929 server logs (khash/run-test.log vs c++11/run-test.log): at N=50M khash 5.460 s CPU and 172.457 MB versus std::unordered_map 22.220 s and 493.762 MB, about 4.1x less CPU time and 2.9x less memory (derived from log data); at N=10M 0.652 s versus 2.972 s (4.6x, derived). The run-test-1 pair is two different variants: khash/test-1.c stores a {key,count} struct in a khash set (no separate value array), 4.724 s / 136.742 MB, while c++11/test-1.cpp uses emplace, 22.872 s / 493.363 MB at N=50M (4.8x, derived). The later 191228-server.tgz run shows the same picture: khash 4.061 s / 171.488 MB versus std::unordered_map 17.211 s / 519.270 MB at N=50M (about 4.2x CPU, 3.0x memory, derived from log data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 5.4.0 per udb2 README for the server run; khash/Makefile builds with '$(CC) -O2 -Wall' and c++11/Makefile with '$(CXX) -O3 -Wall -std=c++11' (verified in the 2018 Makefile at commit 539d6d0, unchanged in substance since), so the baseline got the higher optimization level. libstdc++ is inferred from gcc on Linux, not stated.
hardware: Linux server, Xeon E5-2683 v3 2.0GHz, 35MB cache, 640GB memory (udb2 README)
tradeoffs: Single-header C macro library (KHASH_INIT instantiates types and functions per key/value type), so no templates, RAII, or iterator stability; open addressing with 32-bit bucket indices (khint_t), values stored in a separate array and relocated on resize; deletion leaves tombstones. Pointers or references into the table are invalidated by insertion. Keys and values must be trivially copyable plain types; custom types need hand-written hash and equality macros. The klib README also advertises kbtree.h (B-tree ordered map), ksort.h, and kvec.h, but no numeric comparison against std::map, std::sort, or std::vector was reachable here (their blog posts are on blocked wordpress).
caveats: The benchmark lives in a separate repo (attractivechaos/udb2, same author, 35 stars, no license file) and the numbers are inside the linked tgz (udb2-lynx-log/khash/run-test.log and c++11/run-test.log); the README itself shows only plots. The 180929 run is from 2018 with gcc 5.4.0 and an old libstdc++ (unordered_map's node-based design has not changed since). udb2 vendors khash.h 0.2.8, identical to klib's current khash.h apart from comments. Only 32-bit integer keys and values (keys pre-scrambled with hash32, then an identity hash in both tables), counting workload; says nothing about string keys or lookup-only loads; a deletion variant exists for khash in 191228-server.tgz but has no std::unordered_map counterpart. The timed loop also includes key generation (about 0.12 s over the 50M sequence, small). CPU time is getrusage user+sys, single run per N. The run-test-1 pair compares a khash set-of-struct variant against an emplace-based std::unordered_map, not like for like. The README's 'results vary with machines' warning applies: the Google Cloud n1-standard-1 run uses different hardware. udb2 also lists many other maps (absl, ska, tsl, robin_hood, unordered_dense, verstable, khashl and others), most of which beat khash on the 2023 runs; khash is far from the fastest option, only clearly faster than std::unordered_map.

name: uthash
workload: Third-party C/C++ hash-table benchmark (uthash v2.3.0 vs std::unordered_map among 15 tables): tables grown to 20,000,000 keys at max load factor 0.875 with a shared MurmurHash3-finalizer/FNV-1a hash, measuring insert, erase and replace of existing keys, erase and lookup of existing and nonexisting keys, and iteration, for three key/value shapes (32-bit/32-bit, 64-bit/448-bit, 16-char string/64-bit).
claimed_speedup: Article text: "uthash's iteration is about twice as fast as std::unordered_map's iteration (albeit still extremely slow)". Heatmap for 0-20M keys (total time relative to the fastest table, std::unordered_map vs uthash): iterate 87.83 vs 37.39 (32-bit keys), 24.67 vs 10.53 (64-bit key/448-bit value), 79.94 vs 30.64 (string keys), i.e. 2.3-2.6x (derived from page data); erase existing 11.26 vs 7.79, 9.84 vs 6.10, 3.21 vs 2.41, i.e. 1.3-1.6x (derived from page data); erase nonexisting 5.25 vs 3.72, 5.83 vs 3.91, 2.43 vs 1.93, i.e. 1.3-1.5x (derived from page data); lookup nonexisting 3.67 vs 3.22, 3.96 vs 3.24, 2.32 vs 1.83, i.e. 1.1-1.3x (derived from page data); insert 64-bit/448-bit 4.91 vs 4.11 and string 2.87 vs 2.61 (1.1-1.2x, derived from page data); string-key lookup existing 1.59 vs 1.38 and replace 1.52 vs 1.46 (1.04-1.15x, derived from page data). uthash is NOT faster for 32-bit-key insert (6.75 vs 6.39), 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit replace (3.80 vs 2.71, 2.90 vs 2.34), or 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit lookup of existing keys (2.58 vs 2.28, 2.45 vs 2.41).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, C++20, -O3 -DNDEBUG (README build line: g++ -I. -std=c++20 -static -O3 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wpedantic main.cpp)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, frequency locked at 90%
tradeoffs: Macro-based intrusive hash table: every item embeds a 56-byte UT_hash_handle (per the benchmark article), node-based separate chaining like std::unordered_map, rudimentary API with the user writing much of the scaffolding. By default keys are hashed and compared byte-by-byte, which is unsafe for structs with padding bytes. Pure C, single header, BSD-1-Clause.
caveats: The numbers are a third-party comparison; uthash's own repo carries no benchmarks and never claims to beat std::unordered_map. The article's author concludes uthash 'should be avoided due to all-around poor performance' (it is far slower than open-addressing tables) and says its comments about std::unordered_map's poor performance also apply to uthash; the win over std::unordered_map is mixed. Heatmap figures are totals over the 0-20M-key run normalized to the fastest table, and the ratios here are derived from them. In the 0-200,000-key run (docs/result_2024-05-28T04_06_21.csv) uthash is slower than std::unordered_map for most insert, lookup and replace cases (for example 32-bit lookup of existing keys at N=200,000: 35,300 vs 15,700 in the CSV's time units, 2.25x slower, derived from CSV data), while at N=200,000 its iteration is faster only for the 64-bit/448-bit and string keys (derived from CSV data). Benchmarked version is uthash v2.3.0; the repo is now at v2.4.0. Run on Windows with MinGW-w64, so libstdc++ behaviour (including std::unordered_map growth policy) is specific to that build. The published article lives on github.io, which was blocked here; the numbers were read from the article source docs/index.md in the benchmark repo.

name: libcuckoo (cuckoohash_map, efficient/libcuckoo)
workload: Concurrent multi-threaded insert/lookup/mixed workloads on 120M 8-byte-key/8-byte-value pairs (Figure 1, 4-core, 1:1 read:write) and large-scale insert/lookup throughput on a 16-core machine
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed (EuroSys'14): on a 16-core machine the design executes 'almost 40 million inserts and more than 70 million lookup operations per second'; Figure 1 (4-core, 120M keys, 1:1 read/write) places it well above the C++11 std::unordered_map bar, though no exact std::unordered_map multiplier is printed as text (only 'up to 2.5x' vs Intel TBB concurrent_hash_map is quoted numerically)
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (4-core Haswell) @ 3.4GHz, 32KB L1D / 256KB L2 / 8MB L3, 16GB DDR3 (main experiments); a separate 16-core machine is used for the headline ~40M insert/~70M lookup number
tradeoffs: Adds per-bucket spinlock/version-counter overhead irrelevant for single-threaded use; find() returns via out-parameter rather than iterator; requires locked_table() for safe bulk iteration; mainly wins when there is real concurrent contention, not necessarily in single-threaded use
caveats: The repo's universal-benchmark (tests/universal-benchmark) compiles only LIBCUCKOO, with no std::unordered_map baseline. The std comparison comes from the EuroSys'14 paper's Figures 1-2, where the multiplier is only visual. The only explicit numeric speedup ('up to 2.5x') is against other concurrent tables such as Intel TBB. The paper treats std::unordered_map as a single-writer table: Section 2.3 says such tables 'allow only one writer at a time', and Figure 2 runs it under a global lock or TSX lock elision. So the win shows multi-core scalability, not a faster single-threaded operation. The compiler, flags, and std library are not stated in the paper.
