name: Collections-C CC_HashTable (also CC_List, CC_Deque, CC_TreeTable)
baseline: std::unordered_map<int, void*> (also std::map, std::list, std::deque; the same run also compares GNOME glib 2.63.0 GHashTable/GTree/GList/GQueue and cdcontainers)
workload: Google Benchmark loops of N = 4 to 122,880 random-int operations on containers holding void* values: map insert, remove and search by key, iterator traversal; list push-front, push-back and insert-in-middle; deque push-front, push-back and insert at a random position. Each timed loop also calls a std::mt19937 random-number function per operation.
claimed_speedup: No ratios are written in the repo; it publishes SVG graphs only. Values read from the plotted points of those SVGs at N = 122,880 (derived from page data, approximate): CcHashTable vs std::unordered_map insert about 10.2 ms vs 49.4 ms (4.8x), remove 6.8 ms vs 24.9 ms (3.7x), search 8.1 ms vs 16.6 ms (2.0x), iterator traversal 2.2 ms vs 3.2 ms (1.5x); CcTreeTable vs std::map insert 44.5 ms vs 85.9 ms (1.9x), search 45.4 ms vs 84.3 ms (1.9x), traversal equal; CcList vs std::list push-back 5.1 ms vs 12.5 ms (2.4x), push-front 5.2 ms vs 12.3 ms (2.4x), insert-middle 5.8 ms vs 12.4 ms (2.2x); CcDeque vs std::deque push-back 4.6 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.3x), push-front 4.1 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.5x), random-position insert 337 ms vs 2560 ms (7.6x). CcTreeTable lookups are slower than std::unordered_map at large N (about 45 ms vs 17 ms for search), and glib's GHashTable beats CcHashTable on traversal and search.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. CMakeLists.txt defines Release flags '-O3 -flto -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti' (C: '-O3 -flto'), but run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so as published the benchmark binary (which instantiates the std containers) gets no -O flag, and Collections-C, built as an ExternalProject with the same empty build type, had only '-Wall -Werror' in its 2016-2019 CMakeLists.txt. Google Benchmark v1.5.0, glib 2.63.0, Collections-C pinned only to 'master' (late-2019 snapshot).
hardware: Quad-core Intel Core i7-7820HQ (3.9 GHz max), Linux 4.15.0-72-generic x86_64 (README 'Equipment' section)
tradeoffs: Generic containers store void* pointers (or sized variants), so there is no type safety and values need boxing or casting; the C library is LGPL-3.0 (library-linking terms apply). Insertion into CcHashTable and CcTreeTable needs a user hash and comparison function. Allocations use malloc per node like std::list and std::map.
caveats: Third-party but competing: the benchmark repo belongs to the author of the rival cdcontainers library (1 star, 17 commits, last updated 2019-12-27). Numbers exist only as matplotlib SVG graphs; the figures were recovered from the SVG point coordinates (re-checked: they match). Likely unoptimised build: run.sh sets no build type, and the per-operation times at N=122,880 (about 400 ns per std::unordered_map insert, 700 ns per std::map insert, 100 ns per std::list push_back, 135 ns per std::unordered_map lookup, derived from page data) are several times what optimised libstdc++ usually achieves, which is consistent with -O0 builds where header-only C++ templates lose far more than a precompiled C library; the speedups may largely measure that, so treat them as unreliable (inference, not proven). Insert, push-front, push-back and insert-middle loops call a std::mt19937 random function per operation; search, remove and traversal use a pre-shuffled vector instead. GetRandomPos constructs uniform_int_distribution<unsigned int> from SIZE_MAX, which narrows to a = b = UINT_MAX, so the deque 'random position' is always UINT_MAX % size (deterministic, but the same for every library). The std side stores int and the C side stores int cast to void*, with std::hash<int> as the C++ hash and cdc_hash_int for the C tables. Collections-C was built from an unpinned 'master' of December 2019 using the old unprefixed API (hashtable_add, deque_add_last); the library has since been renamed to the cc_ prefix, so the benchmark code does not build against current master and the numbers predate later changes. glib's GHashTable beats CcHashTable on search and traversal, and CcTreeTable is far slower than std::unordered_map for lookups. LGPL-3.0-or-later: static linking carries relinking obligations. No std::vector comparison exists.

name: CYBHash

claimed_speedup: README states 'approximately 10 times faster than std::unordered_map'; the repo's own GitHub description separately states 'approximately 5-30 times faster than std::unordered_map' -- the two first-party figures are inconsistent, and no benchmark script, raw numbers, or workload size is published.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++17 -mbmi2 -O3 -DNDEBUG (from the repo's test.sh; not stated as the configuration behind the README's 10x figure)
tradeoffs: Only applicable to a narrow, domain-specific key space (Chinese futures/stock/option ticker symbols that can be packed into an int64); it is closer to a specialized key-encoding trick than a general-purpose hash map, and has no license, so the code cannot legally be reused/copied (study-only).
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo, so all rights are reserved by default. The speedup claim differs between the README ('approximately 10 times') and the repo description ('approximately 5-30 times'). name: parallel-hashmap (phmap)
workload: Inserting up to 100 million key/value pairs (two 8-byte integers) into phmap::flat_hash_map vs std::unordered_map, per the project's online design writeup.
claimed_speedup: Writeup: "the Abseil flat_hash_map is significantly faster that the default stl implementation, typically about three times faster". That quote is literally about absl::flat_hash_map vs VS2017 std::unordered_map. phmap's own flat/parallel maps are graphed as nearly indistinguishable from it, and parallel_flat_hash_map is slightly slower for small tables and converges above ~80M values. Repo raw data (benchmark/results/output_stl_flat_par), 100M random inserts: std::unordered_map 48.38 s vs phmap::flat_hash_map 14.41 s vs phmap::parallel_flat_hash_map 14.47 s, ~3.4x (derived from repo data).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 MSVC (cl -EHsc -DNDEBUG -O2 per benchmark/Makefile), 64-bit, run from Cygwin
tradeoffs: flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set move keys and values in memory, so pointers/iterators are invalidated on mutation, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; node_hash_map avoids that at some speed/memory cost; the parallel_* variants add multithreading support and lower peak resize memory at the cost of being slightly slower for small tables. The author now steers new users to the C++20 successor repo 'gtl' (also by greg7mdp, not filed separately here since it shares the same design and no independent benchmark was found for it).
caveats: The '~3x faster' sentence in the writeup refers to Abseil's flat_hash_map, of which phmap is a header-only derivative. The phmap-vs-std number comes from the repo's raw results CSV and graphs, not from a sentence. No CPU model is stated anywhere, so it is capped at Tier C. The benchmark is insert-only with random 8-byte integer keys on MSVC 2017 STL only (no libstdc++/libc++). The results date from ~2019.

name: ska::flat_hash_map / ska::bytell_hash_map
workload: Successful/unsuccessful lookups, inserts (with/without reserve), erases, and mixed insert/erase sequences, on int and string keys with 4-, 32-, and 1024-byte values.

Tessil 2017 shootout raw CSV: flat_hash_map successful lookups 1.34-4.17x faster than std::unordered_map, inserts 0.84-3.18x. In his 2017 post the author claims 'I have the fastest lookups of any hashtable I could find', with results as graphs only.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 13, -O3 -march=native (Ankerl 2022)
hardware: Intel i7-8700 locked at 3200 MHz, Manjaro Linux (Ankerl 2022)
tradeoffs: Robin Hood hashing with a log2(n) probe-count cap bounds worst-case lookup but adds complexity; default policy uses prime sizing (max load factor 0.5), power-of-two policy available as an alternative.
caveats: The author's 2017 post is graph-only, states no compiler or hardware, and predates bytell_hash_map (added in a 2018 post). name: CPath

claimed_speedup: Wall time 0.082-0.083s for CPath (recursion/emplace, C and C++) vs 0.147s for `find`, 0.237s for Python os.walk, 0.284s for Cute Files, 0.294s for TinyDir, 0.626s for `tree`. name: reckless
workload: Caller-side log-call latency in four scenarios. (1) Single-threaded periodic calls that never fill the buffer. (2) A call burst that fills the buffer. (3) Disk I/O: 2048 log entries interleaved with writing 64 GiB of data. (4) A Mandelbrot computation that logs ~1M lines with 1-8 worker threads (total runtime over 100 runs, overhead vs no-op). Baselines are std::fstream (std::flush after each line) and fprintf (fflush after each call), plus spdlog, g3log and Boost.Log.
claimed_speedup: Relative average call latency (reckless = 1.00). Periodic calls: fstream 41.32, stdio 43.77, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42, g3log 78.19. Call burst: spdlog 1.93, fstream 2.36, stdio 2.55. Disk I/O: stdio 17.01, spdlog 23.82, fstream 5719.93. Mandelbrot overhead: single thread fstream 10.73, stdio 12.21, spdlog 9.21; 8 threads fstream 4.62, stdio 3.70. The page concludes: 'For low loads, the speed advantage over a simple fprintf can be a factor of 40.'
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 (stated on the benchmark page). The benchmarks are built with tup (benchmarks/Tupfile.lua + Tuprules.lua), which on Linux compiles with g++ -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 -Wall -Werror unless DEBUG=yes (then -O0). The page itself does not restate the flags.

name: mexce
baseline: native compiler-generated C++ code for the same expressions (statically compiled)
workload: Compile and evaluate a suite of 44,229 scalar math expressions at run time (SSE2 and x87 backends), average evaluation time per expression and total evaluation time, versus the same expressions compiled natively.
claimed_speedup: README table on GitHub Actions CI (Ubuntu runner, 44,229 expressions): average evaluation 6.0 ns for the SSE2 backend versus 7.0 ns for natively compiled code; total evaluation 27.2 ms versus 32.7 ms (1.20x, derived from page data); SSE2 plus fast-math 6.0 ns and 26.8 ms (1.22x, derived from page data); x87 backend 8.0 ns and 34.8 ms, slower than native (0.94x, derived from page data); average compile time 174 us per expression for SSE2 and 135 us for x87. README: the SSE2 backend 'performs on par with or faster than native compiler-generated code'.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark target built Release with -O3 -DNDEBUG (GCC and Clang) or /O2 (MSVC) per CMakeLists.txt; the README table does not say which compiler produced the numbers
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu runner (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only; the SSE2 backend calls libm for transcendentals, the x87 backend uses 80-bit internal precision with more exact results; runtime compile cost of 135 to 177 microseconds per expression; executable memory (mmap or VirtualAlloc) required; fast-math option changes NaN and Inf semantics; optional protected-expression mode needs libsodium.
caveats: First-party numbers from a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner with no CPU model; the CI matrix builds the benchmark with both GCC and Clang (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and the README does not say which produced the table. The table was written in commit cb358747 (2026-01-11, 'Add SSE2 scalar backend') and has not been re-measured since; the repository's own analysis/improvement_report.md (2026-06-10, a 35-agent analysis run) later found master bugs including B1, a miscompilation in emit_sse2_libm_binary_call where a binary libm call at virtual-stack depth 3 received (arg2, arg2) (logb(a, b + logb(2,x)) returned 2.321928 instead of 2.807355), B2 (the documented '>' operator threw at parse time), B3 (one leaked executable page per constant fold) and B4 (SSE4.1 roundsd emitted with no CPUID gate, so it crashes on pre-SSE4.1 CPUs); current mexce.h has the corrected B1 register move but still no CPUID check for roundsd. The averages are whole nanoseconds (6 versus 7 ns is a one-count difference), so the total-eval ratio of 1.20x is the more precise figure. Fairness: the native baseline is one static function per expression called through a function-pointer table and built with -O3 but no -march, -msse4.1 or -fno-math-errno flag, so the compiler cannot emit roundsd for floor/ceil/round/trunc while mexce does; part of the win may come from that ISA difference. The run_benchmarks target uses 100 iterations per expression with a median of 7 round-robin rounds. There is no comparison with other expression evaluators or JITs (exprtk, muparser, tinyexpr, asmjit-based evaluators), so the claim is parity with native code, not a win over a competitor. analysis/asmd_optimizer_benchmark_summary.csv (an earlier stage) lists avg_runtime_ns 11 to 12 against compiler_runtime_ns 10 to 11, i.e. slower than native then. analysis/performance_acceptance.md (GCC 13.3.0, Clang 18.1.3, MSVC 19.44) reports evaluate medians of 6.5 to 7.6 ns but compares only mexce commits against each other, not against native code. 6 stars, single author.

name: Coost co/log
workload: Time or write speed for continuously printing 1 million log lines, single thread against glog on four platforms, and 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads against spdlog on Linux and Windows.
claimed_speedup: vs glog (1 thread, 1 million logs, write speed): win2012 HDD 1.6MB/s vs 180MB/s (112.5x), win10 SSD 3.7MB/s vs 560MB/s (151.3x), mac SSD 17MB/s vs 450MB/s (26.4x), linux SSD 54MB/s vs 1023MB/s (18.9x). vs spdlog (seconds for 1 million logs): linux 1 thread 0.087235 vs 2.076172 (23.8x), 8 threads 0.302088 vs 3.963644 (13.1x); windows 1 thread 0.117704 vs 0.461156 (3.9x), 8 threads 0.406025 vs 1.417387 (3.5x).
hardware: Platforms named only as win2012 HDD, win10 SSD, mac SSD, linux SSD; CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: co/log is part of the coost base library (flags, coroutines, JSON, RPC, allocator in one package), so using it means pulling in coost's flag system and runtime; requires a C++17 compiler.
caveats: First-party README numbers only: no compiler, flags, library versions or CPU models. The benchmark/ directory (atomic, idgen, main, mem, rand, string, time, xtoa) has no log test; test/log.cc -perf times 1 million single-threaded log::info calls and reports separately the time to the in-memory cache and the time after log::close() flushes to file, and test/jbm.cc times co/json only (str() measured once, parse averaged over -n runs), so neither the glog, spdlog nor rapidjson side, nor the 2-8 thread runs, can be reproduced from the repo, and the README does not say whether co/log's figures are cache time or file time. co/log buffers and flushes asynchronously (per test/log.cc), while spdlog's configuration (sink, sync or async mode, version) is not stated, so the spdlog rows may compare async against sync logging. The glog rows are write speeds on different storage (HDD/SSD) and OS combinations. Coost also publishes co/json vs rapidjson (twitter.json minified, stringify/parse in microseconds: win 569/924 vs 2089/2495, mac 783/1097 vs 1289/1658, linux 468/764 vs 1359/1070, claimed 1.4-3.6x) with the same tier-C caveats. [retier] First-party numbers; the spdlog harness lives on the separate `benchmark` branch (benchmark/log_bm.cc, linked only from readme_cn.md). It times co/log's asynchronous in-memory path against spdlog 1.8.5 basic_logger_mt, a synchronous mutex file sink (not spdlog's async logger), and the Linux rows ran under WSL per benchmark/readme.md (spdlog 2.08 s on WSL vs 0.46 s native Windows), so the 13-24x over spdlog is mostly WSL file I/O plus async-vs-sync. Numbers predate the current API (old LOG<< / log::exit), the Windows row differs between the two READMEs, no glog harness exists anywhere, and json_bm.cc also times simdjson but the README omits those rows. co/log is lossy under overload (drops the oldest half of its buffer past max_log_buffer_size 32 MB; the benchmark never counts written lines), the logger thread starts only from the flag::parse hook, timestamps lag up to 128 ms, and it installs process-wide signal handlers. Also publishes co/json vs rapidjson (1.4-3.6x) with the same tier-C caveats.

name: Discount
workload: Convert an 11 MB Markdown file (Pro Git first edition sources concatenated across localizations) to HTML; wall time is the difference between running with the input and with no input, median of ten runs, in the cmark project's benchmark table.
claimed_speedup: discount 1.86 s vs Markdown.pl 2921.24 s (about 1570x faster, derived from page data); vs peg-markdown 5.45 s (about 2.9x faster, derived from page data); vs Python markdown 291.25 s (about 157x, derived from page data); vs PHP markdown 20.82 s (about 11x, derived from page data). In the same table cmark takes 0.36 s and sundown 0.34 s, both about 5x faster than discount.
hardware: 'ancient Thinkpad running Intel Core 2 Duo at 2GHz' (cmark benchmarks.md)
tradeoffs: Implements the original Markdown syntax (README: passes MarkdownTest_1.0, no CommonMark conformance claim) plus extensions; C library with command-line tools. Faster than scripting-language Markdown implementations but about 5x slower than cmark and sundown on the same input.
caveats: The numbers come from the cmark project's own benchmarks.md (tag 0.18), measured on an old Core 2 Duo laptop, not from Discount's repo, which has no benchmark. Discount version, compiler and flags are not stated; the benchmark driver is the public 'make bench' target in the cmark Makefile (time -p with and without input, median of ten runs) and the input is built from the public progit/progit repository. The cmark 0.13 table gave discount 1.705 s on the same input; Discount stayed in the table (1.85 s) through cmark 0.29.0 and was dropped at 0.30.0, when the table was re-run on an i9 MacBook Pro with only commonmark.js, cmark and md4c. The Markdown.pl figure (2921.24 s) is identical in every table from 0.13 to 0.29.0, so it was apparently measured once and carried over rather than re-run beside each Discount timing. Markdown.pl is a regex-based Perl reference implementation, so beating it is a weak result; Discount is not the fastest C Markdown library (sundown 0.34 s and cmark 0.36 s are about 5x faster in the same table, and hoedown 0.21 s in later tables). The measured Discount is a 2014-era release; the repo is now at 3.0.2.0.

name: ExprTk
baseline: muParser 2.2.4 (also FParser 4.5, TinyExpr, ATMSP, METL, MathExpr, MTParser, Lepton, muparserx)
workload: Evaluate pre-parsed expressions (parse once, evaluate many times) with variables a, b, c, x, y, z, w; each of 74 expressions in bench_expr.txt evaluated 5,000,000 times, ranked per expression, points summed.
claimed_speedup: README example summary (bench_expr.txt, 74 expressions, 5,000,000 iterations each): ExprTk (double) 901 points, score 100; muparser 2.2.4 517 points, score 37; FParser 4.5 584 points, score 43; TinyExpr 354 points, score 31; atmsp 1.0.4 530 points, score 38. Per-expression example: ExprTk 39.963 ns versus muparser 2.2.4 47.358 ns on '(a^2/sin(2*pi/b))-a/2' (about 1.18x, derived from page data). Score is the mean over expressions of (ExprTk time / parser time) x 100 per src/ParserBench.cpp, so score 100 versus 37 means muparser runs on average at 37% of ExprTk's per-expression speed, about 2.7x (derived from page data); the README itself only says the reference parser is ExprTk.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 1913 (Visual Studio 2017, toolset v141), Release|Win32 (32-bit) per math-parser-benchmark-project_msvc2017.vcxproj: Optimization MaxSpeed (/O2), InlineFunctionExpansion AnySuitable, IntrinsicFunctions, FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed, WholeProgramOptimization, FloatingPointModel Precise, NDEBUG, _SECURE_SCL=0 (flags are not printed in the results log; the vcxproj read is the current HEAD). The repo .pro file builds with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -fopenmp -O3.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W 0 @ 3.10GHz, 8 cores / 16 logical, L3 20480 KB
tradeoffs: Header-only (very large single header, long compile times), runtime parse into an expression tree with optional constant folding; supports scalars, vectors, strings, loops and user functions. Heavy template use hits compile time and binary size.
caveats: The shootout suite is maintained by ExprTk's own author, so it is first-party even though code, compiler, flags and CPU are public. Score is the arithmetic mean of per-expression time ratios against ExprTk (failed rounds count 0), so it is inflated by expressions ExprTk constant-folds or special-cases; single-expression gaps are much smaller (1.18x over muparser on the README example). The README summary is labelled an example and does not match the committed 2018 bench_expr.txt log (logs/shootout_20180421_00.zip, Shootout_20180420_182359.txt: ExprTk 885 points score 100, muparser 2.2.4 523 points score 38, FParser 4.5 score 43). In the same zip's bench_expr_complete.txt run (6617 expressions, 100000 iterations) ExprTk scores 100 versus muparser 2.2.4 score 28, FParser 4.5 32, TinyExpr 15, METL 42. muparserSSE (float, AsmJit JIT) out-scored ExprTk (double) on 5 of the 8 2018 logs (score 110 to 168) and won on points in bench_expr_complete (78987 versus 77945); it ranks lower elsewhere mainly because its float results fail the precision check. Several rival parsers are old versions bundled in the repo ('may contain outdated versions'; muparser 2.2.4 predates the 2.3 series), and the published runs are 32-bit MSVC only. Last-commit date is the year-stamped commit date from the GitHub commit feed (2025-01-01 is how the author dates commits). [retier] First-party suite (src/ParserBench.cpp, 32-bit MSVC 1913 runs only, logs stop in 2018): the score is a mean of time ratios inflated by constant-folded expressions; recounting the 2018 logs gives a per-expression median of 3.4x vs muparser 2.2.4 on bench_expr.txt (range 1.05-15.8x), 1.5x on random_with_functions and 4.1x on bench_expr_complete, with the best double rival (METL/FParser) at 1.2-2.5x. The harness hard-wires ExprTk as the correctness reference, so rivals that disagree are disqualified while ExprTk never can be, and ExprTk gets an extra untimed pass (double rivals barely affected; float builds, ExprTkFloat included, lose rows). muparserSSE (AsmJit JIT, float) won bench_expr_complete on points and was faster on 5,580 of the 6,198 expressions it passed. name: trigno_simd_cpp (SIMD trigonometric approximations, Goyal & Arora)
workload: 1000 random double-precision angles in [-1e6, 1e6] (fixed seed 2024873), each evaluated 1e5 times; wall-clock execution time of proposed piecewise SIMD sin/cos/tan vs inbuilt C++ std::sin/cos/tan
claimed_speedup: Mean speed-up ratio (std_time/observed_time) vs inbuilt: sin 5.49x, cos 5.52x, tan 4.44x
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++17 -mavx2 -mfma -O3 -march=native
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX (8 cores/16 threads, 3301 MHz max as reported), 2x16 GB (32 GB) DDR 3200 MHz, Windows 10 Home Single Language 64-bit
tradeoffs: Approximate (piecewise rational sin/cos with max relative error ~0.004; tan max absolute error ~0.27 near asymptotes vs 148+ for a degree-9 Taylor baseline); not IEEE correctly-rounded; internally uses a fast inverse-square-root (FISR) hack in place of sqrt/division; the published API is scalar (one angle in, one double out) even though the implementation uses AVX2/FMA internally, so real batched throughput may differ from the reported per-call microbenchmark
caveats: First-party arXiv preprint (cs.MS, Feb 2025), not peer-reviewed. The functions are low-accuracy approximations: the paper reports max abs error 1.5e-3 for sin/cos and 0.27 for tan (max rel error ~3.7e-3 to 6.4e-3), so they are not drop-in replacements for std::sin/cos/tan. The authors' own SIMD Taylor-5 variant was faster (5.83x sin). The benchmark times 1e5 repeated calls on the same single angle through a function pointer (scalar per-call latency, not array throughput). The toolchain is MinGW-w64 g++ on Windows (README: 'MinGW Makefiles'), so the libm under test is the Windows/MinGW CRT, not glibc. The paper calls the baseline 'inbuilt C++ functions' and the code passes ::sin/::cos/::tan. The repo has 7 stars.

name: Vc (SIMD Vector Classes)
baseline: Sequential reference loop that calls an out-of-line scalar kernel per element (kernel_reference.cpp is compiled as a separate translation unit without LTO, so the loop cannot be auto-vectorized) using std::exp, std::log and std::sqrt from <cmath> (GCC 5.3.0 libstdc++ forwarding to glibc libm), built with -O3 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma
workload: Euro-Par 2016 SIMD kernels run on one thread over 8192 doubles with AVX2 (SIMD width 4): simple (sqrt/log/exp wrapper), conditional math call, early return, nested branching, and while loop with varying trip count; the Vc 1.2.0 version (simd_class_vectorization) is compared with the sequential reference.
claimed_speedup: Third-party data (mean time per loop iteration, GCC 5.3.0, Haswell, 1 thread, SIMD width 4), Vc (simd_class_vectorization) vs sequential std:: reference, ratios derived from page data: simple EXP 7.8586e-09 s vs 2.477e-08 s (3.15x), simple LOG 8.14221e-09 vs 3.58324e-08 (4.40x), simple SQRT 6.41381e-09 vs 1.14677e-08 (1.79x); conditional_math_call EXP 2.27x, LOG 2.39x, SQRT 5.07x (3.3077e-09 vs 1.67538e-08); early_return EXP 2.87x, LOG 3.16x, SQRT 4.30x; nested_branching EXP 1.56x, LOG 1.64x, SQRT 2.19x; while_loop EXP 1.34x, LOG 1.62x, SQRT 0.78x (Vc slower: 5.97054e-08 vs 4.6563e-08). In the same logs plain OpenMP 4.x 'omp declare simd' (explicit_vectorization) reaches only 1.00-1.09x and is slower than Vc in all 15 cases, the paper's enhanced OpenMP version beats Vc in 8 of 15 cases, and hand-written AVX2 intrinsics (manual_vectorization) beat Vc in 12 of 15 cases (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GNU 5.3.0, Vc 1.2.0; makefile.gnu in flwende/simd_benchmarks: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++11 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -fopt-info-vec-optimized -mavx2 -mfma -D__AVX2__ -DBENCHMARK_FUNC_<F>_<F> -DSIMD_WIDTH_LOGICAL_REAL64=4 -DDEBUG, plus -DCONDITIONAL_CALL for all executables (notes.txt); Vc linked from $(VC_ROOT)/lib/libVc.a. The makefile and the data come from the same August 2016 commits (notes dated 2016-08-15, last commit 2016-08-16).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2680v3 (Haswell) at 1.9 GHz, Cray aprun with --p-state=1900000
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; packaged in Debian and Arch Linux and listed in CERN LCG
tradeoffs: Explicit SIMD value types (float_v, double_v) written into the code, so algorithms must be restructured for data parallelism; supports x86 SSE2 to AVX2 only (AVX-512, NEON and MIC support removed or never finished); the project is in maintenance mode and points users to std-simd (std::experimental::simd in GCC 11+ libstdc++).
caveats: Vc's own README and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the evidence is third-party data from the Euro-Par 2016 paper 'Portable SIMD Performance with OpenMP 4.x Compiler Directives' (Wende et al.), whose subject is OpenMP, not Vc. The baseline is a deliberately scalar loop: the reference kernel sits in a separate translation unit and is called once per element with std::exp/std::log/std::sqrt, so the gains measure 4-wide SIMD with Vc's vector math (and one call per 4 elements) against scalar libm with one call per element, not against an auto-vectorized loop. Vc is slower than the reference on while_loop SQRT (0.78x) and hand-written intrinsics beat Vc in 12 of 15 single-thread cases. Only single-thread width-4 GNU logs were read (threads12, SIMD width 8, Intel 16.0.3, Clang 3.9.0(pre), KNC and KNL logs not read). Arrays are small (n = 8192 doubles, cache-resident) and the -DCONDITIONAL_CALL build adds a per-element mask to every kernel. The HEAD build.gnu sets VC_AVAILABLE=no, so reproducing the Vc rows needs VC_AVAILABLE=yes and VC_ROOT set. The data is from Vc 1.2.0 (2016); Vc is now 1.4.x and its README says it is in maintenance mode and no longer actively developed (pull requests with bug fixes are still reviewed), recommending std::simd (experimental in GCC 11 libstdc++) instead. The Vc authors' own paper and Kretz's dissertation were unreachable (host blocked), so no first-party numbers were checked. The data repo has only 9 commits and 6 stars.

name: SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)
baseline: <cmath> (scalar libm, represented in the paper by FDLIBM as the reference scalar implementation)
workload: Reciprocal throughput (ns per call) of 256-bit vectorized double-precision SLEEF 3.4 (plus Vector-libm and Intel SVML) vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3. A single-threaded tight loop makes 10^10 calls over pre-generated, uniformly random arguments in each listed domain. The calling loop was compiled without optimization so calls are not elided (the libraries use their -O3 flags), and it is timed with clock_gettime.
claimed_speedup: Table 2, reciprocal throughput in ns per call, 1-ulp variants. SLEEF is the 256-bit AVX2 vectorized function (each call evaluates 4 doubles); FDLIBM 5.3 is scalar (1 value per call). sin [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x per call). cos [0,1e+100]: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x). tan [0,1e+100]: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x). log [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x). exp [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x). pow: 69.40 vs 55.53 (~1.25x). On the fast-path domain [0.4,0.5], scalar FDLIBM is FASTER per call (sin 4.927 vs 11.43, cos 11.42 vs 13.75, tan 7.819 vs 17.30), as it is for acos (12.07 vs 16.09) and atan (10.16 vs 22.12). Per element (dividing by 4 lanes), SLEEF is faster in every 1-ulp row. (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: SLEEF and FDLIBM compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma; Vector-libm compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize -ftree-vectorizer-verbose=1 -fno-math-errno; SVML via Intel C Compiler 19 with -fimf-max-error=1.0/4.0
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 CPU @ 3.40GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (physical PC, no VM)
tradeoffs: Vectorized code takes the slow path for a whole SIMD register if any lane needs it; library offers a 1-ULP and a faster 3.5-ULP accuracy tier as a speed/accuracy tradeoff; on narrow argument domains the scalar-equivalent speed roughly ties FDLIBM rather than beating it, the win is concentrated in wide-domain/branchy cases and true vector (multi-lane) throughput.
caveats: Table 2 compares SLEEF's 4-wide AVX2 vector functions against scalar FDLIBM. It is not a like-for-like scalar replacement of std::sin/std::exp: the gains need vectorized call sites, and SLEEF's scalar entry points are not in the table. Per call, FDLIBM beats vector SLEEF on narrow-domain sin/cos/tan and on acos/atan. FDLIBM is a reference libm, not glibc's libm or the libm behind libstdc++/libc++/MSVC <cmath>. The benchmark loop was built unoptimized for every library alike. The sleef.org benchmark page compares only against SVML. The Table 2 harness for FDLIBM is not in the repo.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "vectorized math library faster than std::exp std::sin benchmark C++" led to the SLEEF arXiv paper; repo confirmed via gh api repos/shibatch/sleef

verification.tier_reason: A peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TPDS vol. 31 no. 6, June 2020; arXiv 2001.09258) gives Table 2 reciprocal throughputs for SLEEF vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3, with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on an i7-6700 with Turbo off. The Table 2 harness is not published: SLEEF 3.4.0's src/libm-benchmarks has only SLEEF/SVML benches, not FDLIBM, and master no longer has that directory. So it is not A.
verification.notes: The record misread Table 2. Its 'narrow domain parity, sin 11.43 vs 11.41' pairs two SLEEF cells (the [0.4,0.5] and [0,6.28] rows); the actual FDLIBM value for narrow-domain sin is 4.927, so FDLIBM wins per call there. The record also hid that the comparison is SIMD-vs-scalar. The tier stays B; the verdict is downgrade because the claim needed substantive correction. The metadata (BSL-1.0, 853 stars, last commit 2025-12-25, active) is correct.

name: Axiom (C++ tensor library)
baseline: Eigen3 element-wise Array ops (A.array().sin()/cos()/exp()/log() on float32 MatrixXf)
workload: Element-wise unary math ops (exp, log, sqrt, sin, cos, tanh, abs, neg, relu, sigmoid) over a 4096x4096 tensor, GB/s throughput, vs Eigen3, PyTorch, NumPy
claimed_speedup: sin: 26.0 GB/s (Axiom) vs 11.0 GB/s (Eigen3), ~2.4x (derived from page data); cos: 25.2 vs 11.0, ~2.3x (derived); exp: 23.0 vs 16.4, ~1.4x (derived); log: 17.0 vs 13.1, ~1.3x (derived). Same table shows sqrt and tanh as SLOWER than Eigen3, so the win is op-specific, not universal
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the benchmark doc. The top-level CMakeLists.txt adds -O3 -DNDEBUG (+ -mcpu=apple-m1 on Apple arm64) for Release builds with Clang/GCC. The compiler version and the build type actually used are not stated.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (per README headline); the benchmark doc's own 'Test Environment' section only states 'Darwin 25.3.0, arm64'
tradeoffs: Not a std::-drop-in: NumPy/PyTorch-like whole-tensor API, no scalar single-value entry point; on macOS Axiom itself delegates BLAS-level and possibly vectorized-math work to Apple's Accelerate framework, so part of the win may reflect Accelerate/vForce vs Eigen's own vectorization rather than a novel Axiom algorithm; several unary ops (sqrt, tanh) are slower than Eigen3 in the same table
caveats: On macOS, Axiom's float32 sin/cos/exp/log/sqrt dispatch straight to Apple Accelerate vForce (vvsinf/vvcosf/vvexpf/vvlogf in src/backends/cpu/cpu_operations.cpp and vdsp.cpp). The measured win over Eigen3 is therefore Apple Accelerate's, not Axiom's own kernels. A code comment says Accelerate is internally parallelized, while the Eigen3 comparison binary does not link Accelerate. PyTorch beats Axiom on exp, log, sin, cos, sqrt and sigmoid in the same table. The benchmark is first-party and auto-generated (make benchmark, 2026-02-21). The doc's Test Environment gives only 'Darwin 25.3.0 arm64'. 'M4 Pro' appears only in the README matmul headline. The baseline is Eigen3, not std::transform+<cmath>.

name: FANN (Fast Artificial Neural Network Library)
baseline: Lightweight Neural Network (lwnn 0.6) and Jet's Neural Library (jneural 1.05)
workload: Execution time per connection (nanoseconds) for fully connected four-layer ANNs with equal layer sizes (doubling from 1 neuron; 128 neurons per layer is the headline case), each size executed continuously for 20 seconds, on an AMD Athlon XP 1600+ (1400 MHz) and on a 206 MHz StrongARM iPAQ H3600 without an FPU, from Steffen Nissen's 2003 FANN report.
claimed_speedup: AMD Athlon, four layers of 128 neurons: "the fann (thres) library is 238.583 times faster than the jneural library and the fann library is 164.388 times faster than the jneural library"; table: lwnn 4.007 ns per connection (127.074x jneural), jneural 509.138 ns, so standard fann is about 3.10 ns and about 1.29x faster than lwnn (derived from page data). At 512 neurons: fann 64.867x jneural (about 8.07 ns, derived) versus lwnn 8.662 ns and jneural 523.175 ns, so fann is about 1.07x lwnn (derived from page data). At 8 neurons lwnn (11.962 ns) is faster than standard fann per the text. iPAQ, 128 neurons: fann (fix) 188.134 ns per connection versus jneural 13,108.617 ns, "almost 70 times faster than the jneural library and more than 40 times faster than the lwnn library"; the 2.7x remark compares fann (fix) on the iPAQ with jneural on the Athlon. README: "up to 150 times faster execution than other libraries" (no baseline named).
compiler_and_flags: Same compiler and compile options for all three libraries per the report; compiler and flags not named on the page
hardware: AMD Athlon XP 1600+ (1400 MHz, 256 KB L2) and 206 MHz Intel StrongARM iPAQ H3600, both Linux
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; packaged in Debian, Fedora and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Multilayer perceptrons only (RPROP, Quickprop, batch, incremental, Cascade2), CPU only, no GPU or convolutions; fixed-point mode exists for FPU-less devices; cache-optimised layout. LGPL.
caveats: Author's own 2003 report, measured on 2003 hardware against two obscure libraries (jneural, lwnn); no comparison with any current ML library. The benchmark programs (performance.cc, benchmark.sh) are printed in the report's appendix B.3.3/B.3.4 but are not in the current repo (no benchmarks directory), and the compiler and flags are not named (only 'same compiler and the same compile-options'). Table values come from the LaTeX ALT text of image tables on the page (lwnn 4.007 ns and 127.074x, jneural 509.138 ns at 128 neurons; lwnn 8.662 ns, jneural 523.175 ns at 512). The 238.583x headline uses fann (thres), a threshold activation that does not compute the sigmoid, so it is not the same computation as the baselines; the like-for-like figure is 164.388x for standard fann. Against lwnn the win is small (about 1.3x at 128 neurons, about 1.07x at 512) and lwnn is faster at 8 neurons. The README '150 times' figure names no baseline.

name: FastMath C++ Library (fast_math_cpp)
baseline: <cmath> single-precision (float) overloads (std::sinh, std::tanh, std::atanh, std::atan2, std::pow, std::acos, std::log10, std::tan, std::exp, std::log, etc.), backed by glibc libm (sinhf, tanhf, ...)
workload: 1,000,000 scalar single-precision (float) calls per function across 28 function/domain combinations (trig, hyperbolic, exp/log family, pow, rounding). Each result is the best of 25 runs with the two implementations interleaved run by run. Benchmarked on x86_64 (GCC 11.4, WSL2) and Raspberry Pi 4 (GCC 12.2); the Pi column takes the minimum over two recorded runs. A batch/array API (1M elements per call) for sin/cos/sincos/atan2 is measured separately.
claimed_speedup: Scalar float calls vs std:: (glibc) at identical flags, x86_64 / Raspberry Pi 4. sinh 2.96x/3.94x, tanh 2.94x/3.91x, atanh 2.42x/2.49x, atan2 2.18x/1.63x, integer pow base^2 2.02x/4.54x, acos 1.76x/1.57x, log10 1.45x/2.20x, tan 1.44x/1.40x. 21 of 28 scalar measurements match or beat std on each platform. Slower cases: sincos [-2pi,2pi] 0.88x/0.63x, sin [-2pi,2pi] 1.03x/0.73x, cos [-2pi,2pi] 1.04x/0.82x, sincos [-pi,pi] 0.71x on the Pi, fractional pow 0.84x/0.90x. exp/log/log2/sqrt are 0.94x-1.01x because they forward to std. Batch API vs std loops: atan2 6.16x/3.48x, sincos vs std::sin+std::cos 3.84x/1.97x, sin 2.15-2.28x on x86 but only 0.98-1.06x (parity) on the Pi.
compiler_and_flags: Both library and baseline built with identical flags via the fast_math_bench target: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops
hardware: x86_64: WSL2 (Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2), GCC 11.4, CPU model not stated. Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72): Linux 6.12 aarch64, GCC 12.2.
tradeoffs: Header-only; several functions (exp, log, log2, sqrt) are deliberately thin wrappers over std:: because the author's own polynomial attempts could not beat glibc's table-based implementations; scalar sin/cos/sincos regress vs std on ARM for angles needing range reduction; author documents 5-10% run-to-run variance and treats anything under 1.1x as a tie.
caveats: The API is float-only, so the baseline is the float std:: overloads (glibc *f functions), not double precision. The x86 column ran under WSL2 with no stated CPU model. The README warns that run-to-run variance is 5-10% and that some Pi std-library rows moved up to ~70% between runs. The batch sin API is only at parity with std::sin on the Pi. Very small personal project (2 stars). The README is unusually open about parity and slower cases.

Cellular: AVX512 851, AVX2 1283, SSE4.1 2679, SSE2 2959 versus FastNoise 2979 and LibNoise 58125. Simplex: AVX512 129, AVX2 294 versus FastNoise 1194. Cubic SSE2 3516 versus FastNoise 2979 (slower). Versus LibNoise (derived from page data): Perlin 9.3x (AVX512), 4.2x (AVX2), 1.7x (SSE2); cellular 68x (AVX512), 45x (AVX2), 20x (SSE2). name: GLM (glm::mat4 add and multiply)
baseline: Eigen (Matrix4f, 2011 snapshot eigen-eigen-13a11181fc5a); CML 1.0.2 also measured
workload: Element-wise addition and multiplication of lists of 4x4 float matrices (10 matrices per call, call repeated 1,000,000 times per cell, so 10M matrix operations per cell), wall time with gettimeofday, on a 2011 MacBook Pro and a stock HTC Desire phone.
claimed_speedup: Android HTC Desire, milliseconds, lower is better. armeabi-v7a: GLM additions 1506 vs Eigen 2181 (1.45x, derived from page data), multiplications 2189 vs 5143 (2.35x, derived from page data). armeabi-v7a with NEON: additions 1407 vs 2145 (1.52x, derived from page data), multiplications 3108 vs 5113 (1.65x, derived from page data). Author: 'GLM is the fastest on the HTC Desire with both ABIs' (plain armeabi is a tie: additions 10256 vs 9944, multiplications 59008 vs 59460). Opposite result on the SSE x86 build: Eigen additions 30 vs GLM 76, multiplications 86 vs 400.
compiler_and_flags: GCC, version not stated. CMakeLists Release flags -g0 -O2 (README: all tests -O2 except the non-SSE laptop build, which is -O0); x86 build adds -msse2 -msse3 -mssse3 -msse4.1 -msse4.2 -fopenmp; Android builds (NDK android-9 platform) add -mfloat-abi=softfp -mfpu=neon.
hardware: i7 2.2 GHz early-2011 MacBook Pro (Mac OS X Lion); stock HTC Desire (Android 2.2) with a 1 GHz Qualcomm QSD8250
tradeoffs: Header-only, GLSL-style API; SIMD paths are opt-in through GLM_FORCE_* configuration and aligned types; no expression templates or lazy evaluation, so chained operations create temporaries. GLM is a graphics-oriented library and not a general linear-algebra package.
caveats: Weak and old evidence: a single hobbyist repo (42 stars, 15 commits, no licence shown) from 2011-2012 that vendors GLM 0.9.3.B, CML 1.0.2 and an Eigen 3 snapshot; current GLM 1.0.3 and Eigen 3.4+ behave differently. Only 4x4 float add and multiply were measured. On the tested Intel CPU with SSE, Eigen is 2.5x (additions) and 4.7x (multiplications) faster than GLM, and the author chose Eigen for that reason. The GLM win is on 2010 phone ARM cores (armeabi-v7a) and the plain armeabi column is a tie. The README's non-SSE laptop column is an -O0 build (GLM 2375/7337 vs Eigen 8065/22404) and is not a meaningful comparison. The README says 1 million matrices times 10 repeats but src/Driver.cpp runs 10 matrices times 1,000,000 repeats. The Eigen test matrices set only the diagonal (off-diagonals not initialised in the generator). Compiler and NDK versions not stated, no repeats or variance. Second source (not used for the numbers): RasterDuck/vectormathbench intermediate-benchmarks.md (AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows, compiler not stated, 17 stars, GPL-3.0; BENCHMARKS.md there is empty) shows GLM ahead of DirectXMath on some vector composites (SSE4.2 ns/op: complex operation 1 1.51 vs 3.20, perspective matrix construction 2.20 vs 14.60) but behind on matrix-matrix multiply (22.13 vs 4.70) and model-matrix construction (160.76 vs 41.89); its README concludes Realtime Math and DirectXMath are generally faster than GLM. GLM's own test/perf programs only compare its scalar and SIMD paths and publish no numbers; the GLM README has no benchmark section.

name: Klein
baseline: GLM (glm::quat multiplication; glm::dualquat converted with mat3x4_cast and applied to a glm::vec4), with RTM (Realtime Math) as a second reference
workload: Static llvm-mca analysis (100 iterations, dispatch width 6, Skylake model) of the compiled SSE assembly for two routines marked with mc_ruler MC_MEASURE regions in perf/klein_perf.cpp, perf/glm_perf.cpp and perf/rtm_perf.cpp: rotor (quaternion) composition and motor (dual-quaternion) application to a point; no run time is measured.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md llvm-mca totals per 100 iterations: rotor composition Klein 821 cycles / 2400 instructions vs GLM 1522 cycles / 5700 instructions (1.85x fewer cycles, derived from page data) vs RTM 824 cycles / 2300 instructions (parity); block reciprocal throughput 8.0 vs GLM 14.0 vs RTM 7.0. Motor application to a point: Klein 1831 cycles / 5900 instructions vs GLM dual-quat 5435 cycles / 14100 instructions (2.97x fewer cycles, derived from page data); block reciprocal throughput 13.5 vs 38.5. docs/index.md: 'Klein's performance is fully competitive with state of the art kinematic and math libraries built with traditional vector and quaternion formulations.'
compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. perf/CMakeLists.txt builds the analysed regions with mc_ruler (an llvm-mca harness that needs clang; version not stated) only in a Release build; the klein target adds -msse3; glm_perf.cpp uses GLM 0.9.9.7 (fetched by tag) with no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS or other GLM SIMD define and no -msse flag; RTM is fetched at origin/master.
hardware: No run-time hardware: llvm-mca static analysis with the Intel Skylake scheduling model (SKLPort0-7 resources, dispatch width 6) for every listing.
tradeoffs: Specialised to 3D projective geometric algebra P(R*_{3,0,1}) with SSE (SSE3 required, SSE4.1 optional) rather than a general vector library; SSE intrinsics only in this version (README requires an SSE3 processor). Points, lines, planes, rotors and motors share one algebra, so motors replace separate quaternion and dual-quaternion code.
caveats: The only numbers are first-party llvm-mca cycle estimates; docs/perf.md itself says llvm-mca 'cannot be used as a proxy for predicting performance'. No run-time measurements are published: perf/ is the mc_ruler harness that produces these llvm-mca reports, not a timing benchmark. The GLM baseline is scalar: glm_perf.cpp defines no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS (GLM 0.9.9.7) and gets no -msse flag, and its listings are movss-based with stack spills, so GLM's own SIMD path was not used. The GLM motor routine converts the dual quaternion with glm::mat3x4_cast on every call, which inflates its count against Klein's direct motor-point application. Against RTM, the best SIMD baseline, rotor composition is a tie (821 vs 824 cycles), and no RTM motor routine is given. Compiler version unstated (mc_ruler requires clang). The project site jeremyong.com/klein is blocked here; the docs were read from the repo's docs/ folder. Repo archived on 2024-08-02 with the README saying it was paused for lack of time. [retier] Evidence is llvm-mca static cycle estimates (Skylake model), not measured run time, from docs/perf.md. The GLM baseline is scalar (0.9.9.7, no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS; its SIMD quaternion multiply is commented out, so the rotor row is representative). name: libdivide
baseline: hardware integer division (compiler-emitted DIV/IDIV with a runtime divisor)
workload: Sum of quotients of an array of random numerators divided by one runtime divisor (benchmark default type u64; u16/s16/u32/s32/s64 selectable), timed for hardware division and for libdivide scalar, branchfree, vector and vector-branchfree dividers plus divider generation; minimum of 30 runs per divisor, with every libdivide result checked against the hardware quotient sum.
claimed_speedup: README: 'a speedup of up to 10x for 64-bit integer division and a speedup of up to 5x for 32-bit integer division', more with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON/SVE vectors. README sample output (integer type, CPU and compiler not stated; the benchmark's default type is u64): for divisor 1 (algo 0, no magic number) hardware divide 9.684 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.792 ns (12.2x, derived from page data) and vector 0.426 ns (22.7x, derived from page data); powers of two 2 and 4 (also algo 0) give 11.5 to 11.6x scalar and 21.3x vector (derived from page data); for divisors 3, 5 and 6 (algo 1, multiply-by-magic-number path) libdivide scalar 1.349 to 1.355 ns versus 9.074 to 9.078 ns (6.7x, derived from page data), vector 1.334 ns (6.8x, derived from page data) and branchfree 1.609 ns (5.6x, derived from page data). Author's 2021 blog (snippet only): Intel Xeon 8275CL, divisor 7, u64 hardware 6.998 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.891 ns (7.9x, derived) and AVX512 0.492 ns; u32 hardware 2.298 ns versus scalar 0.872 ns (2.6x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build by default (CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG on GCC/Clang) with -march=native when supported, -fno-lax-vector-conversions, and compiler auto-vectorization disabled for the benchmark target (-fno-tree-vectorize on GCC, -fno-vectorize on Clang, chosen by the C compiler's ID); compiler not stated for the README sample.
tradeoffs: Only pays off when the divisor is a runtime value reused many times (a hot loop); compilers already turn compile-time constant divisors into multiply and shift. Building a divider costs a few to a few tens of nanoseconds (the 'gener' column, 1.3 to 29 ns in the sample). Branchfree divider cannot take unsigned divisor 1 and uses more instructions; signed types are slower than unsigned; x86 64-bit vector division is much slower than 32-bit for lack of a vector multiply.
caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark program is public, but the README's sample output names no CPU, compiler or integer width, so it is tier C. The largest ratios in the sample (12.2x scalar, 22.7x vector) are for divisor 1 and powers of two, where libdivide reduces to a shift; ordinary divisors on the multiply path give about 6.7x scalar in the same sample, and the README sample omits algo 2 divisors (those needing the add step, such as 7), which the author's 2021 blog (snippet only, Xeon 8275CL) measured at 7.9x for u64 and 2.6x for u32. Generating a divider costs 29 ns for multiply-path divisors in the sample, about three hardware divides, so the divisor must be reused. The README's 90-cycle 64-bit divide latency describes older x86 parts; recent Intel and AMD cores and Apple M1 have much faster dividers (the author's own M1 benchmark post and a 2021 D-forum thread, snippet only, discuss this), so the 10x figure is likely smaller on current hardware (not measured here). The baseline is the compiler-emitted hardware divide for the built-in '/' operator with a runtime divisor, not a C++ library facility. An independent user report on an AMD Zen+ CPU (D forum, snippet only, unverified) gave u32 1.156 ns hardware versus 0.399 ns libdivide.

name: libfixmath
baseline: software single-precision float arithmetic (add, sub, mul, div) as compiled by avr-gcc for ATmega128 (avr-libc/libgcc soft-float; toolchain version unstated)
workload: Per-call cycle counts (min/avg/max) for Q16.16 fix16_add, fix16_sub, fix16_mul and fix16_div versus the same operation on C float, over generated test cases, on a simulated 8-bit AVR ATmega128 built with -O2 -DFIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT.
claimed_speedup: Average cycles from results-avr.ods (columns inferred as min/avg/max from benchmarks/interface.c print()): fix16_add 67 vs float add 135 (2.0x faster, derived from page data); fix16_sub 75 vs float sub 135 (1.8x faster, derived from page data). Not faster: fix16_mul 377 vs float mul 140 (2.7x slower, derived); fix16_div 637 vs float div 450 (1.4x slower, derived). The sheet also lists fix16_sqrt 706 and fix16_exp 3240 average cycles against float sqrtf/expf rows of 8 cycles, which are measurement artifacts and not a comparison. The README only states that the FIXMATH_FAST_SIN option 'runs at 159% the speed' of libfixmath's own accurate sine (self-comparison).
compiler_and_flags: avr-gcc -Wall -mmcu=atmega128 -std=gnu11 -O2 -DFIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT (from benchmarks/Makefile; gcc and avr-libc versions not stated). The Cortex-M3 target uses arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m3 -mthumb -O2 under QEMU, but no results file for it is committed.
hardware: Simulated ATmega128 in simulavrxx 1.0rc0 or newer (cycle counts from the simulator); no real hardware, host machine not stated.
tradeoffs: Q16.16 only (range about -32768 to 32767.99998, resolution 1/65536); optional lookup tables cost 32 KB for exp and 80 KB for trigonometry unless FIXMATH_NO_CACHE is defined; overflow checking and rounding are on by default and can be disabled by macros; sin/cos accuracy is about 2.1% (2.3% with the fast option).
caveats: Mixed result from the project's own spreadsheet: fixed point wins only add and subtract (about 2x) and loses multiply (2.7x slower) and divide (1.4x slower) to avr-libc/libgcc software float on this 8-bit target; only the add/sub rows support a 'faster' claim. The spreadsheet has no column headers (its embedded chart labels the columns only 'Sloupec C/D/E', Czech for 'Column C/D/E'); min/avg/max is inferred from benchmarks/interface.c print(), which the AVR build links. It states no avr-gcc, avr-libc or simulavr version. The timing harness has no compiler barriers: the float sqrtf and expf rows (8 cycles min/avg/max) show avr-gcc moved those libm calls out of the timed region, so no sqrt or exp comparison is valid; the add/sub/mul/div float rows (80-499 cycles) look like real soft-float calls. fix16_add/fix16_sub are timed as out-of-line calls with overflow checking (FIXMATH_NO_OVERFLOW unset); with that option they become static inline plain integer adds. The file was added by contributor maruncz in PR #33 (commit 0c88e55, merged 2021-05-03, ods metadata 2021-05-01), the same PR that fixed fix16_div failing unit tests under GCC >= 9 and an overflow corner case; whether the div row was measured before or after that fix is not stated, and fix16.c changed again on 2023-08-08 (FIXMATH_NO_HARD_DIVISION refactor), so the numbers may not match current code. The Makefile also has a Cortex-M3 QEMU target, but no ARM results are committed. A Wikipedia statement that libfixmath atan2 takes 26.3% of float time on a Cortex-M0 was seen only as a WebSearch snippet (en.wikipedia.org EGRESS_BLOCKED) with no benchmark code or source in the repo; unverified. Fixed point is compared only with float, not with another fixed-point library. The README FIXMATH_FAST_SIN '159% the speed' figure is a self-comparison. README says 'Not actively maintained, pull requests welcome' although commits landed 2026-02-04 and 2026-07-13 (fix16_asin/atan2 boundary cases, fix16_to_int overflow).

name: SIMD Everywhere
baseline: unvectorized (scalar) implementation of the same program (VVenC/VVdeC ported from x86 SSE/AVX to Arm)
workload: Fraunhofer HHI VVenC encoder and VVdeC decoder (H.266/VVC) whose x86 SSE/AVX intrinsics were translated to Arm Neon automatically through SIMDe, compared with the unvectorized build.
claimed_speedup: More than 200% performance gain over unvectorized code on Arm (search-result text of the Arm Community blog post 'Part 1: Porting to Arm Intrinsics with SIMDe'; snippet only). A separate arXiv paper (2309.16509, 'SIMD Everywhere Optimization from ARM NEON to RISC-V Vector Extensions', snippet only) reports 1.51x to 5.13x over the original SIMDe on XNNPACK for an RVV-enhanced SIMDe, which is a different baseline.
stars_or_usage: 3.1k stars; used by Bowtie 2, MMseqs2, OBS Studio, wabt, vvenc/vvdec, vectorscan, Firefox (WASM SIMD128 builds), plink2 and over 30 other projects listed on its wiki
tradeoffs: Header-only portable implementations of x86 (MMX to AVX-512), NEON, WASM SIMD128 and other intrinsic sets; use the native instruction when available, otherwise a fallback that depends on compiler auto-vectorization (README strongly recommends -O3 and OpenMP SIMD pragmas via -fopenmp-simd or SIMDE_ENABLE_OPENMP). Some fallbacks are slow on a given target and which of two code paths is faster varies by target (wiki FAQ), so porting needs per-target benchmarking. Intel's char-based signatures become int8_t, which can need minor source changes.

The baseline is the program's own scalar fallback, not one of the category baselines (std::valarray, std::transform, std::reduce, <cmath>), and the gain is that of SIMD vectorization rather than of SIMDe over another SIMD route; SIMDe's translation has overhead versus hand-written Neon (the AWS Graviton SIMD guide advises rewriting hot paths in native Neon after a SIMDe port, and Fraunhofer later hand-optimized VVdeC with arm_neon.h). name: GNU gperf
baseline: std::unordered_map<std::string_view, int> (std::hash in the perfect_hashing harness; boost::hash in the qlibs/mph README nanobench tables)
workload: qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness: random alphanumeric string keys (length 1-8 or exactly 8; 1-32 and 1-1024 keys) known at compile time, size x 100,000 lookups from a pre-built vector with 100%, 50% or 0% hits (misses are runs of '.'), total time per binary (median of 3 runs, checksums asserted equal across targets); gperf generated with %compare-strncmp, %language=C++, %enum, %readonly-tables, %global-table, %struct-type and --multiple-iterations=1. Secondary: the qlibs/mph README nanobench tables (5, 6 or 100 random-string keys, ns per lookup) and Kronuz/constexpr-phf's string-dispatch benchmark on Xapiand's 192 field-type names.
claimed_speedup: GNU gperf's own manual and README give no lookup numbers; all numbers are third-party. (1) qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness on an i7-12650H, plotted total time for size x 100,000 lookups, values read off the notebook's plots (derived from page data, about +/-0.01 s): 1024 string keys of length 1-8, all hits: std::unordered_map ~2.14 s vs gperf ~0.46 s, ~4.7x ('clang++-19' panel), ~2.06 s vs ~0.48 s, ~4.3x ('g++-13' panel), i.e. ~21 ns vs ~4.5 ns per lookup; 1024 keys of length exactly 8, all hits: ~1.58 s vs ~0.32 s, ~4.9x (~1.62 vs ~0.33 s in the other panel); 1024 keys of length 1-8, all misses: ~0.66 s vs ~0.11 s, ~6x (~0.70 vs ~0.11 s); 32 keys of length 1-8, all hits: ~0.052 s vs ~0.0125 s, ~4x ('clang++-19') and ~0.049 vs ~0.010 s, ~5x ('g++-13'). In the same harness mph is about 2-3x faster than gperf on hits (~0.15 s at 1024 keys), while gperf edges mph on 1024-key all-miss runs (~0.11 s vs ~0.13 s). (2) qlibs/mph README nanobench tables, ns/op gperf vs std::unordered_map (boost::hash): clang++: 5 keys len 4 7.70 vs 5.56 (gperf 1.38x slower), 5 len 8 7.70 vs 13.45 (1.75x faster), 6 len 2-5 7.94 vs 15.28 (1.92x), 100 len 8 8.04 vs 15.32 (1.91x), 100 len 1-8 13.06 vs 19.34 (1.48x); g++: 5 len 4 7.69 vs 5.29 (gperf 1.45x slower), 5 len 8 7.92 vs 13.36 (1.69x), 6 len 2-5 9.13 vs 17.56 (1.92x), 100 len 8 7.75 vs 15.01 (1.94x), 100 len 1-8 11.20 vs 25.35 (2.26x) (ratios derived from page data). (3) Kronuz/constexpr-phf README, 192 Xapiand field-type names: gperf 14 ns/op vs std::unordered_map 29 ns/op (2.07x, derived from page data) and std::set 82 ns/op; gperf is the fastest row there, ahead of constexpr-phf (18-21 ns).
compiler_and_flags: perfect_hashing harness: notebook CXXFLAGS -std=c++20 -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native, plus -fconstexpr-steps=1000000000 -ftemplate-depth=1024 from the Makefile; panels are labelled clang++-19 and g++-13, but the Makefile hard-codes CXX=clang++-18, which overrides the CXX environment variable the notebook passes, so both panels were most likely built with clang++-18; gperf version not stated (the Dockerfile does not install it). README tables: clang++ and g++ (versions not stated), -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mbmi2. constexpr-phf: GCC 11, -O3, x86_64.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12650H (notebook /proc/cpuinfo), pinned with taskset to logical CPU 1, Turbo Boost on, intel_pstate powersave governor (pyperf system tune output); the README tables state no CPU, and constexpr-phf says only x86_64.
stars_or_usage: GitHub mirror has 0 stars; used by the GNU C, GNU C++, GNU Pascal and GNU Java compilers and GNU indent to recognise reserved words (gperf README and manual)
tradeoffs: Build-time generator that emits C or C++ source (switch or table form) for a fixed keyword set; the generated code is not covered by the GPL (manual, 'The Copyright of the Output'), but the generator is GPL. Works on selected character positions, so it handles small and medium sets well; gsauthof/phashtable's README reports it does not terminate in a reasonable time on 1.4 million ISINs and gave a 10% table fill on smaller sets, and rurban/Perfect-Hash's README says it cannot deal with certain anagrams. Non-minimal tables by default.
caveats: All evidence is third-party and comes from competing perfect-hash libraries (qlibs/mph, Kronuz/constexpr-phf), both of which also show their own library beating gperf on hits. The perfect_hashing harness's compiler labels are unreliable (Makefile hard-codes clang++-18; identical binaries in both panels per the wave1-phf qlibs/mph record), the machine ran with turbo on and the powersave governor, the plots must be read off pixels, the 1024-key runs stream a size x 100,000 lookup vector (~100M string_views) so per-lookup times may sit near a memory floor, and the misses are runs of '.' that gperf rejects on length or its first table probe, so the all-miss rows are cheap rather than adversarial. In the README nanobench tables the std::unordered_map baseline uses boost::hash (benchmark/benchmark.cpp), the gperf output is pasted into lambdas and edited to return an index, and gperf loses to std::unordered_map on 5 four-character keys (1.4x slower with both compilers). The qlibs.github.io page carrying the same plots is blocked here; the notebook and its embedded plots were read through raw.githubusercontent.com. libstdc++ is inferred (Ubuntu jammy Docker image, no -stdlib flag). Schmidt's 1990 USENIX C++ paper 'GPERF: A Perfect Hash Function Generator' was not reachable. gperf's output is not under the GPL (manual section 'The Copyright of the Output'): generated tables take the licence of the keyword input, so the GPL-3.0-or-later licence covers the generator only. The repo URL is an unofficial GitHub mirror (0 stars) that stops at gperf 3.2 (last commit 2022-02-08); WebSearch snippets (snippet only) show upstream releases 3.2.1 and 3.3 (3.3 packaged by IPFire in a patch dated 2025-05-24, NEWS: gperf itself 2-2.5x faster), so the mirror lags GNU Savannah, which is blocked here. Not a minimal perfect hash for large key sets: gperf targets small keyword sets and its tables keep empty slots (e.g. 5 keys in an 8-slot table in the README harness).

The README's license line says MIT, but the LICENSE file, the GitHub sidebar and the src/ftoa.cpp header are Apache-2.0, so the license is recorded as Apache-2.0. The bench/ directory vendors third-party code (schubfach, ryu, dragonbox, fmt, yy, zmij, teju, uscale, jnum) under their own licenses; the library sources do not need it. std::to_chars is not benchmarked. Ryu (ulfjack d2s_buffered_n) stands in for it and prints its own exponent format (1.1E-6), so output formats differ across rows; the harness comment in bench/util/benchmark.cpp itself calls the comparison 'somewhat unfair' for this reason. Cycles are yybench tick counts scaled by cycles per tick, best of several runs, with each converter called through a function-pointer table, so only ratios are meaningful. In the newer result files (GCC 15.2.0 and Clang 21.1.6 on the 7840H, Apple clang 17 on M1), the xjb64_comp, yyjson and jnum rows sit at the null-function level in every dataset (about 8 cycles on x86, 3.0 on M1). bench/xjb/xjb_i.hpp and bench/yy/yy_i.hpp compile xjb64_comp and yyjson to a 'return buf' stub when USE_xjb_comp or use_yyjson is 0 (the yy header says it is set to 0 to cut compile time), so those rows did no work in those runs. jnum has no such stub, and its near-null value is unexplained. The cited xjb64 and ryu rows are unaffected, and the GCC 13.3.0 file (last updated 2025-12-20) has real values in every row. Results differ by compiler. With Clang 21.1.6 on the same CPU, xjb64 is 71.1 vs ryu 132.5 cycles (about 1.9x); with GCC 15.2.0 it is 55.7 vs 144.4 (about 2.6x) (derived from page data). The HTML result files predate later algorithm updates. The README's current charts (v1.5.0, 2026-04-13; icpx 2025.0.4 on the 7840H, Apple clang 21 on M1/M5) are SVGs only. PR #22 (2026-07-25, 'Fix buffer overflow') raised src/ftoa.cpp's documented output-buffer requirement from 33 to 34 bytes after a one-byte overrun for negative doubles with 16 integer digits in XJB_NO_MEMMOVE mode. Per the PR's file view, it also added a missing NEON store in to_ascii16 and debug-only bounds checks. Callers that sized buffers to the old 33-byte figure must update. The fix touched src/, not the bench copy that produced the cited numbers, and per the PR file view it does not change the release x86 conversion work, so the numbers are not treated as measured on code later fixed for a hot-path bug.

name: emio
workload: emio::scan with compile-time or runtime format strings (nothing, simple int, 64-bit int, hex) versus sscanf, run with Catch2 BENCHMARK in test/benchmark/bench_scan.cpp.
claimed_speedup: "Scanning on the other hand is around twice as fast then scanf." (docs/DESIGN.md, Performance section). Formatting is stated to be "round about 1.5 - 2 times slower than fmtlib" and "similar to printf (e.g. for integer types)".
tradeoffs: Targets bare-metal and RTOS embedded systems: no exceptions (returns emio::result), works without heap, about 5 kBytes versus 191 kBytes of flash for fmt on a one-line format (38 times smaller, per DESIGN.md). Supports fewer features than fmt. C++20 required (GCC 11-13, Clang 16-17 tested). Library is labelled beta.
caveats: Single first-party prose sentence in docs/DESIGN.md ('Scanning on the other hand is around twice as fast then scanf'); no result table, compiler, flags or CPU are given and no benchmark output is committed. The DESIGN.md points to 'the benchmark tests inside the CI': the CI matrix (GCC 11-13, Clang 16-19 on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners) runs ctest --verbose in both Debug and Release builds, so it is unknown which build or compiler the 2x figure came from, and the CI logs could not be opened here. In test/benchmark/bench_scan.cpp the sscanf cases are mislabelled 'snprintf'; the four cases are a 445-character literal-only format, a single-digit int, a 19-digit int64 and a 16-digit hex uint64, each with a compile-time and a runtime format string, and the claim does not say whether the runtime-format path (parsed sequentially, which DESIGN.md calls a performance overhead) is also 2x. The sscanf baseline is the C library (glibc on the CI runners), not a C++ standard library. Its own DESIGN.md says formatting is about 1.5-2x slower than fmtlib and similar to printf, so the speed win is scanning only; the headline win is binary size (about 5 kB vs 191 kB for fmt, 38x smaller). No independent measurement was found (one web search). [retier] One prose claim in DESIGN.md (scanning about 2x faster than sscanf) with no compiler, flags or CPU; the numbers exist only in CI logs (Debug and Release both run; the gcc-14/clang-19 matrix jobs have no install step, so they build with the runner's default compiler). bench_scan.cpp labels its sscanf rows 'snprintf' and its 'scan nothing' row times one memcmp against sscanf's whitespace-skipping format interpretation. Correctness: the overflow check in detail::parse_int (include/emio/reader.hpp) rejects only when value*base+digit wraps below the previous value, so '5000000000' scans into uint32_t as 705032704, '30000000000000000000' into uint64_t as 11553255926290448384 and hex '1FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF' as 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (about 75% of 10-digit values above UINT32_MAX accepted; signed paths hit overflow UB; unit tests try only max+1 and max*10); benchmark inputs are in range, so the measured rows are unchanged. No float scanning; formatting (Dragon4) is self-reported 1.5-2x slower than fmt.

workload: Seven scenarios from the FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6 test/performance programs, each formatting into a std::string per iteration with functional equivalents for the other libraries: (1) 'My name is {0} {1}; I am {2} years old; call me {0}' (cvu.ex.1); (2) name, int age, float height for five records (name_age_height); (3) one int from INT_MIN to INT_MAX (one_integer); (4) one pointer (one_pointer); (5) three strings with repeats (scenario1); (6) ten strings, including a 1000-char one, formatted twice (ten_strings_twice); (7) three strings and one int (three_strings_one_integer). claimed_speedup: Times relative to FastFormat.Format (above 1.0 means FastFormat.Format faster), averaged over five platform/compiler rows, scenarios 1-7: 'Streams (snprintf())' 1.49, 0.83, 1.15, 0.66, 1.63, 6.87, 1.64; IOStreams 3.28, 2.16, 5.08, 2.41, 2.82, 9.96, 2.86; Boost.Format 10.29, 5.18, 12.10, 5.57, 8.68, 17.27, 8.94; Loki.SafeFormat 2.28, 1.36, 2.03, 1.35, 2.17, 5.47, 2.16; FastFormat.Write 0.74, 0.84, 0.61, 0.81, 0.70, 0.88, 0.71. Page summary: faster than Streams by 15-580% except scenarios 2 and 4 (17% and 34% slower); faster than IOStreams by ~100-900% in all cases; faster than Boost.Format by ~400-1650%; FastFormat.Write is ~25% faster than FastFormat.Format and faster than all competitors except in scenarios 2 and 4. Headline: 5-17 times faster than Boost.Format, 1.5-5.5 times faster than Loki.SafeFormat.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.1, GCC 4.2, Visual C++ 6, Visual C++ 9; optimisation flags not stated
tradeoffs: Type-safe, no format-string parsing for the Write API; relies on the STLSoft and Pantheios-style support libraries and sink objects; Format (replacement-based, I18N friendly) is slower than Write (concatenation-based). Needs its own inserter functions for user types.
caveats: Author's own page from the 2008-2009 era (FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6; GCC 4.1/4.2, Visual C++ 6/9); no CPU, RAM, optimisation flags or date are given. The printf-family win comes from the MSVC CRT rows: on the two Ubuntu/GCC rows glibc snprintf beat FastFormat.Format in 11 of 14 cells (FastFormat.Format won only scenario 6 on both and scenario 3 on x86; derived from page data), and the page itself reports FastFormat.Format 17% and 34% slower than snprintf on average in scenarios 2 and 4. FastFormat.Write beat glibc snprintf in 10 of 14 GCC cells, losing scenarios 2 and 4 (derived from page data). The averages mix platforms and compilers. The current repo's harness (test/performance/*, updated February 2024) times ::sprintf into a 10001-char stack buffer followed by a std::string construction, while the page labels the column snprintf(). The IOStreams column is the C++ standard library (libstdc++ of GCC 4.1/4.2 and the Visual C++ 6/9 library), so the C++ comparison is direct but on toolchains that are 15+ years old. The ACCU Overload 91 article (June 2009) could not be opened (egress blocked); a web search snippet reports about 3x faster than printf-family, 6x faster than IOStreams and 17x faster than Boost.Format. Requires the header-only STLSoft 1.9.121+ library. The only commit since February 2024 is 'Boilerplate (#4)' (2026-08-04), so 'active' reflects project scaffolding, not new performance work.

name: S+ tree (Algorithmica static B-tree array layout)
baseline: std::lower_bound (primary), std::set (bench code binsearch/set.cc actually uses std::multiset), absl::btree
workload: Point/predecessor lookup over sorted arrays of 32-bit integers up to 2^25 (~33.5M) elements; reciprocal-throughput microbenchmark (batched independent queries) on an AMD Zen 2 CPU with Clang 10
claimed_speedup: Reciprocal throughput. The S+ tree is up to 15x faster than std::lower_bound; the S-tree variant is up to 8x (article). The repo README says ~15x over std::lower_bound for small cache-resident arrays and ~8x for large arrays (>1e6). The S+ tree is up to 30x faster than std::set on the same lower-bound queries, and the S+ tree with pointers is ~15x faster than Abseil's B-tree for large arrays (article). The article says the real-latency speedup is 'not that impressive'.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 10; binsearch/Makefile: clang++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native
hardware: AMD Zen 2 CPU
tradeoffs: Static structure: no insert/delete support without a full rebuild, so it is not a drop-in replacement for a mutable std::set; SIMD/AVX and layout choices are microarchitecture-tuned; requires branchless/permutation tricks that add code complexity
caveats: Headline speedups are reciprocal-throughput numbers from batches of independent queries; the author explicitly notes that single-query real latency (with data dependencies) shows a much smaller gain ('not that impressive'), so most of the win is instruction-level parallelism across queries rather than lower per-lookup latency; repository has no LICENSE file or stated license

name: libart (Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: red-black tree (the ART paper's own in-memory red-black-tree implementation, algorithmically what std::map/std::set are built on, but not literally libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map)
workload: single-threaded lookups of existing random 32-bit-integer keys in an index of 65K, 16M, and 256M keys, both dense and sparse key distributions (also a 12-thread/8-way-software-pipelined variant at 16M keys), from the ART paper's micro-benchmarks
claimed_speedup: From the ART paper's Fig. 10 (single-threaded lookups of random existing 32-bit keys; derived from page data: read off bar chart, approximate; measures the paper authors' ART, not libart): 65K keys: ART ~108M lookups/s dense, ~35M/s sparse vs red-black tree ~7.5M/s (~14x dense, ~4.7x sparse); 16M keys: ART ~20M/s dense, ~10.7M/s sparse vs RB ~1.2M/s (~17x / ~9x); 256M keys: ART ~10.1M/s dense, ~6.8M/s sparse vs RB ~0.65M/s (~15x / ~10x). The paper's chained hash table beats ART on sparse keys at every size; in Fig. 11 (16M keys, 12 threads, 8-way software pipelining) ART dense ~195M/s vs hash table ~132M/s, but ART sparse ~110M/s is slower than the hash table. The paper's 1.6-1.7x (ART) and 1.2x (HT) figures are speedups from software pipelining, not ART-vs-HT ratios.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.6 (optimization flags not stated in the text)
hardware: Intel Core i7 3930K, 6 cores/12 threads, 3.2GHz (3.8GHz turbo), 12MB shared L3 cache, 32GB quad-channel DDR3-1600 RAM, Linux 3.2 x86-64
stars_or_usage: 836 stars; the ART algorithm (the paper's implementation, not libart) was integrated into the HyPer main-memory database per the paper
tradeoffs: keys are limited to fixed-width binary-comparable encodings (signed integers, floats, and strings all need a transform to sort correctly bitwise); path compression and lazy expansion are required to bound worst-case space to ~52 bytes/key; libart (this repo) is an independent open-source C99 implementation of the paper's algorithm, not the authors' original benchmark artifact
caveats: libart has no benchmarks of its own (repo has only src/ and tests/); all numbers come from the ART paper (ICDE 2013), which measured the authors' own ART and own red-black tree ('two textbook data structures'), not libart and not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC std::map; values are read off bar charts; the paper removed path compression for the 32-bit-key micro-benchmarks; the paper's hash table beats ART on sparse keys; libart last commit 2021-02-11 (abandoned).

name: tlx::btree_map / btree_set / btree_multimap (STX B+Tree lineage)
workload: Random-integer multiset (and, in 2013, map/multimap) tests: insert-only, insert+find+erase, and find-only on pre-filled trees. n runs from 125 to 4,096,000, 32,768,000 or 65,536,000 depending on the run, doubling each step. Several B+ tree slot sizes (4-256) are tested against the libstdc++ red-black tree and hash tables.
claimed_speedup: 2007 run: for n > 1,024,000 items, the red-black tree (libstdc++ multiset) needs almost twice as much time as a B+ tree with 32 slots.
