name: Yomm2
baseline: C++ virtual member function call (closed dispatch via vtable)
metric: latency (average time per dispatched call, unit not stated on the page)
workload: Google Benchmark loop picking a random hierarchy out of 100, then a random object (or two for arity 2) out of 1000 per hierarchy with randomized allocation sizes, and calling one virtual function or the equivalent open method; ordinary-inheritance and virtual-inheritance variants.
claimed_speedup: Only the virtual_ptr rows beat the baseline. In docs/benchmarks/v010500.euclid.clang.md (clang 16.0.6, release build, 100 hierarchies of 1000 objects, run 2024-04-26), arity 1 with an ordinary base: virtual function 60.1, direct virtual ptr 10.5 (ratio 0.18), indirect virtual ptr 12.2 (0.20). Arity 2 with an ordinary base: virtual function 93.2, direct virtual ptr 19.4 (0.21), indirect 20.5 (0.22). That is about 5x lower time per call (derived from page data); the page gives no time unit. With virtual inheritance, the virtual_ptr rows are about 2.1x slower than the virtual function (arity 1: direct 156.9 vs 74.3; arity 2: 231.9 vs 107.3). Every other open-method row is slower than the virtual function: ratios 1.09-1.62 with an ordinary base and 2.05-2.47 with a virtual base. The Performance section of ORIGINAL-README.md says that dispatching a method with one virtual argument takes 15-30% more time than the equivalent virtual member function, and that virtual_ptr makes dispatch 'even faster - three instructions and two memory reads'.
compiler_and_flags: clang 16.0.6, build type release (CMake Release; exact flags not stated in the result file)
hardware: host 'euclid', '16 X 3300 MHZ CPUs' (CPU model not stated; cache sizes printed with implausible units: L1 Data 32768 KiB x2, L2 524288 KiB x2, L3 4194304 KiB x8)
stars_or_usage: 382 stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Open (non-intrusive) multi-methods for C++17 with multiple dispatch on several arguments, which virtual functions cannot do; needs class registration and a runtime update() call that builds dispatch tables (about 75K runtime). Plain-reference dispatch costs 9 instructions and 7 memory reads vs 2 and 2 for a virtual call; virtual_ptr is a fat pointer (extra pointer size) that carries the vptr. Dispatch through virtual bases needs a dynamic cast and is 2-5x slower than virtual functions.
caveats: Weak evidence of 'faster'. The repo was archived on 2026-03-04 and is superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90). The current README is a retirement notice saying YOMM2 'was' a library, and the original documentation now lives in ORIGINAL-README.md. The author's own text there says open methods are almost as fast as virtual functions and take 15-30% more time with plain references. The benchmark page shows ratios of 1.09-1.62 for every non-virtual_ptr row with an ordinary base (for example, arity 1: basic policy 80.4 vs virtual function 60.1), and 2.05-2.47 with a virtual base. The 0.18-0.22 ratios for virtual_ptr come from a layout effect in tests/benchmarks.cpp. The virtual_ptr rows copy a fat pointer, which already carries the vtable pointer, out of a contiguous vector (population::vptr_draw / ivptr_draw; the vectors are built during allocation, outside the timed loop). The virtual-function row dereferences a randomly chosen heap object (population::draw returns *objects[dist(rnd)]), so cache misses on the object dominate the baseline. In real code that touches the object, the gap would shrink. With virtual inheritance, virtual_ptr dispatch is about 2.1x slower than the virtual function. The result file gives no time unit, no compiler flags and no CPU model; its cache sizes are printed with implausible units (L1 Data 32768 KiB). The benchmark source excludes g++ ('Don't benchmark g++ until this is fixed', GCC bug 85282). The 'much faster than other implementations' claim in docs/articles/performance.md has no numbers. First-party measurement, so tier C. [retier] Project's own tests/benchmarks.cpp (Google Benchmark, no CPU model): ordinary open-method dispatch is 1.09-2.47x slower than virtual functions. The only faster rows (virtual_ptr 0.18-0.22x) copy prebuilt fat pointers from a contiguous vector and call empty overriders that never read the object, while the virtual-function row loads the vptr from one of 100,000 random heap objects and pays the cache miss; with a virtual base, where the object must be touched, virtual_ptr turns 2.1x slower. avg is the Google Benchmark mean minus a no-dispatch baseline (dev/bmutils.py); the odd cache sizes are byte counts printed as KiB; alloc_dist is declared but never used. Issue #36 (duplicate overrider crashes at call time). Archived 2026-03-04, superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90), whose docs claim no speed-up over virtual functions. No spec category fits; filed with the fat-pointer and delegate libraries under smart-pointers-and-refcount.

name: SimdQuickHeap
workload: MonotoneConstantSize workload, i64 keys, n=2^25: build heap via (push∘pop∘push)^n, then 10n interleaved pop/push operations with monotone-increasing keys, timed per element.
claimed_speedup: Table 1, MonotoneConstantSize, i64 keys, n=2^25: SimdQuickHeapAvx2 35.6 ns/elem and SimdQuickHeapAvx512 32.2 ns/elem vs Rust std BinaryHeap 439.6 ns/elem, i.e. ~12.3x and ~13.7x (derived from page data). At small n (2^10) the gap is small: 27.1 / 23.5 vs 27.4 ns/elem. Abstract: 1.2-1.7x as fast as the monotone radix heap (the next-best competitor) and 1.4-2.8x as fast as the superscalar sample queue (S3Q). The README says up to 10x faster than binary and d-ary heaps.

tradeoffs: The 12-13x figure is on a monotone-key workload engineered to be near-degenerate for comparison-based heaps; the general win over the next-best rival (S3Q) is a more modest 1.4-2.8x. Needs AVX2/AVX512 for full speed. No run against an actual GCC/Clang/MSVC std::priority_queue was performed -- only against Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap and several boost::heap variants.

The largest multiplier is against Rust's own BinaryHeap, not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC std::priority_queue (C++ std::priority_queue was not tested; Boost 4-ary heap was). The speedup is small while the heap fits in cache. It supports only i32/u32/i64/u64 keys, needs AVX2 or AVX-512, and the benchmarks need nightly Rust. The C++ bindings are LLM-generated. name: cpp_batched_random
workload: Fisher-Yates shuffle of std::vector<uint64_t> (10,000 and 1,000,000 elements) driven by std::mt19937_64. std::shuffle is compared with batched_random::shuffle_2, which draws two bounded indices from one 64-bit random word using multiplication-based, nearly-divisionless bounded generation.
claimed_speedup: vs std::shuffle with std::mt19937_64. Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 15 (libc++): 12.4 vs 2.4 ns/element at 10,000 elements and 12.0 vs 2.5 ns/element at 1,000,000 elements (~4.8-5.2x, derived from page data; the author says 'four to five times faster'). Linux, Intel CPU (model not stated), GCC 12 (libstdc++): 2.2 vs 1.7 ns/element at 10,000 and 3.5 vs 2.7 ns/element at 1,000,000 (~1.3x, derived from page data; the author says 'about 30% faster').
compiler_and_flags: Apple/LLVM 15 (M2 run); GCC 12 (Linux run); -std=c++17 -O3 per the linked benchmark Makefile
hardware: Apple M2 MacBook; Linux machine with an Intel processor whose model is not stated
tradeoffs: Only benefits shuffles driven by a 64-bit-output RNG (e.g. std::mt19937_64); speed advantage shrinks for very large arrays and grows for small/medium ones; adds an extra header dependency vs calling std::shuffle directly.
caveats: The blog numbers were measured with the 2024 prototype header (batched_random::shuffle_2 in lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog/2024/08/16), the direct predecessor of this repo (created 2025-09). They are not from this repo's current batched_random::shuffle. The gain depends on the standard library: ~4.8-5.2x against libc++ but only ~1.3x against libstdc++, which already uses Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded method. The peer-reviewed paper (arXiv:2408.06213, SPE 55(1) 2024) reports 1.4-4.7x (Xeon Gold 6338, LLVM 16) and 1.5-3.9x (Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 14). Those paper numbers compare a C implementation against the authors' own unbatched C Fisher-Yates that already uses an efficient bounded-integer method, not against std::shuffle. The header requires a 64-bit URBG and uses static_assert to check it. The repo is dual-licensed MIT and Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception.

workload: Single-chip raw random byte-stream generation throughput (GB/s) and cycles-per-byte, counter-based generators (Philox, Threefry, ARS) vs conventional PRNGs including the C++0x std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: ARS-7 (AES-NI hardware-accelerated): 11.1 GB/s vs std::mt19937_64: 6.1 GB/s (~1.8x, derived from page data) on the Intel CPU tested; Threefry-4x64-20 (no special hardware needed): 6.4 GB/s vs 6.1 GB/s (~1.05x, derived from page data, i.e. only marginally faster without AES-NI)

caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Salmon, Moraes, Dror & Shaw, 'Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1,2,3', SC11) with a benchmark table (Table 2) that states CPU model and compiler but not flags. The hardware dates from 2011 (Westmere Xeon X5667). On the CPU, only the AES-NI generators (ARS-5 17.8 GB/s, ARS-7 11.1 GB/s) and Threefry-4x64-12 (11.2 GB/s) clearly beat std::mt19937_64 (6.1 GB/s). The recommended portable Threefry-4x64-20 is roughly a tie (6.4 GB/s), and the Philox variants are slower on the CPU (for example Philox4x32-10 at 3.4 GB/s and Philox4x64-10 at 3.9 GB/s). The large wins in the paper are on GPUs, where there is no C++ std baseline. GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is standard BSD-3-Clause text.

workload: 5-10 billion-iteration tight loop generating random bytes summed into an anti-optimizer accumulator, timed with QueryPerformanceCounter, CPU clock locked to remove turbo-boost noise.
claimed_speedup: 27.45 GB/s (single-stream) / 34.35 GB/s (dual-stream) for AESRand vs 0.858 GB/s for std::mt19937 (~32x / ~40x throughput; derived from page data in BenchmarkResults.md); on a cycles-per-iteration basis, 3.69 cycles/iter (32 bytes/iter) vs mt19937's 14.76 cycles/iter (4 bytes/iter), ~4x fewer cycles per call (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (toolset v141, Windows build); the build configuration used for the benchmark is not stated. The repo's Release|x64 config sets MaxSpeed (/O2), intrinsics, whole-program optimization, and AVX2.

name: TRE
baseline: PCRE2 interpreted pcre2_match, no JIT (page labels it PCRE2 10.10; the published harness tarball bundles PCRE2 10.20-RC1)
workload: Find all non-overlapping matches of 15 regex patterns over the ~20 MB Mark Twain e-book mtent12.txt (carriage returns converted to newlines), restarting each search at the previous match end; best of 5 runs per engine, wall time in ms, engines built with default options. The HTML output prints only times, so match counts per engine are not shown on the page.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, not a project claim. x86-64 Linux, Intel Xeon 2.67GHz: TRE 0.8.0 beats interpreted PCRE2 on [a-zA-Z]+ing (954 ms vs 1373 ms, 1.44x, derived from page data) and .{0,2}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) (3425 ms vs 5164 ms, 1.51x, derived from page data) and ties on .{2,4}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) (5248 ms vs 5298 ms). x86-32 Linux run: 892 ms vs 1740 ms (1.95x), 3641 ms vs 6726 ms (1.85x), 5700 ms vs 7107 ms (1.25x), all derived from page data. x86-64 Windows, Intel Core i5 3.2GHz: 567 ms vs 773 ms (1.36x) and 2170 ms vs 2970 ms (1.37x), derived from page data, but slower on .{2,4}(...) (3298 ms vs 2965 ms). On the remaining 12 of 15 patterns (13 of 15 on Windows) TRE is slower than interpreted PCRE2, by up to 97x on Twain (486 ms vs 5 ms, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.2 (Linux runs) / GCC 4.4.7 (Windows run). The page states only -O3; the harness MakeGlobals sets CFLAGS = -g -O3 -Wall, which the tre/ and pcre2/ sub-Makefiles include, so both engine libraries and the driver are built with -g -O3 -Wall. Bundled TRE 0.8.0 config: TRE_WCHAR and TRE_MULTIBYTE on, TRE_APPROX off; bundled PCRE2 10.20-RC1 with SUPPORT_UNICODE and SUPPORT_JIT. TRE called via tre_regcomp(REG_EXTENDED|REG_NEWLINE) and tre_regnexec; PCRE2 via pcre2_compile(PCRE2_MULTILINE, newline ANYCRLF) and pcre2_match.
hardware: Intel Xeon 2.67GHz (Linux, 64-bit and 32-bit runs); Intel Core i5 3.2GHz (Windows); exact CPU SKU not stated
tradeoffs: POSIX leftmost-longest matching with correct submatches, approximate (agrep-style) matching, wide-char and binary-safe APIs, thread safe, regexec does not allocate from the heap (README). No Perl-style backtracking semantics, so results can differ from PCRE2 on alternation; backreferences are exponential.
caveats: The evidence is a third-party comparison page by the author of the PCRE2 sljit JIT (Zoltan Herczeg, page last modified 2015-08-23), not a TRE claim, and TRE is not faster overall: it loses to interpreted PCRE2 on 12 of 15 patterns (up to 97x on Twain, 486 ms vs 5 ms), to PCRE2-JIT by up to 964x ([a-q][^u-z]{13}x, 1928 ms vs 2 ms) and to RE2 by up to 162x (Twain, 486 ms vs 3 ms), all derived from page data. Its wins come on patterns where the PCRE2 backtracker gets no start-of-match optimisation ([a-zA-Z]+ing, .{0,2}(alternation)); .{2,4}(alternation) is a 1 percent tie on x86-64 Linux and a loss on Windows. Against pcre2_dfa_match TRE wins 7 of 15 patterns on x86-64 Linux, but DFA mode is not the default. Versions are from 2015 (TRE 0.8.0; the page says PCRE2 10.10 while the published harness bundles PCRE2 10.20-RC1); current TRE and PCRE2 were not measured. Engines were not tuned (default options). PCRE2 uses leftmost-first Perl semantics and TRE leftmost-longest POSIX semantics, and the harness does not print match counts, so equal work per engine is not demonstrated. CPU is given only as 'Intel Xeon 2.67GHz' with no model number. Heng Li's regex benchmark (lh3lh3.users.sourceforge.net/reb.shtml) reportedly shows TRE third on alternation patterns but was not opened, so it is not used. [retier] Not faster overall: wins 2-3 of 15 patterns vs interpreted PCRE2 (1.44x, 1.51x), loses up to 97x and up to 964x vs PCRE2-JIT. Harness compiles TRE with REG_NEWLINE, so [^u-z] and [^"'] rows stop at newlines unlike PCRE2/RE2/Oniguruma (the RE2 win on [a-q][^u-z]{13}x is not like for like); match counts dropped from the HTML. 2015 versions, CPU only 'Xeon 2.67GHz', POSIX vs Perl semantics. Open #143 heap OOB read in tre_regaexecb, #101 REG_NOTBOL bug.

name: Unformat
workload: Parsing 'Harry is 18 years old and weighs 67.8 kilograms' against '{} is {} years old and weighs {} {}' into string_view, int, float and string_view, timed with Google Benchmark (unformat_benchmark.cpp). The std::regex leg uses regex_search with a 4-group pattern, then stoi/stof and std::string copies. The README usage example '{} is {} years old.' is not the benchmarked input.
claimed_speedup: Unformat: 32.6 ns (11.5 ns using the compile-time constexpr make_format path) vs std::regex (StdRegex in the benchmark): 3269 ns -- roughly 100x-284x faster; the project's own description claims 'up to 300x faster than std::regex'.
hardware: 32 x 2420 MHz CPUs (exact CPU model and OS not stated)
tradeoffs: Not a general regex engine -- only handles fixed brace-delimited '{}' format-string extraction of basic types (similar to a type-safe scanf), with no wildcards, character classes, alternation, or quantifiers, so it cannot replace std::regex for general pattern matching; the win mainly reflects avoiding std::regex's NFA-compilation/allocation overhead for a task regex is overkill for.
caveats: The StdRegex benchmark constructs (compiles) std::regex inside the timed loop on every iteration, so the 3269 ns includes pattern compilation plus std::string/stoi/stof conversions. That inflates the gap versus a precompiled regex, and the '300x' claim should be read with this in mind. The README does not state the compiler, optimization flags or OS (only 32 x 2420 MHz CPUs). The same run also shows std::stringstream at 391 ns and sscanf at 677 ns. This is typed parsing of a fixed format, narrower than general regex matching.

name: ankerl::svector (martinus/svector)
workload: Small-vector micro-benchmarks with nanobench, one container per process, median of 9 processes: building 7 inline elements, push_back, emplace_back and insert of std::string, random access, swap, shuffle and sort of 1000 std::string; also object size (sizeof 8 bytes holding 7 inline uint8_t).
claimed_speedup: Build 7 inline elements: 1.26 ns per element vs std::vector 3.85 ns (about 3.1x, derived from page data); insert at front of std::string vector 1320.2 ns vs 1415.2 ns (about 7%); shuffle plus sort of 1000 std::string 31305 ns vs 35435 ns (12%, the only gap the README says exceeds run-to-run noise); emplace_back std::string 22.64 ns vs 23.52 ns (within noise). Slower than std::vector at push_back uint8_t (0.66 vs 0.30 ns, 2.2x), random operator[] (0.67 vs 0.57 ns) and swap of 7 inline uint64_t (2.15 vs 1.66 ns). Object size 8 bytes with 7 inline uint8_t vs 24 bytes with none for std::vector.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1.1, -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG, boost 1.90.0, abseil 20260107.1; meson release build
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, pinned to one core with taskset
tradeoffs: Tagged-pointer design: one byte of overhead, 7 inline bytes in an 8-byte object, at most 127 inline elements, little-endian targets only, no fancy-pointer allocators, move is noexcept only when the element move is, insert of several elements gives only the basic guarantee. Every operation branches on direct or indirect mode, which costs instructions on bookkeeping-only operations. Swap is element-wise for inline storage, not three pointer exchanges.
caveats: The win over std::vector is concentrated in workloads that stay inside the inline storage (std::vector must allocate) and in std::string element work; on pure bookkeeping with trivially copyable elements svector loses to std::vector (push_back 2.2x slower, subscript about 18% slower, swap slower) and loses to absl::InlinedVector at filling inline storage (0.48 ns per element). Several differences are inside the stated run-to-run spread (under 3%, about 6-7% for std::string workloads): the bolded emplace_back std::string win (22.64 vs 23.52 ns, 3.9%) and the insert-at-front std::string win (1320.2 vs 1415.2 ns, 6.7%) are within or at the edge of that spread even though the README bolds them; only build-7-inline (3.1x) and shuffle+sort (12%) clearly exceed it. The last commit date is a dependabot bump; the last functional commit is 2026-08-05. libstdc++ is implied by gcc (test/bench/solo.cpp comments refer to libstdc++ string swapping), not stated as a version. Young container maintained by one person. [retier] Own harness (test/bench/solo.cpp, gcc 16.1.1 -O3, Ryzen 9 7950X): wins only inline-storage and string work. The headline 3.1x build-7-inline row is against a std::vector that is never reserved (it starts empty and reallocates at 1/2/4/8, 4 mallocs per vector; no reserve(7) baseline is measured), and the 12% shuffle+sort lead runs std::sort on raw storage, so the container design does not explain it; the two bolded wins (emplace_back string 3.9%, insert-front string 6.7%) sit inside the stated ~7% noise. Slower than std::vector on push_back (2.2x), subscript (18%) and swap. v1.0.x had data-corruption bugs fixed in v1.1.0 (2026-07-28): push_back(v[0]) segfault #50, erase(it,it) and empty-range insert blanking elements #65/#66, double destroy #68; Conan Center still lists only 1.0.2 and 1.0.3. The 1-byte overhead holds only for 1-byte T (8 bytes when alignof(T) is 8).

name: plf::colony (plf::hive)
workload: Independent microbenchmark suite (fill/back-insertion, linear search, random insert, randomized iterate-and-erase at 1%/50% erasure probability, sort, destruction) across element sizes from 8B to 4096B on GCC/libstdc++.
claimed_speedup: "three orders of magnitude faster than the vector and deque" at 1% iterate-and-erase with 1024B elements; "the colony in this case is about 361'143 times faster than the vector!" at 50% erasure, largest configuration (verbatim from post). For fill/back-insertion of 8B elements the post says "almost three times slower is the colony" vs vector-with-reserve (32B: "almost the same with less margin"). Linear search: colony "even 50% slower than the list container".
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.9.4, -std=c++11 -march=native -O2
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 @ 3.4GHz, Gentoo Linux
tradeoffs: Unordered container: element insertion order is not preserved and elements are not indexable by position like vector's operator[]; higher per-element memory overhead (skip-field metadata) than vector; key advantage is that erase() never invalidates other iterators/pointers/references (unlike vector/deque), which is what makes bulk random erasure O(1) per element instead of O(n).
caveats: Benchmark dated 2017 on GCC 4.9.4 (dated compiler); the headline 361,143x figure is specific to a 50%-random-erasure iterate/erase workload on large (multi-KB) elements at whatever container size the author's graph reached, and reflects colony's O(1) erase vs. vector/deque's O(n) erase-and-shift -- an asymptotic-complexity artifact, not a representative 'typical workload' multiplier; for simple sequential fill of small/medium elements the same post reports colony as slower than std::vector. Only libstdc++ (GCC) was exercised in this post, not libc++ or MSVC STL. The library's own site (plflib.org/colony.htm, colony v6.11, GCC 9.2 x64, Intel Xeon E3-1241 Haswell, -O2 -march=native, benchmark source in the colony downloads section) shows qualitatively consistent rankings (colony/list leading insertion and erasure, vector leading iteration) but presents numbers as graph images rather than machine-readable text, so it was used only as corroboration, not the primary citation. The library has since been forked/renamed to plf::hive (github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_hive, 179 stars, also active) to track the pending std::hive standardization proposal (P0447); both repos are maintained in parallel by the same author and the cited benchmark evidence applies to both implementations.
found_via: Blogs / talks (CppCon, C++Now, Meeting C++, C++ on Sea, personal engineering blogs): HN Algolia search for "plf colony container" surfaced Baptiste Wicht's blog post "C++ Containers Benchmark: vector/list/deque and plf::colony" (baptiste-wicht.com, May 2017), cross-checked against plflib.org/colony.htm.

name: CTL (C Container Template Library)
baseline: libstdc++ containers (std::vector, std::list, std::deque, std::set, std::unordered_set, std::string) from g++ 10.2.1
workload: tests/perf microbenchmarks with int elements, sizes up to about 25,000: push_back, pop_back, push_front, iterate, sort, insert, erase and clear per container, plus a compile-time and memory bar chart of the C11 build against the C++ STL build.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no ratio in text; its log-scale PNG plots show CTL as solid lines and the STL as dotted lines. Read off the plots at about 25k int elements (approximate, derived from page data): CTL roughly equal to the STL for vector, list, forward_list, set, unordered_set and priority_queue push/insert, erase and iterate, and for deque push_back and iterate; wins are str push_back about 3-4x faster than std::string push_back (about 16 us vs 60 us), priority_queue top about 7x faster (about 8 us vs 60 us for an O(1) operation) and unordered_set erase about 1.3x faster; losses are deque pop_back and pop_front about 3-4x slower (about 60 us vs 17 us), vector sort about 1.5x, deque sort about 2x, forward_list sort about 1.2x and string sort about 35x slower. The compile chart labels CTL 'tests/perf/perf_compile_c11.c' 60.12 KB and 117752k RSS against 'perf_compile_cc.cc' 43.944 KB and 153612k RSS (about 23% less compiler memory, derived from page data), with both bars at about 1.7 s.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 10.2.1 20201125 (Red Hat 10.2.1-9), -O3 -march=native (from the plot titles)
tradeoffs: Header-only macro-templated containers for C99/C11 (one include per element type), 24 container types, fat bounds-checked iterators, default max_size of 2^32 bytes and anti-DoS hash policies; the unordered_set uses a security-oriented collision policy that trades speed for safety. Only the lower-than comparator is officially supported with algorithms.
caveats: This is a weak claim: the project's stated goal is STL-compatible C containers with security and verification features, and the plots show parity rather than wins, with sorts and deque pops clearly slower. The README says only 'C is roughly comparable to C++'; the unordered_set doc says 'Overall the STL unordered_set performance is bad, and our is also not much better.' The compile chart shows equal compile time (about 1.7 s each) and a larger stripped CTL binary (60.12 KB vs 43.944 KB), with only compiler memory lower. No ratio appears in text; all figures were read off embedded PNG plots, so they are approximate. The plots were last regenerated in February-March 2021 (last docs/images commit 2021-03-26, GCC 10.2.1), so they predate about five years of changes (new hashmap policies, swisstable work in 2026); the str and set graphs are not in gen_images.sh's default list. Hardware is not stated; each point is a single wall-clock run per size; results are first-party. Only int (and char for str) elements are measured. As the README notes, the C++ functions are partly dynamically loaded from libstdc++.so.6 while the C versions are compiled into the binary. GitHub shows the repo as forked from glouw/ctl; the README lists a renamed API and 254 methods as improvements over the original.

name: libcdada
baseline: libstdc++ std::set, std::map and std::list (native C++ code on the same libstdc++)
workload: test/benchmark.cc: 500,000 uint32_t keys from test/array.s3 (also wrapped in 69-byte and 444-byte structs) inserted then erased in set and map, and push_back then pop_back in list (and stack), each pass repeated 10 times; RDTSC ticks summed and divided by 500,000 x 10, so the table is average ticks per operation. The std::set/std::map baseline does find() then a hinted insert/erase to mimic cdada's E_EXISTS/E_NOT_FOUND semantics. Thread runs under SCHED_FIFO max priority. Measures libcdada's wrapper overhead over libstdc++.
claimed_speedup: No speedup claimed. README: 'Reasonable performance - comparable to libstdc++'. Table (average ticks per op, std vs cdada): uint32 set insert 752 vs 746, erase 698 vs 743; uint32 map insert 830 vs 809, erase 722 vs 1009; uint32 list push_back 20 vs 28, pop_back 17 vs 20; 69-byte set insert 1410 vs 1623 (custom container 1433); 69-byte list push_back 42 vs 67 (custom 44), pop_back 22 vs 40 (custom 25); 444-byte custom containers within about 4 percent except map erase 1472 vs 2021.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (libcdada configured with ../configure, per doc); compiler name and version not stated, only 'Standard Debian10 libstdc++ package'; benchmark source test/benchmark.cc
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U 1.80GHz/4.6GHz, 16GB DDR4 2667 MHz, cpufreq governor set to performance
tradeoffs: C API wrapper over libstdc++ containers, so it needs the C++ runtime; default containers support 1-256 byte keys padded to a power of two (custom containers for larger or unpadded keys); not thread-safe; POSIX build with autotools; values are copied by value through a void* API.
caveats: Not a faster-than-std result: the doc is an overhead measurement of a C wrapper built on libstdc++ itself, and cdada is level with libstdc++ only on uint32 set/map inserts (within about 3 percent, in the noise) and on custom containers for large structs. It is slower on most other rows: uint32 map erase about 1.4x slower, list push_back about 1.4x slower, 69-byte list pop_back about 1.8x slower, 444-byte map erase about 1.37x slower (derived from page data). One 'random execution' of the binary, no variance given; compiler version missing; Debian 10 era libstdc++ only (no libc++ or MSVC STL). The 'list' rows time push_back/pop_back, not insert/erase. README calls map a hashmap, but it is backed by std::map. Not thread-safe. Kept for the C-callable container wrapper role.

name: pbtools
baseline: Google Protocol Buffers C++ (libprotobuf 3.6.1) and protobuf-c
workload: Encode and decode of two protobuf messages from a proto derived from Google's protobuf benchmark messages (benchmark/benchmark.proto, java_package com.google.protobuf.benchmarks): 'Message' wrapping Message1 with a 566-byte wire size and Message3 with a 106-byte wire size, 2,000,000 iterations each, per library; whole-process time per row.
claimed_speedup: Encoding (Message plus Message3, 2,000,000 iterations each): pbtools -O2 1.457 s vs Google protobuf C++ -O3 2.231 s (about 1.53x, derived from page data) and vs protobuf-c -O3 1.892 s (about 1.30x, derived from page data). Decoding: pbtools -O2 1.594 s vs Google -O3 1.997 s (about 1.25x, derived from page data) and vs protobuf-c -O3 2.508 s (about 1.57x, derived from page data). With -O2 -flto pbtools encodes in 1.319 s and decodes in 1.239 s. At -Os pbtools encodes in 3.398 s, slower than protobuf-c -Os (1.970 s) but faster than Google -Os (3.713 s); at -Os pbtools decodes in 1.749 s vs Google 2.350 s and protobuf-c 2.609 s. An earlier run (September 2019, all at -O3, replaced in commit 6000b5f) had pbtools at 1.118 s encode and 1.069 s decode.
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ 8.3.0 with -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections (benchmark/common.mk); per-row flags in the README tables: pbtools -O2, -O2 -flto, -Os, -Os -flto; protobuf-c -O3, -O3 -flto, -Os, -Os -flto (libprotobuf-c linked statically); Google -O3 and -Os (generated code and main only, linked against a shared libprotobuf 3.6.1 whose own build flags are not stated). The -O3 rows come from the September 2019 run when common.mk had OPT_SPEED = -O3; commit 6000b5f (2020-01-16) switched OPT_SPEED to -O2 and re-ran only pbtools, nanopb and flatbuffers.
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-4510U CPU @ 2.00GHz
tradeoffs: Generates C source from proto3 files with a Python generator; no malloc/free, all allocations come from a caller-supplied workspace (arena) that cannot be freed, so repeated-field lengths cannot change after allocation; generates functions instead of tables, so executable size grows faster than table-driven libraries (README: text 17484 B vs nanopb 21256 B for the benchmark program, but growth is steeper); proto3 only, options, services (gRPC), reserved fields and public imports are not implemented; char must be 8 bits.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party, single run per row, no variance reported, small messages only, and the toolchain is old (gcc 8.3.0, Google libprotobuf/libprotoc 3.6.1 as a distro shared library, protobuf-c version not stated). The headline mixes two runs: the Google and protobuf-c -O3 rows date from September 2019 (common.mk then had OPT_SPEED = -O3), while the pbtools -O2 rows come from a January 2020 re-run (commit 6000b5f switched to -O2 and the top-level benchmark Makefile only rebuilds nanopb and pbtools), so the baselines were not re-measured against the pbtools version shown; the current Makefiles would build every library at -O2. Harness differences favour pbtools: its encode loop fills a fixed stack workspace and stores pointers to string literals, Google's encode loop constructs a fresh heap-allocated benchmark::Message every iteration (no Arena, although the proto sets cc_enable_arenas) and copies both ~230-byte strings before SerializeToString into a std::string, and protobuf-c encodes through pack_to_buffer with a ProtobufCBufferSimple callback rather than its direct pack() call (stack structs, no malloc on encode). On decode protobuf-c mallocs and frees the whole message tree per iteration (unpack with the default allocator), Google reuses one message object, and pbtools copies strings into its arena workspace. At -Os pbtools encoding is slower than protobuf-c (3.398 s vs 1.970 s). FlatBuffers decodes in 0.100 s (-O2) only because it decodes lazily. The repo's guessed baseline (msgpack) is wrong: msgpack is not in the benchmark. No commits since 2023-06-04. [retier] Headline mixes a September 2019 -O3 run for Google protobuf 3.6.1 and protobuf-c with a January 2020 -O2 rerun of pbtools only (commit 6000b5f). Baselines handicapped: Google loop heap-allocates a fresh message with no Arena and validates UTF-8 while pbtools never validates; protobuf-c uses pack_to_buffer and mallocs per decode; baseline runtimes are prebuilt distro libraries. pbtools loses at -Os encode (3.398 vs 1.970 s). Security: packed fixed-width repeated fields with a payload length not a multiple of the element size write past the arena allocation (read in lib/src/pbtools.c, untested). N-byte encode buffer holds N-1 bytes; NUL-terminated strings; proto3 only; abandoned since 2023-06-04.

README also says the built-in JSON archive is about 40% faster than BitSerializer's own RapidJSON-based JSON archive, and that wrapped third-party formats (RapidJSON, PugiXml, RapidYAML) cost about 5% against their native APIs.
tradeoffs: Header-style C++17 library; types need a Serialize function or KeyValue mapping per class (non-intrusive). MsgPack, CSV and the new built-in JSON archive have no external dependencies; the RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML archives pull in those libraries. Streams straight to and from the model with no intermediate DOM, so it cannot do arbitrary DOM manipulation the way nlohmann::json can.
caveats: Benchmark source is public (benchmarks/archives: main.cpp, benchmark_base.cpp, competitors/nlohmannjson_benchmark.h) but no compiler, flags or CPU model are stated anywhere in the repo or README, and the committed report JSON and chart carry no machine information, so it is a first-party result with partial methodology (tier C, not A). The only nlohmann::json row is MsgPack: competitors/nlohmannjson_benchmark.h also defines a NlohmannJson-Json (text JSON) class, but main.cpp never runs it, so there is no nlohmann JSON text row. The baseline converts the struct into a nlohmann::json DOM (whose objects are std::map nodes) and then calls to_msgpack/from_msgpack, while BitSerializer maps the struct straight to bytes; the README itself calls Serializer-vs-Parser comparisons 'not entirely fair', and the README text never quotes the nlohmann numbers (they appear only in the report JSON and chart). No dedicated MsgPack library (msgpack-c/cpp, cereal, glaze, zpp_bits) is compared, so 'best-in-class' MsgPack speed is unsupported. Correctness: the harness validates the loaded model against the source after every load stage (ValidateTargetModel), so round-trip correctness is checked, but serialized bytes are not compared across libraries and the committed output-size report (last changed 2025-05-01) has no NlohmannJson-MsgPack row. The committed speed report has no row for the new built-in JSON archive (BitSerializer::Json::JsonArchive), so the README's 'about 40% faster than the RapidJSON-based archive' claim has no committed numbers. Against RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML the BitSerializer archives are within about 5% or slightly slower, not faster (RapidJson save 14103 vs 13636, load 11957 vs 11149 fields/ms), so the speedup claim holds only for MsgPack against nlohmann. The 33x and 22x ratios are derived from the report's two numbers. Results are the minimum time per stage over a 30 s window after a 10 s CPU warm-up, which favours best-case numbers for every library equally. [retier] First-party benchmark: BitSerializer reuses a 16384-byte pre-reserved output string while the nlohmann side rebuilds a std::map DOM per call, grows to_msgpack's vector from empty and copies it, without sax_parse; best single run on a cache-hot ~13 KB payload (3.8 us vs 126 us), compiler/CPU/nlohmann version unstated. MsgPack timestamp 96 field order swapped (seconds before nanoseconds), interop bug. Archives are compiled libraries, not header-only; ostream paths 7.6x slower.

name: iguana (struct_pb)
workload: Monster message (game-monster struct with nested fields), serialize and deserialize loops of iguana::to_pb / from_pb against protobuf's generated code, in benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp (bench3).
claimed_speedup: In the benchmark monster scenario struct_pb serialization is 2.4x protobuf and deserialization is 3.4x protobuf (README text lang/struct_pb_intro.md, translated from Chinese: 'serialization speed is 2.4 times protobuf, deserialization 3.4 times').
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the claim. In-repo CMakeLists.txt: default build type Release with CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE '-O3' plus '-Wall -pthread -g' (no -DNDEBUG), C++17 by default, libstdc++ unless LINKLIBC++; protobuf is whatever find_package(Protobuf) finds.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17/C++20 (C++26 reflection path with GCC 16.1); structs defined in C++ with YLT_REFL / YLT_REFL_PB instead of .proto files and protoc. Protobuf support is proto3 binary wire only: no proto2 required fields, extensions, custom options or services, no proto3 JSON or text format; official conformance runs only the binary subset.
caveats: First-party claim in a Chinese-language doc; the numbers carry no hardware, compiler version or protobuf version, and the doc points to 'the benchmark in struct_pack' (alibaba/yalantinglibs) for reproduction. The identical 2.4x / 3.4x sentence is in yalantinglibs' struct_pb docs (website/docs/zh and en/struct_pb/struct_pb_intro.md), where struct_pb is iguana re-exported (include/ylt/struct_pb/struct_pb_impl.hpp: 'namespace struct_pb = iguana;'); yalantinglibs' published struct_pack charts (Alibaba Clang 13, Xeon Platinum 8163) cover struct_pack, not struct_pb. The in-repo benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp prints iguana/protobuf ratios from a high_resolution_clock around whole loops (default 100000 iterations) but commits no results; deserialization allocates a fresh object per iteration for both libraries, and the parsed objects are never used, so the header-only from_pb could be partly optimised away while protobuf's out-of-line ParseFromString cannot (a risk, not demonstrated). The claim may predate the current code, which was refactored heavily (C++26 reflection; a draft JSON DOM parser PR #386 is still open). The README FAQ answer 'Is iguana high performance? Yes, because it is based on compile-time reflection' has no numbers. No JSON-versus-RapidJSON or other numbers found in README or docs. The claim is about the protobuf binary wire format, so binary-schemas fits better than serialization-json.

name: protobuf-c
workload: Encode plus decode of one 494-byte protobuf message (all scalar widths, floats, strings, bytes, eight numeric arrays, a nested struct, an array of structs, Unicode strings) in the arena's c-embedded host target (languages/c-embedded). Each timed iteration packs the same statically built message into a preallocated buffer and then unpacks it: protobuf-c mallocs the decoded tree and frees it every iteration, and nanopb decodes into a memset stack struct with fixed-size fields set in nanopb/message.options. 500,000 iterations by default (bench.sh), best of 5 runs with a 10 s cooldown between runs.
claimed_speedup: Arena 'Embedded - throughput' table: protobuf-c 328.0 MB/s (663,929 msg/s) vs nanopb 61.9 MB/s (125,240 msg/s), about 5.3x on both metrics (derived from page data). Older corroboration in the pbtools benchmark (eerimoq/pbtools benchmark/README.rst, gcc 8.3.0, Intel Core i7-4510U): encoding protobuf-c -O3 1.892 s vs nanopb -O2 9.580 s (about 5.1x) and decoding 2.508 s vs 6.433 s (about 2.6x) (derived from page data), with nanopb driven through its callback API. In the same pbtools table protobuf-c encodes faster than Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1 at -O3 (1.892 s vs 2.231 s, about 1.18x) but decodes slower (2.508 s vs 1.997 s, about 0.80x) (derived from page data). No msgpack comparison found.
compiler_and_flags: gcc from the arena's Ubuntu 26.04 devcontainer (version not stated). The bench driver and the generated code are built with -Os -flto -std=c99 (languages/c-embedded/setup.sh). nanopb's runtime (git tag 0.4.9.1) is compiled from source at -Os -flto, but protobuf-c is linked with -lprotobuf-c against the distro's prebuilt libprotobuf-c (libprotobuf-c-dev), so the protobuf-c runtime's version and build flags are not stated and are not -Os.
tradeoffs: Wire-compatible with Google protobuf, so it needs protoc plus protoc-gen-c and a C runtime; decoded messages are allocated through a pluggable allocator (malloc by default), unlike nanopb's static allocation; the arena README calls it 'desktop-class' and ranks it for reference against footprint-oriented nanopb, so code size is larger than nanopb's.
caveats: Third-party numbers from a rival codec's benchmark arena (SofaBuffers, 0 stars) in which protobuf-c and nanopb are both baselines of the 'Embedded' throughput table, where speed is explicitly not the ranking metric. Host CPU and compiler version are not stated, so the run is not reproducible as published (the harness code is public). The build is asymmetric in protobuf-c's favour: every codec's bench driver and generated code are built -Os -flto and nanopb's runtime is compiled from source at -Os -flto, but protobuf-c's runtime is the distro's prebuilt libprotobuf-c linked with -lprotobuf-c, so its hot code runs at the distro's (unstated) flags; pbtools' own rows put nanopb at -Os about 1.35x (encode) to 1.5x (decode) slower than at -O2 (derived from page data). The c-embedded loops re-encode the original static message every iteration, not the freshly decoded one as the arena README describes for its maxspeed targets. One message shape, one unnamed host, and the 5.3x ratio compares two rows of one table. The older pbtools benchmark corroborates the direction but drives nanopb through its callback API (strings and sub-messages via pb_encode_string and pb_encode_submessage callbacks), mixes runs (protobuf-c -O3 rows from September 2019, nanopb -O2 rows re-run in January 2020 after commit 6000b5f switched common.mk to -O2), statically links an unstated libprotobuf-c version, and shows protobuf-c decoding about 1.26x slower than Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1 (derived from page data). The GLD.SerializerBenchmark C suite also lists protobuf-c, but according to the search record its protobuf-c row times a shared in-tree proto3 wire codec rather than protobuf-c itself (not re-checked by the verifier), so it was not used. No benchmark or performance numbers exist in the protobuf-c README. Last commit 2025-04-07 (release 1.5.2); the GLD suite author opened a benchmark-fairness review request (#803, 2026-07-17) and a spec-compliance report for 1.5.2 (#810, 2026-09-14), both still open. [retier] Baseline is nanopb, not MessagePack. Arena figures (328.0 vs 61.9 MB/s) run by rival codec SofaBuffers; nanopb built from source at -Os -flto while protobuf-c is the prebuilt distro library; pbtools table also links -static -lprotobuf-c for every flag row. Matched build might give roughly 3.5-3.9x (derived, unmeasured). vs Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1: about 1.18x faster encode, 1.26x slower decode. Unpack has no recursion-depth limit and no proto3 UTF-8 check; open allocation overflow #796/#799; builds fail against protobuf 34/35 and C++20. Development continues on the next branch (2026-08-22).

name: Protocol Puffers (protopuf)
baseline: Google protobuf C++ (libprotobuf with protoc-generated classes; version not stated)
workload: Google Benchmark on one small message, Class{name, 3 x Student{id, name}} (45 bytes on the wire): encode into a 64-byte array and decode from a 45-byte buffer, protopuf vs protobuf SerializeToArray / ParseFromArray.
claimed_speedup: Per call: encode 17.2 ns (unsafe_mode) and 29.7 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 68.0 ns, about 4.0x and 2.3x faster; decode 188 ns (unsafe_mode) and 217 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 244 ns, about 1.30x and 1.12x faster (ratios derived from page data; times from the 'Before' table of PR #53).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated beyond 'Release mode': the PR author introduces the tables as 'Here is a benchmarks (in Release mode)'; compiler, version, exact flags, CPU and protobuf version are not given. test/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt prints '[TIP] Release mode is expected in benchmark test'.
stars_or_usage: 207 stars; packaged in vcpkg and Conan Center (README badges)
tradeoffs: Messages are described as C++20 template types instead of .proto files (no code generator), so it needs GCC 11+, Clang 12+, MSVC 14.29+ or Apple Clang 17+ and compile times grow with templates; wire format is protobuf-compatible both ways. unsafe_mode skips bounds checks while safe_mode adds out-of-bounds checking and is slower. The README lists the supported field types but no benchmark section.
caveats: Numbers come from a contributor's (basiliscos) pull-request description (PR #53, opened 2025-07-08, still open) and not from the README, docs or CI. The PR says only that the runs were 'in Release mode' and omits CPU, compiler, flags and the protobuf version. The harness source is public (test/benchmark/main.cpp), so a rerun is possible, but the published figures are not fully specified. The same PR's decode optimization (145 ns unsafe, 162 ns safe) is unmerged, and review found a length-counting bug in it (it decremented an item count instead of a byte count), so only the 'Before' figures are used. Harness flaws: the encode loops pass neither the output buffer to DoNotOptimize nor call ClobberMemory, so stores from the header-only, fully inlined protopuf encoder could be eliminated, while protobuf's SerializeToArray is an out-of-line library call that also runs ByteSizeLong first. Both decoders are handed the whole 64-byte array (45 wire bytes plus 19 zero bytes) and neither result is checked; since tag 0 is invalid in protobuf, ParseFromArray should end with an error after parsing the real data. The message is tiny (45 bytes, all strings within small-string length), and both decode loops construct a fresh message per iteration (protobuf without an Arena). The unsafe_mode rows skip bounds checks, so the headline 4.0x encode ratio is with checks off; safe_mode gives 2.3x on encode and only 1.12x on decode. The README has no benchmark section, and the protopuf.surge.sh docs were not reachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED in the search session). [retier] First-party PR #53 numbers ('Release mode' only; no CPU, compiler or protobuf version; PR unmerged). Encode output never passed to DoNotOptimize (inlined encoder may be partly eliminated); decode buffer zero-padded with protobuf's ParseFromArray failure ignored; protobuf run without Arena; 4.0x headline is unsafe_mode; 45-byte message. safe_mode throws on wire types 3/4/6/7; varint decode uncapped; unpacked repeated scalars dropped (#47); little-endian only; no oneof (#14).

name: Tachyon.JSON v6
baseline: nlohmann::json (also compared against simdjson and Glaze)

name: utl::json (part of the UTL header-only library collection)
baseline: nlohmann::json (also PicoJSON; beats RapidJSON on serialization tasks only, loses to it on most parsing tasks)
workload: Parsing and serializing minimized/prettified JSON test files (strings.json, numbers.json, twitter.json, apache_builds.json, database.json) with a benchmark harness comparing utl::json, nlohmann, PicoJSON, and RapidJSON
claimed_speedup: Faster than nlohmann::json at parsing: 2.2x on twitter.json (402.89 vs 182.76 op/s), 2.4x on apache_builds.json (2,134.76 vs 881.03 op/s), and about 4x on strings.json and numbers.json (derived from page data). Faster than nlohmann at serializing by about 1.6-1.9x on twitter.json and apache_builds.json (e.g. twitter.json minimized: 834.42 vs 440.27 op/s), 1.5x on numbers.json, and 2.4x on strings.json (derived from page data). Vs RapidJSON, utl::json wins only strings.json parsing and most serialization runs. The author says that an experimental flat-map object type (not the shipped default) 'allowed utl::json to beat RapidJSON on all serializing tasks and significantly closed the gap of database.json parsing'. RapidJSON is still 1.30-1.40x faster at parsing database.json in that run.
tradeoffs: Uses std::map for JSON objects by default, which the author states is the main performance weak point on object-heavy documents; JSON values map onto standard containers (std::map/std::vector/std::string) for STL interoperability rather than a custom optimized container, trading some speed for simplicity.
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags appear on the benchmark page (nanobench tables showing relative %, ms/op, op/s, and err% only), so the methodology is self-reported and partial. The 'relative' column is relative to utl::json, and >100% means faster. RapidJSON beats utl::json on parsing on every file except strings.json: numbers.json 1.29-1.45x, twitter.json 2.07-2.22x, apache_builds.json 1.63-1.72x, database.json 1.30-1.40x. It also roughly ties utl::json at serializing apache_builds.json (100.5%). The consistent win is only against nlohmann and PicoJSON. The database.json/flat-map result uses a configuration the author rejected, so it does not describe the shipped library. The page also warns that Clang/libc++ below version 20 falls back to a much slower number parser (no std::from_chars).

name: cmp
baseline: msgpack-c (msgpack C API, v1.3.0 in the shootout)
workload: Encoding (write test) of randomly generated schemaless data (2367-byte small and 248571-byte large MessagePack objects) into a growable buffer in the ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks suite, with the hash cost subtracted. CMP's incremental reader is also timed, but msgpack-c has no incremental-parser row in the suite, so only the write test is a like-for-like comparison against the baseline.
claimed_speedup: No speed win exists. The project only says 'Fast, Lightweight, Flexible, and Robust' (no numbers). The independent shootout shows CMP v14 slower than msgpack C 1.3.0 on write: 7.33 us vs 6.42 us (small) and 660.19 us vs 544.24 us (large) on the AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop; 89.75 us vs 69.21 us (small) and 9206.05 us vs 8142.64 us (large) on a Raspberry Pi. CMP is the smallest MessagePack build on the desktop (3232 vs 4088 bytes for write) but not on the Raspberry Pi size build (2324 vs 1528 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux, -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG, each test run 7 times for 10 s, best and worst dropped
hardware: AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop; first-generation Raspberry Pi Model B rev2 (ARMv6)
tradeoffs: No internal buffers and no heap allocation, about 4k lines in cmp.c/cmp.h, C89, user supplies read/write/skip callbacks (no growable buffer, no tree parser). Small and portable rather than fast.
caveats: Not faster than the named baseline. Every write row in the shootout (README and full-results-extended.md) has CMP v14 slower than msgpack C 1.3.0: desktop 7.33 vs 6.42 us small and 660.19 vs 544.24 us large; Raspberry Pi 89.75 vs 69.21 us and 9206.05 vs 8142.64 us; the extended results add an Intel Celeron 2957U Chromebook with 14.01 vs 11.90 us small and 1463.82 vs 1338.33 us large. Both write tests produce the same output hash (1a9c6681 small, b4ac134d large), so the numbers are real. CMP has no tree parser; its incremental reader is faster than msgpack C's tree unpacker on large data (533.46 vs 750.87 us desktop, 5713.58 vs 10287.89 us Raspberry Pi, derived from page data) but slower on small desktop data (7.43 vs 6.47 us), and that is a cross-category comparison, not a like-for-like win. The shootout was written by the author of MPack (a competitor; its own disclaimer says it may be biased), dates from 2016 (GCC 5.3.0, CMP v14, msgpack-c 1.3.0; the MPack README's feature table now lists CMP v19 and msgpack-c v3.3.0), and the CMP write test uses a harness-supplied growable buffer (buffer.h) because CMP has none, which the author notes is unfair for embedded comparisons. CMP's only measured advantage is code size in the desktop speed build (3232 vs 4088 bytes for write); in the Raspberry Pi -Os build msgpack C is smaller (1528 vs 2324 bytes). No numbers anywhere support a speed claim; candidate for the not-faster shortcoming list.

name: bstring
baseline: C standard library char* string functions (strcpy, strcat, strchr, strstr, strcspn, memmove)
workload: Upstream Bstrlib's cbench.c example (examples-09282006.zip): operations per second for assignment, char extraction, scan, concatenation (250 appends of a 60 character string plus '!!' into one growing buffer, buffer reset each iteration) and replace, bstring C API against plain char* code (strcpy, strchr, strstr, strcspn, strcat, memmove/memcpy). The same page also benchmarks upstream's C++ wrapper CBString against std::string with cppbench.cpp.
claimed_speedup: Bstrlib C API as percent of char* Clib speed (100% is parity), columns WATCOM C 11.0c / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / gcc 3.3.3 Cygwin / gcc 3.3.3 Power 4 SUSE: concatenation 21700% / 23700% / 21200% / 9260% / 3980%; assignment 182% / 198% / 218% / 89% / 91%; scan 214% / 125% / 159% / 209% / 89%; char extraction 95% / 96% / 101% / 102% / 113%; replace 147% / 114% / 125% / 101% / 86%. Same page, CBString over std::string (WATCOM + STLport / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / g++ 3.3.3 Cygwin / g++ 3.3.3 Power 4): char * assignment 93% / 248% / 264% / 537% / 132%; char extraction 63% / 118% / 123% / 132% / 100%; scan 155% / 143% / 178% / 274% / 192%; concatenation 187% / 21100% / 19400% / 1330% / 200%; replace 144% / 95% / 110% / 108% / 135%.
compiler_and_flags: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c (with STLport for C++), Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0 (4.0 99026), gcc/g++ 3.3.3 on Cygwin and on SUSE Linux. The page says only that the compiler must be set to 'a reasonable maximum performance setting', for most compilers 'a flag such as -O2'; the makefiles shipped in examples-09282006.zip use gcc -O3 (Makefile.gccXnix), MSVC /O2 (plus /Ob2 for C++) and Intel /Ox /Ob2, but the page does not say these were the flags used.
hardware: Athlon XP 1.620GHz (all Windows/Cygwin columns); Power 4 1GHz (SUSE Linux column)
stars_or_usage: 175 stars (msteinert fork); upstream websnarf/bstrlib 570 stars; packaged in many distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Length-prefixed string struct (slen, mlen, data) that stays NUL-terminated for interop with char* code, so length is O(1) and appends amortize, at the cost of a header and a different API from <string.h>. Dual licensed BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0 (user's choice). This fork is pure C: it removed upstream's C++ wrapper (CBString, bstrwrap) and the const_bstring type, and adds Meson build, Check tests, fuzzing and CI.
caveats: The numbers are for upstream Bstrlib (websnarf/bstrlib, last commit 2016-11-02), measured with 2000s era compilers on a 1.62GHz Athlon XP and a 1GHz Power 4; the msteinert fork is described as binary compatible but was not re-benchmarked, and the CBString versus std::string rows apply only to upstream because the fork dropped the C++ wrapper. First-party project page with percentages only (no raw ops/s), no date, and flags not tied to the run, so tier C. The page's cbench.c/cppbench.cpp links point at the dead cvs.sourceforge.net; the code is in examples-09282006.zip on the SourceForge downloads page. The large concatenation ratios come from the baseline calling strcat repeatedly on a growing buffer (rescanning the whole string every call, quadratic) while bstring tracks length; a C program that keeps its own end pointer would not lose this much. The scan row is not like for like: in cbench.c the char* test runs strchr '.', strstr "123" and strcspn "sm" over the 60-character TESTSTRING1, which contains neither '.' nor "123" (both calls scan the whole string), while the bstring test searches the 25-character 'Dot. 123. Some more data.', where '.' and "123" are found within the first six characters; the scan percentages therefore overstate bstring. The std::string comparison used old STLs (WATCOM with STLport, Visual C++ 6.0 and Intel C++ 6.0 sharing Microsoft's STL, g++ 3.3.3 libstdc++); the page itself attributes the 19400-21100% concatenation results to Microsoft's STL implementing concat as O(m+n), so they reflect a since-fixed library defect rather than a lasting advantage. std::string was faster or equal in some rows (char extraction 63% with STLport, replace 95% with Visual C++ 6.0, assignment 93% with STLport) and the C API loses on assignment and replace in some columns (89%, 91%, 86%). The fork's own README claims 'improved overall performance of common string operations' and doc/comparisons.md discusses performance qualitatively, with no numbers.

name: shoco
baseline: smaz (short-string compressor); also gzip and xz command-line tools
workload: Compress and decompress English words: all words in /usr/dict/share/words versus smaz, and /usr/share/dict/words (4,953,680 bytes) compressed as one file with the included shoco command-line tool versus gzip and xz.
claimed_speedup: README: shoco 'is typically faster by at least a factor of 2' than smaz; example 0.325s (smaz, 28% average compression) versus 0.145s (shoco, 33% average compression) for compress plus decompress of all words in /usr/dict/share/words (about 2.2x, derived from page data). Versus gzip and xz on /usr/share/dict/words: shoco 0.070s compress / 0.010s decompress / 3,393,975 bytes; gzip 0.470s / 0.048s / 1,476,083 bytes (6.7x and 4.8x faster, derived from page data); xz 3.300s / 0.148s / 1,229,980 bytes (47x and 15x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README timings; the repo Makefile builds with $(CC) -std=c99 -O3 -Wall plus user CFLAGS, and the README says it was only tested with gcc/clang on x86_64 Linux.
tradeoffs: Entropy coder for short ASCII strings built on a compiled-in bigram model (default model tuned for English words; a Python script generates new models from your own data). Compression ratio is far worse than gzip or xz on larger inputs (3.39 MB versus 1.48 MB and 1.23 MB on the 4.95 MB word list); output never grows for plain ASCII input but non-ASCII input can; copy-in C files (shoco.c, shoco.h, shoco_model.h), no packaging.
caveats: First-party numbers measured 'on my computer' (README, 2014): no CPU, compiler, flags or OS version stated, no run count. The smaz row has no committed harness; the shoco 0.145s figure equals the 'user' time of the README's own test_input example on /usr/share/dict/words (479,828 lines), and test_input.c times fgets input, compress, decompress and a strcmp check per line, so the two sides may not have been timed the same way. The gzip/xz table times whole processes of the shoco-bin command-line tool, which compresses the 4.95 MB file in one call including file I/O; the README calls whole-file use 'not a strong point of shoco', gzip/xz levels are not stated, and gzip/xz reach far better ratios (1.48 MB and 1.23 MB vs 3.39 MB), so that comparison is not like for like. The baseline is not a C++ standard facility. The numbers predate the March 2015 'Prevent buffer overflows in decompression' fix and the December 2015 end-of-string fix. Open issue #28 (2017, unanswered) reports an AFL/AddressSanitizer global-buffer-overflow read in shoco_decompress() on malformed input (24 bytes before chrs_by_chr_and_successor_id), so decompressing untrusted data is unsafe; open issue #35 reports some ASCII strings (e.g. 'My-Nam3-iZ-H@5eeB-M33R') failing to compress. The README begins 'This project is unmaintained. You should use ZStandard nowadays'; the last code change is the 2015-12-08 merge of pull request #17, and the 2026-02-16 commit only marks the project unmaintained. No independent speed benchmark of the C library against smaz was found (a search surfaced only ratio comparisons by Unishox2 and a third-party smaz speed-up blog). The README's '/usr/dict/share/words' path is the author's typo for /usr/share/dict/words. [retier] First-party 'on my computer' numbers: the test_input driver is built without -O3 and its timing includes fgets/strlen/strcmp per line; no smaz harness; gzip/xz rows time whole processes at unstated levels (shoco ratio 68.5% vs 29.8%/24.8%). Security: decoder reads packs[] past PACK_COUNT for lead bytes 0xF0-0xFF (CVE-2017-11367, #28, fix PR #34 unmerged) and crafted pack-2 bytes read outside the successor table; shoco_compress 1-byte over-read (#15/#16). Unmaintained since 2015; Python 2 model generator; default model lacks digits and spaces.

name: CDRC atomic_weak_ptr (concurrent_deferred_rc)
baseline: just::thread's atomic<weak_ptr> (commercial third-party implementation of the C++20 std::atomic<std::weak_ptr> interface)
workload: Ramalethe & Correia lock-free concurrent doubly-linked queue using atomic weak back-pointers; P threads repeatedly pop-then-reinsert an element, P = 1 to 192, on a 4-socket 72-core machine
claimed_speedup: CDRC atomic weak pointers vs just::thread: 4.2x faster at P=8 and 10x faster at P=192 (paper Sec. 5.2). At P=1 (off-plot), the paper says the hand-tuned 'original' manual-reclamation queue is 4.5x faster than CDRC and 67x faster than just::thread, which puts CDRC ~15x ahead of just::thread at P=1 (derived from page data: 67/4.5). Versus the manual original, CDRC is 4.5x slower at P=1, 19% slower at P=8, and 33% slower at P=192.
hardware: 4-socket 72-core machine, 4x Intel Xeon E7-8867 v4 @ 2.4GHz, 2-way hyperthreading, 45MB L3 cache, 1TB RAM
tradeoffs: Requires a C++20-concepts-capable compiler; full benchmark reproduction needs jemalloc + NUMA-aware setup; library is research-grade (from the CDRC/acquire-retire papers), not a drop-in std::shared_ptr replacement, and uses more memory than manual reclamation in oversubscribed scenarios.
caveats: The paper's 67x figure at P=1 is the manual 'original' implementation vs just::thread, not CDRC vs just::thread; CDRC's own P=1 margin is ~15x (derived). The baseline is just::thread, a commercial library of atomic shared and weak pointers, not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL atomic<weak_ptr>. The paper's separate 2x-3x throughput claim is against earlier concurrent reference-counting implementations, not std::shared_ptr. The last commit on the default branch is 2022-07-03 (the repo shows a push on 2024-02-18).

name: observable_unique_ptr / observer_ptr (oup)
workload: Median dereference/creation cost across int, float, std::string, std::array<int,65536> owned objects; oup::observer_ptr dereference vs std::weak_ptr::lock()-based dereference (also compares owner-pointer creation vs std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr)
claimed_speedup: Dereference observer, relative to raw T* = 1 (median across object types). gcc 9.4.0/libstdc++-9/Ryzen 5 2600: weak/shared 3.5 vs observer 1.0 (obs_unique and obs_sealed), ~3.5x. MSVC 16.11.3/MS-STL/i7-7800X: 9.4 vs 1.4 (obs_unique) and 0.8 (obs_sealed), ~6.7x-11.8x. Emscripten 2.0.34/libc++/Node.js 14.15.5/Ryzen 5 2600: 38.7 vs 1.0, ~38.7x. Create observer: 1.6 vs 1.6 (gcc), 5.3 vs 1.6 (MSVC), 14.8 vs 2.3 (Emscripten). (Ratios derived from page data.)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.4.0 (libstdc++-9), MSVC 16.11.3 (MS-STL), Emscripten 2.0.34 (libc++); 'all optimizations turned on (except LTO)', exact flags not listed
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 2600, Linux 5.15.0 (gcc run); Intel i7-7800X, Windows 10.0.19043 (MSVC run); AMD Ryzen 5 2600, Node.js 14.15.5 + Linux 5.1.0 (Emscripten/libc++ run)
tradeoffs: Not thread-safe (no atomic refcount), unlike std::shared_ptr/weak_ptr; no array support; no custom-allocator support; owner-pointer creation itself is 1.1-2.1x SLOWER than std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr in the same table, so the win is specific to the observer/dereference path.
caveats: oup is unique-ownership only and not thread-safe; std::weak_ptr::lock() does atomic refcount work, so part of the dereference advantage comes from dropping thread safety. Creating the owner pointer is slower than std::unique_ptr. The README says the benchmarks were last run for oup v0.7.1, so they may not reflect current code. The Emscripten/libc++ run is WebAssembly on Node.js, not native.

name: BlockQuicksort
workload: Sorting arrays of random 32-bit ints, 10-dimensional double Vectors (Euclidean-norm comparator), and 21-field int Records, measured as elements sorted per second, against GCC's std::sort.
claimed_speedup: More than 80% more elements sorted per second than GCC's std::sort on random ints. Section 4: optimized BlockQuicksort needs ~45 ns/element vs 85 ns/element for std::sort at n=2^28 (+88%), and the duplicate-check variant is almost twice as fast on random ints in [0, sqrt n]. Figure 7 shows smaller but positive gains on Vector and Record for the BlockQS (mo-sqrt n, dc) variant. std::sort wins only on sorted or almost-sorted inputs.
compiler_and_flags: GNU g++ 4.8.4, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i5-2500K @ 3.30GHz, 4 cores, 32KB L1 i/d, 256KB L2/core, 6MB shared L3, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04.4 64-bit

tradeoffs: In-place but not stable; block size (default 128) needs tuning per data type; branch-misprediction-avoidance technique now widely reused (e.g. pdqsort, PPQSort) under more permissive licenses than this repo's GPL-3.0.

name: IPS⁴o (In-place Parallel Super Scalar Samplesort)
workload: Sorting 2^10 to 2^32 uniformly-distributed 64-bit floating point elements (also Pair/Quartet/100Bytes records and skewed distributions), sequential and multi-core, on four different server machines.
claimed_speedup: Sequential (Table 1 of arXiv 2009.13569, average slowdowns relative to the fastest algorithm per input, averaged over the four machines and inputs of at least 2^18 bytes): I1S4o (sequential IPS4o) vs std::sort, Total: double 1.20 vs 2.47, uint64 1.46 vs 2.95, uint32 1.78 vs 3.93, Pair 1.52 vs 2.45; Uniform: double 1.08 vs 2.43, uint64 1.35 vs 3.02, uint32 1.67 vs 4.02. By Total, I1S4o is about 2.06x (double), 2.02x (uint64), 2.21x (uint32) and 1.61x (Pair) faster than std::sort (derived from page data). Fig. 11 (Uniform uint64) shows std::sort off the plot, above I1S4o, on all four machines. Parallel: the paper reports no parallel speedup against std::sort; its parallel speedups (8.37 on A1x16, 40.92 on A1x64, 20.91 on I4x20, 17.49 on I2x16) are relative to sequential I1S4o.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0, -march=native -O3
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (A1x16); AMD EPYC Rome 7702P (A1x64); 2x Intel Xeon E5-2683 v4 (I2x16); 4x Intel Xeon Gold 6138 (I4x20)
stars_or_usage: 135 stars (canonical repo); used as the reference sequential/parallel sorting baseline in numerous follow-up algorithm-engineering papers and benchmark suites (e.g. PPQSort)
tradeoffs: Needs C++14; parallel mode requires OpenMP or std::thread plus TBB and 16-byte atomic compare-and-exchange support (or -mcx16/libatomic); does not compile on Windows; least advantage on already-sorted or low-cardinality inputs where n<=2^15.
caveats: Numbers come from the peer-reviewed ESA 2017 paper (Section 5, Figures 6-8), which used the older SaschaWitt/ips4o code. The ips4o/ips4o repo contains no benchmark code. A separate ips4o/ips4o-benchmark-suite (GPL-3.0) has a std::sort target but is not linked from the repo README and matches the later 4-machine journal version. ips4o/ips4o is a GitHub fork of the now-deprecated SaschaWitt/ips4o and is the maintained successor. The 1.86x std::sort factor applies at n=2^32; DualPivot beats IS4o on AlmostSorted input by 1.70x, and IS4o is slower than BlockQuicksort for n<=2^15. The parallel advantage shrinks to ~1.41x on the 4-socket Intel4S machine. [retier] Table 1 values are average slowdown factors, not direct timings. std::sort is the sequential GCC introsort, so no parallel-vs-std::sort figure exists in the paper.

name: dietlibc (qsort and bsearch)
workload: qsort and bsearch on 1000 random ints, measured in CPU cycles, as recorded in the dietlibc 0.8 changelog entry (2001 or earlier; lib/qsort.c history in the mirror starts 2001-02-11). The qsort that was measured has since been replaced twice (new qsort 2003-11-02, 'faster qsort' 2006-08-16, random pivot via rand_i 2019-01-29).
claimed_speedup: qsort 300010 cycles vs glibc 679414 cycles (about 2.3x fewer cycles, derived from page data); bsearch 553 cycles vs glibc 3352 cycles (about 6.1x fewer cycles, derived from page data). Changelog author: 'I have no idea why glibc is so slow.'
stars_or_usage: 130 stars on the unofficial ensc git-cvs mirror (archived 2023-09-05); packaged by Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, openSUSE per search results
tradeoffs: A libc built for the smallest static Linux binaries (the dietlibc README says to use it for programs that do not need the bloat of glibc). Static linking only, GCC-only, no FreeBSD/Solaris/Windows support (FAQ), GPL-2.0-or-later licence, so statically linked programs carry the GPL. The qsort/bsearch comparison is a data point for the libc's small routines; the project's headline claim is size, not speed.
caveats: First-party, one changelog line from the 0.8 release (2001 or earlier) with no benchmark program, compiler, flags, CPU model or glibc version stated; the author adds 'I have no idea why glibc is so slow.' The measured qsort no longer exists: lib/qsort.c was rewritten on 2003-11-02 ('write new qsort that does not fail so'), again on 2006-08-16 ('faster qsort', the 0.31 'faster qsort' changelog line) and given a random pivot on 2019-01-29, so the 2.3x figure describes code that is gone. The current qsort is a recursive Sedgewick 3-way quicksort with a byte-by-byte swap loop, no insertion-sort cutoff and no recursion-depth bound; glibc's qsort has also changed many times since 2001. Independent counter-evidence (snippet only, nullprogram.com 2016 'Inspecting C's qsort Through Animation', page EGRESS_BLOCKED): glibc's qsort finished the animated sort in 307 frames versus 503 for dietlibc 0.32, and the author calls dietlibc 'optimized for size, which shows through its slower performance'. The bsearch gap (3352 vs 553 cycles for a single lookup in 1000 ints, about 10 comparisons) is far larger than two plain binary searches can differ algorithmically; it probably reflects first-call costs such as lazy PLT binding of a dynamically linked glibc or cold caches, which the changelog does not control for. Size is dietlibc's real selling point and is not benchmarked in the repo. The FAQ says dietlibc can 'improve performance by an order of magnitude for certain programming models' and points to fefe.de/fnord/SPEED; fefe.de was EGRESS_BLOCKED here. The same changelog notes an i386 strlen that is '31% faster, 14% smaller', but its baseline is the older dietlibc C version, not glibc. repo_url is the unofficial ensc git-cvs mirror, archived 2023-09-05 with its last commit on 2019-03-18; upstream lives in CVS at cvs.fefe.de and may be newer (the mirror's CHANGES already has an unreleased 0.35 section). License is GPL-2.0 'or later' per README, so linking it into distributed binaries carries GPL obligations. [retier] 2001 changelog cycle counts (qsort 300010 vs 679414, bsearch 553 vs 3352) from harness t.c (commit 344deb2): one rdtsc call each, glibc's timed call pays sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES) and malloc on first use, bsearch unwarmed. Measured qsort went quadratic on equal keys and measured bsearch read past the array end (fixed 0.10-0.15); qsort rewritten 2003, 2006, 2012 (rand pivot) and 2019. HEAD qsort makes about 1.8x more comparisons than glibc's merge sort on random keys. Mirror archived; upstream last commit 2019-03-18; GPL-2.0-or-later.

name: Indiesort (plf::indiesort)
workload: Sorting vectors or arrays of large structs (496 bytes) with plf::indiesort, which sorts an index/pointer array and then permutes the elements, versus direct std::sort; also sorting std::list contents versus std::list::sort for types under 272 bytes; averaged across all numbers of sorted elements.
claimed_speedup: +146% faster than std::sort on vectors or arrays of large structs (496 bytes), on average across all numbers of sorted elements; crossover is any type larger than 152 bytes. +28% faster than std::list's internal sort on types smaller than 272 bytes.
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++98 through C++20 compatible. Temporary memory of N * (sizeof(pointer) + sizeof(size_t)) for non-random-access ranges and N * sizeof(U) for random-access ranges (U is the smallest unsigned type able to hold N). Not a win for small types: std::sort is faster on vectors and arrays below 152 bytes, and std::list's own sort is faster for types above 272 bytes. Its main use is letting std::sort-style algorithms run on non-random-access containers.
caveats: First-party README numbers only. The README gives no compiler, flags, CPU, element counts or standard library; the repo contains no benchmark code (plf_indiesort_test_suite.cpp is a correctness test with no timing). The methodology pages plflib.org/indiesort.htm and plflib.org/benchmarks_haswell_gcc.htm#sort were EGRESS_BLOCKED; a web search snippet (snippet only) says the benchmarks were run on a Haswell machine with GCC (so libstdc++ is likely but unconfirmed; exact CPU model and flags not seen). Older pages quoted '+130% ... vector with 496 byte structs' (and '~480 bytes'), so the headline figure has moved between releases (README now says +146%). The win only exists for large or non-trivially-movable element types (std::sort is faster below 152 bytes; std::list::sort is faster above 272 bytes), so the average depends on which sizes and element counts the benchmark includes. Extra temporary memory: N * sizeof(U) for random-access ranges, N * (sizeof(pointer) + sizeof(size_t)) otherwise.

name: swenson/sort (sort.h)
workload: Sorting 10,000 random int64_t values (lrand48) once per routine with demo.c, timed with gettimeofday, against libc qsort with a function-pointer comparator.
claimed_speedup: demo.c output on a 2014-era MacBook Pro, 10,000 int64_t: quick sort 579 us vs stdlib qsort 1285 us (about 2.2x, derived from page data); heap sort 592, in-place merge sort 903, merge sort 999, tim sort 1005, shell sort 1054, sqrt sort 1095 and grail sort 1220 us are also below qsort's 1285 us; binary insertion (13,443 us) and selection sort (127,176 us) are far slower; stdlib mergesort 1299 us and heapsort 2109 us are slower than qsort.
compiler_and_flags: Unstated for the README numbers. The Makefile default is CFLAGS ?= -O3 -g -Wall -std=c89 -pedantic -Wno-long-long -Wno-format with CC ?= gcc, which may differ from the README run.
hardware: 2014-era MacBook Pro (CPU model unstated)
tradeoffs: Single C89 header that generates type-specialised routines through #define SORT_TYPE, SORT_NAME and SORT_CMP, so each instantiation adds code size. Comparator inlining is the source of the win over qsort. Includes stable options (timsort, merge sort, grail sort, sqrt sort). Not a C++ std::sort drop-in. The default demo comparator (x - y) is unsafe for integers whose difference can overflow.
caveats: The README table comes from one run (RUNS is 1 in demo.c, timed with gettimeofday at microsecond resolution) of one 10,000-element lrand48 array on an unnamed 2014 laptop, with compiler and flags unstated. The baseline is C qsort calling through a function pointer (and, since the stdlib heapsort and mergesort rows are compiled only on non-Linux, non-Cygwin platforms, macOS/BSD libc qsort), not std::sort or an inlined-comparator sort, so the gap measures comparator inlining more than algorithm quality; qsort is also not in the sorting category's baseline list. The demo uses the subtraction comparator (x - y), safe here only because lrand48 values are non-negative. The table predates later code changes (gallop revert 2020, binary-insertion small sorts 2021, grail and sqrt sort moved to sort_extra.h in 2024), so it reflects older code. Only quick sort, heap sort and in-place merge sort show a clear win; the README itself says results depend on the machine and data. benchmark.c in the repo (100,000 elements, timed loops) is more careful but no results from it are published. [retier] One 10,000-element lrand48 int64 run on a 2014 MacBook Pro with compiler and flags unstated, qsort called through a function pointer (macOS libc), not compared against std::sort. The table is unchanged since commit 47934fc (2014-05-04) and timed the old middle-pivot quick sort with no depth limit (the issue #62 stack-overflow version); the shipping 2019 median-of-5/heap-fallback/sorting-network quick sort has never been re-benchmarked. Comparator results are stored in an int (partition, binary insertion find, in-place merge), so the README's own ((x) - (y)) int64 example truncates differences wider than 32 bits (with more than 16 multiples of 2^32 the all-equal shortcut leaves the range unsorted) and double keys with a subtraction comparator truncate differences below 1.0 to 0; the MEDIAN else branch compares dst[a] with dst[b] instead of dst[c] (pivot quality only, open PR #84); the stress test returns 0 on FAILED; demo and benchmark override SORT_CSWAP with branchless MIN/MAX; tim sort exits on OOM.
